# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# gmp_mpfr_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-low-level-bindings-for-gmp-mpfr-and-mpc)Rust low-level bindings for GMP, MPFR and MPC

The gmp-mpfr-sys crate provides Rust FFI bindings to the following
[GNU](https://www.gnu.org/) arbitrary-precision libraries:

- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)for integers and rational numbers,
- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)for floating-point numbers, and
- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/)for complex numbers.

The source of the three libraries is included in the package.

The gmp-mpfr-sys crate is free software: you can redistribute it
and/or modify it under the terms of the GNU Lesser General Public
License as published by the Free Software Foundation, either version 3
of the License, or (at your option) any later version. See the full
text of the [GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and [GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-features)Basic features

This crate contains three modules:

- `gmp`- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/).
- `mpfr`- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/).
- `mpc`- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/).

The versions provided by this crate release are [GMP](https://gmplib.org/) version 6.3.0, [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)
version 4.2.2, and [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/) version 1.4.0.

If you want a high-level API, consider using [Rug](https://crates.io/crates/rug), a crate
which provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary
precision and correct rounding:

- `Integer`
- `Rational`
- `Float`
- `Complex`

[§](https://docs.rs#name-prefixes)Name prefixes

Since modules and enumerated types provide namespacing, most prefixes
in the C names are removed. However, when the prefix is not a whole
word it is not removed. For example [ mp_set_memory_functions](https://docs.rs/C/GMP/constant.Custom_Allocation.html#index-mp_005fset_005fmemory_005ffunctions)
becomes

[, but](https://docs.rs/gmp/fn.set_memory_functions.html)

`gmp::set_memory_functions`[becomes](https://docs.rs/C/GMP/constant.Integer_Functions.html#index-mpz_005finit)

`mpz_init`[not](https://docs.rs/gmp/fn.mpz_init.html)

`gmp::mpz_init``gmp::z_init`, and [in](https://docs.rs/C/MPFR/constant.MPFR_Basics.html#Rounding-Modes)

`MPFR_RNDN`[becomes](https://docs.rs/C/MPFR/constant.MPFR_Basics.html#index-mpfr_005frnd_005ft)

`enum MPFR_RND_T`[not](https://docs.rs/mpfr/enum.rnd_t.html#variant.RNDN)

`mpfr::rnd_t::RNDN``mpfr::rnd_t::N`. Also, the types [and](https://docs.rs/mpfr/struct.mpfr_t.html)

`mpfr::mpfr_t`[are](https://docs.rs/mpc/struct.mpc_t.html)

`mpc::mpc_t`*not*shortened to

`mpfr::t` or `mpc::t`.[§](https://docs.rs#types)Types

Unlike in the C libraries, the types [ gmp::mpz_t](https://docs.rs/gmp/struct.mpz_t.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/gmp/struct.mpq_t.html)

`gmp::mpq_t`[,](https://docs.rs/gmp/struct.mpf_t.html)

`gmp::mpf_t`[,](https://docs.rs/gmp/struct.randstate_t.html)

`gmp::randstate_t`[and](https://docs.rs/mpfr/struct.mpfr_t.html)

`mpfr::mpfr_t`[are defined directly as structs, not as single-element arrays.](https://docs.rs/mpc/struct.mpc_t.html)

`mpc::mpc_t`[§](https://docs.rs#undocumented-or-obsolete-functions)Undocumented or obsolete functions

The bindings do not cover undocumented or obsolete functions and macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-gmp-mpfr-sys)Using gmp-mpfr-sys

The gmp-mpfr-sys crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys). To use
gmp-mpfr-sys in your crate, add it as a dependency inside
[ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
gmp-mpfr-sys = "1.7"
```
This crate requires rustc version 1.71.0 or later.

If the C libraries have a major version bump with some deprecated functions removed, but no features are removed in the Rust bindings, then gmp-mpfr-sys will have a minor version bump rather than a major version bump. This allows more compatiblity across crates that use the Rust bindings but do not use the C libraries directly.

If on the other hand a dependent crate makes use of internal
implementation details, or includes a C library that directly uses the
header (*.h*) and library (*.a*) files built using C, it can be a good
idea to depend on version `"~1.7"` instead of version `"1.7"` in order
to ensure backwards compatibility at the C level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

The gmp-mpfr-sys crate has two optional features:

- `mpfr`, enabled by default. Required to include the- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)library.
- `mpc`, enabled by default. Required to include the- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/)library. This feature requires the- `mpfr`feature.

The [GMP](https://gmplib.org/) library is always included.

The two optional features are enabled by default; to use features
selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies.gmp-mpfr-sys]
version = "1.7"
default-features = false
features = ["mpfr"]
```
Here only the `mpfr` feature is selected.

[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump.

Experimental features may also not work on all platforms.

There are three experimental features:

- `use-system-libs`, disabled by default. Using this feature, the system libraries for- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/), and- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)and- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/)if enabled, will be used instead of building them from source. The major versions of the system libraries must be equal to those provided by the crate, and the minor versions of the system libraries must be greater or equal to those provided by the crate. There are no restriction on the patch version.
- `force-cross`, disabled by default. Without this feature, the build will fail if cross compilation is detected, because cross compilation is not tested or supported and can lead to silent failures that are hard to debug, especially if this crate is an indirect dependency. As an exception, cross compiling from x86_64 to i686 does not need this feature. (Compiling on MinGW does not have this exception because MinGW does not support cross compilation from 64-bit to 32-bit.)
- `c-no-tests`, disabled by default. Using this feature will skip testing the C libraries. This is not advised; the risk that the GMP sources are miscompiled is unfortunately quite high. And if they indeed are miscompiled, the tests are very likely to trigger the compiler-introduced bug.

[§](https://docs.rs#metadata)Metadata

The gmp-mpfr-sys crate passes some metadata to its dependents:

- `DEP_GMP_LIMB_BITS`contains the number of bits per limb, which is 32 or 64.
- `DEP_GMP_OUT_DIR`contains the path of a directory that contains two subdirectories: the first subdirectory is named- *lib*and contains the generated library (- *.a*) files, and the second subdirectory is named- *include*and contains the corresponding header (- *.h*) files.
- `DEP_GMP_LIB_DIR`contains the path of the- *lib*subdirectory of the- `DEP_GMP_OUT_DIR`directory.
- `DEP_GMP_INCLUDE_DIR`contains the path of the- *include*subdirectory of the- `DEP_GMP_OUT_DIR`directory.

A dependent crate can use these environment variables in its build script.

[§](https://docs.rs#building-on-gnulinux)Building on GNU/Linux

**Warning:** The build system does not support building in paths that contain
spaces.

To build on GNU/Linux, simply make sure you have `diffutils`, `gcc`,
`m4` and `make` installed on your system. For example on Fedora:

`sudo dnf install diffutils gcc m4 make`Note that you can use Clang instead of GCC by installing `clang` and setting the
environment variable `CC=clang` before building the crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#building-on-macos)Building on macOS

**Warning:** The build system does not support building in paths that contain
spaces.

To build on macOS, you need the command-line developer tools. To install them, run the following command in a terminal:

`xcode-select --install`[§](https://docs.rs#building-on-windows)Building on Windows

**Warning:** The build system does not support building in paths that contain
spaces.

You can build on Windows with the Rust GNU toolchain and an up-to-date MSYS2 installation.

To install MSYS2:

-
Install MSYS2 using the [installer](https://www.msys2.org/).
-
Launch the MSYS2 MinGW 64-bit terminal from the start menu.
-
Install the required tools. `pacman -S pacman-mirrors pacman -S diffutils m4 make mingw-w64-x86_64-gcc`

Then, to build a crate with a dependency on this crate:

-
Launch the MSYS2 MinGW 64-bit terminal from the start menu.
-
Change to the crate directory.
-
Build the crate using `cargo`.

Note that you can use Clang instead of GCC by installing
`mingw-w64-x86_64-clang` and setting the environment variable `CC=clang` before
building the crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#cross-compilation)Cross compilation

While some cross compilation is possible, it is not tested automatically, and may not work. Merge requests that improve cross compilation are accepted.

The experimental feature `force-cross` must be enabled for cross
compilation. There is one case which is allowed even without the
feature: when the only difference between host and target is that the
host is x86_64 and the target is i686.

[§](https://docs.rs#caching-the-built-c-libraries)Caching the built C libraries

Building the C libraries can take some time. In order to save compilation time, the built libraries are cached in the user’s cache directory as follows:

- on GNU/Linux: inside `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/gmp-mpfr-sys`or`$HOME/.cache/gmp-mpfr-sys`
- on macOS: inside `$HOME/Library/Caches/gmp-mpfr-sys`
- on Windows: inside `{FOLDERID_LocalAppData}\gmp-mpfr-sys`

To use a different directory, you can set the environment variable
`GMP_MPFR_SYS_CACHE` to the desired cache directory. Setting the
`GMP_MPFR_SYS_CACHE` variable to an empty string or to a single
underscore (`"_"`) will disable caching.

# az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/az/1.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/az/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#numeric-casts)Numeric casts

This crate provides casts and checked casts.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-examples)Quick examples

```
use az::{Az, OverflowingAs, WrappingAs};
use core::num::Wrapping;
// Panics on overflow with `debug_assertions`, otherwise wraps
assert_eq!(12i32.az::<u32>(), 12u32);
// Always wraps
let wrapped = 1u32.wrapping_neg();
assert_eq!((-1).wrapping_as::<u32>(), wrapped);
assert_eq!((-1).overflowing_as::<u32>(), (wrapped, true));
// Wrapping can also be obtained using `Wrapping`
assert_eq!((-1).az::<Wrapping<u32>>().0, wrapped);
```
Conversions from floating-point to integers are also supported.
Numbers are rounded towards zero, but the [ Round](https://docs.rs/struct.Round.html) wrapper can be
used to convert floating-point numbers to integers with rounding to
the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

```
use az::{Az, CheckedAs, Round, SaturatingAs};
assert_eq!(15.7.az::<i32>(), 15);
assert_eq!(Round(15.5).az::<i32>(), 16);
assert_eq!(1.5e20.saturating_as::<i32>(), i32::max_value());
assert_eq!(f32::NAN.checked_as::<i32>(), None);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-casts-for-other-types)Implementing casts for other types

To provide casts for another type, you should implement the [ Cast](https://docs.rs/trait.Cast.html) trait and
if necessary the

[,](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedCast.html)

`CheckedCast`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.StrictCast.html)

`StrictCast`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.SaturatingCast.html)

`SaturatingCast`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.WrappingCast.html)

`WrappingCast`[traits. The](https://docs.rs/trait.OverflowingCast.html)

`OverflowingCast`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.Az.html)

`Az`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedAs.html)

`CheckedAs`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.StrictAs.html)

`StrictAs`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.SaturatingAs.html)

`SaturatingAs`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.WrappingAs.html)

`WrappingAs`[traits are already implemented for all types using blanket implementations that make use of the former traits.](https://docs.rs/trait.OverflowingAs.html)

`OverflowingAs`The cast traits can also be implemented for references. This can be
useful for expensive types that are not [ Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html). For example if you
have your own integer type that does not implement

[, you could implement casts like in the following example. (The type](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html)

`Copy``I` could be
an expensive type, for example a bignum integer, but for the example
it is only a wrapped [.)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.i32.html)

`i32````
use az::{Az, Cast};
use core::borrow::Borrow;
struct I(i32);
impl Cast<i64> for &'_ I {
    fn cast(self) -> i64 { self.0.cast() }
}
let owned = I(12);
assert_eq!((&owned).az::<i64>(), 12);
// borrow can be used if chaining is required
assert_eq!(owned.borrow().az::<i64>(), 12);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-az-crate)Using the *az* crate

The *az* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/az). To use it in
your crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
az = "1.3"
```
The crate requires rustc version 1.85.0 or later.

[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `nightly-float`, disabled by default. This requires the nightly compiler, and implements casts for the experimental- `f16`- `f128`

# facett_osm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-osm/0.1.10/facett_osm/

## Expand description

**facett-osm** — read **OSM GeoParquet** (the `osm2geoparquet` / katana-osm
output) into facett geometry. Each row’s `geometry` column is **WKB** — a
`Point` for nodes, a `LineString`/`Polygon` for ways — which we decode to
`(lon, lat)` points and hand to [ facett_map::MapView](https://docs.rs/facett-map/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map/struct.MapView.html). This is how facett
gets real OSM data (millions of points) for the map component + its tests.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_wkb.html)- wkb
- Decode a WKB geometry blob, appending every `(lon, lat)`vertex to`out`. Handles Point (1), LineString (2), Polygon (3); ignores Z/M + SRID flags.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_wkb_coords.html)- wkb_ - coords
- Decode a single WKB blob into **one geometry’s**`(lon, lat)`vertices (Point → 1 vertex, LineString → its line, Polygon → its exterior ring), preserving the geometry as a unit (unlike`decode_wkb``read_ways``katana_osm_shared::geometry::decode_coords`.
- [map_](https://docs.rs/fn.map_view.html)- view
- Read a GeoParquet straight into a `facett_map::MapView`
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_points.html)- points
- Read up to `max``(lon, lat)`points from a GeoParquet file’s`geometry`(WKB) column. Works on`osm2geoparquet`’s`nodes.parquet`(Points) and`ways.parquet`(LineStrings → their vertices).
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_points_bytes.html)- points_ - bytes
- Like `read_points`**in-memory**GeoParquet (the bytes of a`nodes.parquet`). This is the filesystem-free path the wasm web demo uses: it`include_bytes!`s a clipped region into the binary and decodes it here (the browser has no`std::fs`). Any`Into<Bytes>`works (`&'static [u8]`,`Vec<u8>`).
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_ways.html)- ways
- Read **ways**(LineString / Polygon geometries) from an`osm2geoparquet``ways.parquet`— the SAME WKB`geometry`column`read_points``tags`column for styling. Each row → a`facett_map::Way``(lon, lat)`, projected to Mercator, classified by its OSM tags through`theme`.`max`caps the number of ways (0 = unlimited). Rows with <2 vertices are skipped (graceful — no panic on a degenerate geometry).
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_ways_bytes.html)- ways_ - bytes
- Like `read_ways`**in-memory**`ways.parquet`(the bytes the wasm web demo`include_bytes!`s — no filesystem in the browser).

This is the CPU painter’s- **scissor**: it geometrically confines every face to the widget rect so nothing a 3D/2D pass paints can land outside the component’s own rectangle — independent of whether the host renderer applies the egui clip_rect as a GPU scissor.
- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_tri_frustum.html)- tri_ - frustum
- **Full view-space FRUSTUM clip**(the real fix for the smear) — Sutherland–Hodgman of a triangle against all FIVE relevant frustum planes BEFORE the perspective divide: the near plane- `z >= near`AND the four side planes- `|cx| <= cz·sx`,- `|cy| <= cz·sy`(with- `sx`,- `sy`the projection’s per-axis NDC slopes — for- `project_view`’s focal =- `half_h`,- `sy = 1`,- `sx = half_w/half_h`).
- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_tri_near.html)- tri_ - near
- **View-space near-plane clip**(step 1 of the part-step decomposition) — Sutherland–Hodgman clip of a single view-space triangle against the half-space- `z >= near`, returning the clipped convex polygon’s view-space vertices (0 when the whole triangle sits on/behind the eye, 3 when untouched, 4 when one vertex was behind and split). This runs- **before**the perspective divide so no surviving vertex ever divides by a near-zero / negative depth — the geometric replacement for the old “near-singularity spoke reject” + “screen-extent guard” heuristics that let off-axis near faces smear thousands of px off the rect.

A correct scissor leaves- **0**— this is the bug oracle the spec’s clip stage emits (- `ink_outside_rect == 0`). Pure, so both the emit path and tests call it.

# blueprint_tangle_aggregation_svc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/blueprint-tangle-aggregation-svc/0.2.0-alpha.10/blueprint_tangle_aggregation_svc/

## Expand description

Tangle BLS Signature Aggregation Service

A simple HTTP service that collects BLS signatures from operators, aggregates them once threshold is met, and provides the aggregated result for submission to the Tangle contract.

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
Operator 1 ──┐
Operator 2 ──┼──▶ Aggregation Service ──▶ Aggregated Result
Operator 3 ──┘         │
                       ▼
                 Tangle Contract
```
[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#starting-the-service)Starting the service

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use blueprint_tangle_aggregation_svc::{AggregationService, api, ServiceConfig};
use std::sync::Arc;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let service = Arc::new(AggregationService::new(ServiceConfig::default()));
    let app = api::router(service);
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:8080").await.unwrap();
    axum::serve(listener, app).await.unwrap();
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#api-endpoints)API Endpoints

- `POST /v1/tasks/init`- Initialize an aggregation task
- `POST /v1/tasks/submit`- Submit a signature
- `POST /v1/tasks/status`- Get task status
- `POST /v1/tasks/aggregate`- Get aggregated result

[§](https://docs.rs#operator-flow)Operator Flow

- Someone (often the first operator) initializes the task
- Each operator signs the output and submits their signature
- Once threshold is met, anyone can fetch the aggregated result
- Submit the aggregated result to the Tangle contract

SubAgent → can spawn actor children), runs the prompt on a root session through the same execute path the HTTP API uses, streams events to the terminal, and exits when the whole tree is finished (parent + children, including suspend/resume coordination).
- [subagent_](https://docs.rs/subagent_worker/index.html)- worker
- The `bamboo subagent-worker`actor worker (provision via stdin, serve over WS).`bamboo subagent-worker`— the real actor worker.

# crumbex 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/crumbex/0.2.0

# crumbex

**Polyglot code-intelligence in a single Rust binary.** Parse once, read surgically, map
the architecture, enforce the contract — with zero LLM in the core.

Crumbex parses a codebase **once** into a shared tree-sitter index and serves several
independent, opt-in layers over it: symbol search + surgical line reading, a dependency
graph (god modules, import cycles, communities), a function-level call graph, a cross-repo
service **atlas** with multi-hop feature paths, and cross-repo API **contract** enforcement.
Each layer is a Cargo feature — you pay binary weight only for what you compile.

## Install

```
```
Installs the `crumbex` binary. Building the tree-sitter grammars needs a C compiler (MSVC
Build Tools on Windows, clang via Xcode CLT on macOS, gcc/clang on Linux).

## Usage

Run `crumbex --help` for the full command list.

## Languages

TypeScript · TSX · JavaScript · Go · Python · Rust · Ruby. Adding a language is one tree-sitter grammar plus a query file — the engine never changes.

## Documentation & source

Full guide, worked examples, and roadmap: [https://github.com/Razielini/crumbex](https://github.com/Razielini/crumbex).

## License

Dual-licensed under **MIT OR Apache-2.0**, at your option.

# base64_ng_tokio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64-ng-tokio/1.3.0/base64_ng_tokio/

## Expand description

Optional Tokio async helpers for `base64-ng`.

The crate provides two API tiers:

- read-all/write-all convenience functions, with `*_limited`variants for peer-controlled request or frame boundaries.
- manual `AsyncRead``EncoderReader``DecoderReader`

The streaming readers are implemented as explicit state machines. They do
not use `async fn` internally, so cancellation can only leave data in the
adapter’s fixed pending/output buffers; those buffers are cleared on drop.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

The read-all helpers use temporary `Vec<u8>` allocations and the normal
strict decode path. They wipe those temporary vectors before returning, but
they are not constant-time-oriented token validators or high-assurance
secret decoders. For secret-bearing async frames, collect a bounded frame
under the application’s approved memory policy and decode through
`base64_ng::ct`, staged CT decode, `base64-ng-derive`, or
`base64-ng-sanitization`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Decoder](https://docs.rs/struct.DecoderReader.html)- Reader
- Async reader that streams Base64 input as decoded bytes.
- [Encoder](https://docs.rs/struct.EncoderReader.html)- Reader
- Async reader that streams raw bytes as Base64.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_reader_to_writer.html)- reader_ - to_ - writer
- Reads all Base64 bytes from `reader`, decodes them, and writes decoded bytes.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_reader_to_writer_limited.html)- reader_ - to_ - writer_ - limited
- Reads at most `max_input_len`Base64 bytes from`reader`, decodes them, and writes decoded bytes.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_to_vec.html)- to_ - vec
- Decodes `input`into an owned byte vector.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_reader_to_writer.html)- reader_ - to_ - writer
- Reads all bytes from `reader`, encodes them, and writes the encoded output.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_reader_to_writer_limited.html)- reader_ - to_ - writer_ - limited
- Reads at most `max_input_len`bytes from`reader`, encodes them, and writes the encoded output.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_vec.html)- to_ - vec
- Encodes `input`into an owned byte vector.

# base64_ng_subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64-ng-subtle/1.3.0/base64_ng_subtle/

## Expand description

Optional `subtle::ConstantTimeEq` integration for `base64-ng`.

The core `base64-ng` package stays zero-runtime-dependency. This companion
crate exists for applications that already admit `subtle` and want a
reviewed comparison primitive at the protocol boundary.

Length is treated as public. Mismatched lengths return
[`subtle::Choice::from(0)`] immediately. Use fixed-size protocol tokens when
length must not vary. When the length itself is secret, compare fixed-size
arrays or fixed-width protocol buffers directly with
[ subtle::ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/subtle/2.6.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/subtle/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) instead of this public-length helper.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Subtle](https://docs.rs/trait.SubtleEqExt.html)- EqExt
- Extension trait for comparing `base64-ng`buffers with`subtle`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [subtle_](https://docs.rs/fn.subtle_ct_eq_public_len.html)- ct_ - eq_ - public_ - len
- Compares two byte slices with public length.

# bamboo_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bamboo-server/2026.7.3/bamboo_server/

## Expand description

Unified HTTP server consolidating web_service and agent/server

This module provides a single, consolidated server implementation that:

- Eliminates the proxy pattern from web_service
- Provides direct provider access without HTTP callbacks
- Unifies state management across all endpoints
- Supports all API routes (agent, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini)

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

The server is organized into several key components:

- **app_state**: Unified state management with direct provider access
- **config**: CORS and security header configuration
- **metrics**: Unified metrics infrastructure
- **handlers**: Agent API handlers (chat, execute, events, etc.)
- **controllers**: Multi-provider API controllers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini)
- **services**: Business logic services
- **routes**: Route configuration for all API endpoints
- **server**: Entry points for running the server

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use std::path::PathBuf;
use bamboo_server::run;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let app_data_dir = PathBuf::from("/path/to/bamboo-data-dir");
    run(app_data_dir, 3456).await
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#server-modes)Server Modes

The server supports three modes:

[§](https://docs.rs#1-desktop-mode-default)1. Desktop Mode (Default)

Binds to localhost only, No rate limiting. Perfect for local development.

```
use std::path::PathBuf;
use bamboo_server::run;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let data_dir = PathBuf::from("./.bamboo");
    run(data_dir, 9562).await
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#2-docker-mode)2. Docker Mode

Custom bind address with rate limiting. For containerized deployments.

```
use std::path::PathBuf;
use bamboo_server::run_with_bind;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let data_dir = PathBuf::from("./.bamboo");
    run_with_bind(data_dir, 9562, "0.0.0.0").await
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#3-production-mode-with-frontend)3. Production Mode with Frontend

Serves static files alongside API. Full production setup.

```
use std::path::PathBuf;
use bamboo_server::run_with_bind_and_static;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let data_dir = PathBuf::from("./.bamboo");
    run_with_bind_and_static(
        data_dir,
        9562,
        "0.0.0.0",
        Some(PathBuf::from("./dist")),
    )
    .await
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#route-organization)Route Organization

[§](https://docs.rs#agent-routes-apiv1)Agent Routes (/api/v1/*)

Core agent functionality: chat, execute, events, metrics, MCP.

[§](https://docs.rs#openai-routes-v1)OpenAI Routes (/v1/*)

OpenAI-compatible API for tool integration.

[§](https://docs.rs#anthropic-routes-anthropicv1)Anthropic Routes (/anthropic/v1/*)

Anthropic Claude API compatible endpoints.

[§](https://docs.rs#gemini-routes-geminiv1beta)Gemini Routes (/gemini/v1beta/*)

Google Gemini API compatible endpoints.

# rug 1.30.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rug/1.30.0

# Arbitrary-precision numbers

Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and correct rounding:

- `Integer`
- `Rational`
- `Float`
- `Complex`

Rug is a high-level interface to the following [GNU](https://www.gnu.org/) libraries:

- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)for integers and rational numbers,
- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)for floating-point numbers, and
- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/)for complex numbers.

Rug is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms
of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published by the Free Software
Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later
version. See the full text of the [GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and [GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

## What’s new

### Version 1.30.0 news (2026-04-27)

- Arithmetic operators are now overloaded to work between:
- `Integer`- `MiniInteger`
- `Rational`- `MiniRational`
- `Float`- `MiniFloat`
- `Complex`- `MiniComplex`

- The following method was added to `MiniRational`

### Version 1.29.0 news (2026-03-20)

- The *az*crate[version 1.3](https://docs.rs/az/~1.3/az/index.html).
- The [gmp-mpfr-sys](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys)dependency was updated to[version 1.7](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.7/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html).
- The following methods were added to `Complex`

### Other releases

Details on other releases can be found in [ RELEASES.md](https://gitlab.com/tspiteri/rug/blob/master/RELEASES.md).

## Quick example

```
use ;
let mut int = new;
assert_eq!;
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign;
assert!;
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
int =  - 1;
assert_eq!;
```
- [Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/struct.Integer.html)::- [new](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.new)creates a new- `Integer`
- To assign values to Rug types, we use the `Assign``Assign::assign`[assignment operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#assignment-expressions)as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.`=`
- Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to fit in a
primitive type. To assign such a number to the large types, we use strings
rather than primitives; in the example this is done using
[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)and[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse_radix](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse_radix).
- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types using the
normal comparison operators, for example `int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and primitive types
on either side of the operator, for example `int >> 128`.

## Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two values of
the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive types, conversion to
and from Rug types can be expensive, so the arithmetic operators are overloaded
to work on many combinations of Rug types and primitives. More details are
available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/index.html#using-with-primitive-types).

## Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```
use Integer;
let a = from;
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```
use Integer;
let  = ;
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = from;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/struct.Integer.html). This is covered in
more detail in the documentation’s

[section.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*More details on operators are available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/index.html#operators).

## Using Rug

Rug is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/rug). To use Rug in your crate, add it as
a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.30"
```
Rug requires rustc version 1.85.0 or later.

Rug also depends on the [GMP](https://gmplib.org/), [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/) and [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/) libraries through the low-level
FFI bindings in the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys), which needs some setup to
build; the [gmp-mpfr-sys documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.7/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html) has some details on usage under
[GNU/Linux](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.7/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-gnulinux), [macOS](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.7/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-macos) and [Windows](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.7/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-windows).

# rug - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rug/1.30.0/target-redirect/rug/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-precision-numbers)Arbitrary-precision numbers

Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and correct rounding:

- `Integer`
- `Rational`
- `Float`
- `Complex`

Rug is a high-level interface to the following [GNU](https://www.gnu.org/) libraries:

- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)for integers and rational numbers,
- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)for floating-point numbers, and
- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/)for complex numbers.

Rug is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms
of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published by the Free Software
Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later
version. See the full text of the [GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and [GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

You are also free to use the examples in this documentation without any restrictions; the examples are in the public domain.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-example)Quick example

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let mut int = Integer::new();
assert_eq!(int, 0);
int.assign(14);
assert_eq!(int, 14);
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign(Integer::parse(decimal).unwrap());
assert!(int > 100_000_000);
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign(Integer::parse_radix(hex_160, 16).unwrap());
assert_eq!(int.significant_bits(), 160);
int = (int >> 128) - 1;
assert_eq!(int, 0xfffe_ffff_u32);
```
- [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::- [new](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.new)- `Integer`
- To assign values to Rug types, we use the `Assign``Assign::assign`[assignment operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#assignment-expressions)as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.`=`
- Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to fit in a
primitive type. To assign such a number to the large types, we use strings
rather than primitives; in the example this is done using
[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[parse_radix](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.parse_radix)
- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types using the
normal comparison operators, for example `int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and primitive types
on either side of the operator, for example `int >> 128`.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-with-primitive-types)Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two values of
the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive types, conversion to
and from Rug types can be expensive, so the arithmetic operators are overloaded
to work on many combinations of Rug types and primitives. The following are
provided:

- Where they make sense, all arithmetic operators are overloaded to work with
Rug types and the primitives `i8``i16``i32``i64``i128``u8``u16``u32``u64``u128``f32``f64`
- Where they make sense, conversions using the `From``Assign``bool``isize``usize`
- Comparisons between Rug types and all the numeric primitives listed in 1 and 2 above are supported.
- For `Rational`
- For `Complex`

[§](https://docs.rs#operators)Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```
use rug::Integer;
let a = Integer::from(10);
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!(b, 5 - 10);
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```
use rug::Integer;
let (a, b) = (Integer::from(10), Integer::from(20));
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = Integer::from(incomplete);
assert_eq!(sub, -10);
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html). This is covered in
more detail in the

[section.](https://docs.rs#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*[§](https://docs.rs#shifting-operations)Shifting operations

The left shift `<<` and right shift `>>` operators support shifting by negative
values, for example `a << 5` is equivalent to `a >> -5`.

The shifting operators are also supported for the [ Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html) and

[number types, where they are equivalent to multiplication or division by a power of two. Only the exponent of the value is affected; the mantissa is unchanged.](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)

`Complex`[§](https://docs.rs#exponentiation)Exponentiation

Exponentiation (raising to a power) does not have a dedicated operator in Rust.
In order to perform exponentiation of Rug types, the [ Pow](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.Pow.html) trait has
to be brought into scope, for example

```
use rug::ops::Pow;
use rug::Integer;
let base = Integer::from(10);
let power = base.pow(5);
assert_eq!(power, 100_000);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compound-assignments-to-right-hand-side-operands)Compound assignments to right-hand-side operands

Traits are provided for compound assignment to right-hand-side operands. This
can be useful for non-commutative operations like subtraction. The names of the
traits and their methods are similar to Rust compound assignment traits, with
the suffix “`Assign`” replaced with “`From`”. For example the counterpart to
[ SubAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.SubAssign.html) is

[:](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubFrom.html)

`SubFrom````
use rug::ops::SubFrom;
use rug::Integer;
let mut rhs = Integer::from(10);
// set rhs = 100 - rhs
rhs.sub_from(100);
assert_eq!(rhs, 90);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#incomplete-computation-values)Incomplete-computation values

There are two main reasons why operations like `&a - &b` do not perform a
complete computation and return a Rug type:

- Sometimes we need to assign the result to an object that already exists. Since Rug types require memory allocations, this can help reduce the number of allocations. (While the allocations might not affect performance noticeably for computationally intensive functions, they can have a much more significant effect on faster functions like addition.)
- For the `Float``Complex`

There are two things that can be done with incomplete-computation values:

- Assign them to an existing object without unnecessary allocations. This is
usually achieved using the `Assign``int.`and[assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html#tymethod.assign)(incomplete)`float.`.[assign_round](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html#tymethod.assign_round)(incomplete,[Round](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html)::[Up](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html#variant.Up))
- Convert them to the final value using the `Complete``From``incomplete.`or[complete](https://docs.rs/trait.Complete.html#tymethod.complete)()[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html#tymethod.from)(incomplete)`incomplete.`or[complete](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#method.complete)(53)[Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)::[with_val](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html#method.with_val)(53, incomplete)

Let us consider a couple of examples.

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let mut buffer = Integer::new();
// ... buffer can be used and reused ...
let (a, b) = (Integer::from(10), Integer::from(20));
let incomplete = &a - &b;
buffer.assign(incomplete);
assert_eq!(buffer, -10);
```
Here the assignment from `incomplete` into `buffer` does not require an
allocation unless the result does not fit in the current capacity of `buffer`.
If `&a - &b` returned an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) instead, then an allocation would take
place even if it is not necessary.

```
use rug::float::Constant;
use rug::Float;
// x has a precision of 10 bits
let x = Float::with_val(10, 180);
// y has a precision of 50 bits
let y = Float::with_val(50, Constant::Pi);
let incomplete = &x / &y;
// z has a precision of 45 bits
let z = Float::with_val(45, incomplete);
assert!(57.295 < z && z < 57.296);
```
The precision to use for the result depends on the requirements of the algorithm
being implemented. Here `z` is created with a precision of 45.

Many operations can return incomplete-computation values, for example

- unary operators applied to references, for example `-&int`
- binary operators applied to two references, for example `&int1 + &int2`
- binary operators applied to a primitive and a reference, for example `&int * 10`
- methods that take a reference, for example
`int.`[abs_ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.abs_ref)()
- methods that take two references, for example
`int1.`[gcd_ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.gcd_ref)(&int2)
- string parsing, for example
[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)("12")

These operations return objects that can be stored in temporary variables like
`incomplete` in the last few code examples. However, the names of the types are
not public, and consequently, the incomplete-computation values cannot be for
example stored in a struct. If you need to store the value in a struct, complete
it to its final type and value.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-rug)Using Rug

Rug is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/rug). To use Rug in your crate, add it as

```

```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html). This is covered in
more detail in the

[section.](https://docs.rs#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*[§](https://docs.rs#shifting-operations)Shifting operations

The left shift `<<` and right shift `>>` operators support shifting by negative
values, for example `a << 5` is equivalent to `a >> -5`.

The shifting operators are also supported for the [ Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html) and

[number types, where they are equivalent to multiplication or division by a power of two. Only the exponent of the value is affected; the mantissa is unchanged.](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)

`Complex`[§](https://docs.rs#exponentiation)Exponentiation

Exponentiation (raising to a power) does not have a dedicated operator in Rust.
In order to perform exponentiation of Rug types, the [ Pow](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.Pow.html) trait has
to be brought into scope, for example

```
use rug::ops::Pow;
use rug::Integer;
let base = Integer::from(10);
let power = base.pow(5);
assert_eq!(power, 100_000);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compound-assignments-to-right-hand-side-operands)Compound assignments to right-hand-side operands

Traits are provided for compound assignment to right-hand-side operands. This
can be useful for non-commutative operations like subtraction. The names of the
traits and their methods are similar to Rust compound assignment traits, with
the suffix “`Assign`” replaced with “`From`”. For example the counterpart to
[ SubAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.SubAssign.html) is

[:](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubFrom.html)

`SubFrom````
use rug::ops::SubFrom;
use rug::Integer;
let mut rhs = Integer::from(10);
// set rhs = 100 - rhs
rhs.sub_from(100);
assert_eq!(rhs, 90);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#incomplete-computation-values)Incomplete-computation values

There are two main reasons why operations like `&a - &b` do not perform a
complete computation and return a Rug type:

- Sometimes we need to assign the result to an object that already exists. Since Rug types require memory allocations, this can help reduce the number of allocations. (While the allocations might not affect performance noticeably for computationally intensive functions, they can have a much more significant effect on faster functions like addition.)
- For the `Float``Complex`

There are two things that can be done with incomplete-computation values:

- Assign them to an existing object without unnecessary allocations. This is
usually achieved using the `Assign``int.`and[assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html#tymethod.assign)(incomplete)`float.`.[assign_round](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html#tymethod.assign_round)(incomplete,[Round](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html)::[Up](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html#variant.Up))
- Convert them to the final value using the `Complete``From``incomplete.`or[complete](https://docs.rs/trait.Complete.html#tymethod.complete)()[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html#tymethod.from)(incomplete)`incomplete.`or[complete](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#method.complete)(53)[Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)::[with_val](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html#method.with_val)(53, incomplete)

Let us consider a couple of examples.

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let mut buffer = Integer::new();
// ... buffer can be used and reused ...
let (a, b) = (Integer::from(10), Integer::from(20));
let incomplete = &a - &b;
buffer.assign(incomplete);
assert_eq!(buffer, -10);
```
Here the assignment from `incomplete` into `buffer` does not require an
allocation unless the result does not fit in the current capacity of `buffer`.
If `&a - &b` returned an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) instead, then an allocation would take
place even if it is not necessary.

```
use rug::float::Constant;
use rug::Float;
// x has a precision of 10 bits
let x = Float::with_val(10, 180);
// y has a precision of 50 bits
let y = Float::with_val(50, Constant::Pi);
let incomplete = &x / &y;
// z has a precision of 45 bits
let z = Float::with_val(45, incomplete);
assert!(57.295 < z && z < 57.296);
```
The precision to use for the result depends on the requirements of the algorithm
being implemented. Here `z` is created with a precision of 45.

Many operations can return incomplete-computation values, for example

- unary operators applied to references, for example `-&int`
- binary operators applied to two references, for example `&int1 + &int2`
- binary operators applied to a primitive and a reference, for example `&int * 10`
- methods that take a reference, for example
`int.`[abs_ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.abs_ref)()
- methods that take two references, for example
`int1.`[gcd_ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.gcd_ref)(&int2)
- string parsing, for example
[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)("12")

These operations return objects that can be stored in temporary variables like
`incomplete` in the last few code examples. However, the names of the types are
not public, and consequently, the incomplete-computation values cannot be for
example stored in a struct. If you need to store the value in a struct, complete
it to its final type and value.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-rug)Using Rug

Rug is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/rug). To use Rug in your crate, add it as
a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
rug = "1.30"
```
Rug requires rustc version 1.85.0 or later.

Rug also depends on the [GMP](https://gmplib.org/), [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/) and [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/) libraries through the low-level
FFI bindings in the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys), which needs some setup to
build; the [gmp-mpfr-sys documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html) has some details on usage under
[GNU/Linux](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-gnulinux), [macOS](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-macos) and [Windows](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-windows).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

The Rug crate has six optional features:

- `integer`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Integer`
- `rational`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Rational`- `integer`feature.
- `float`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Float`
- `complex`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Complex`- `float`feature.
- `rand`, enabled by default. Required for the- `RandState`- `integer`feature.
- `std`, enabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`, such as methods that return- `String`
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the- `Integer`- `Rational`- `Float`- `Complex`- `std`feature and the- [serde crate](https://crates.io/crates/serde).

The first six optional features are enabled by default; to use features
selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies.rug]
version = "1.30"
default-features = false
features = ["integer", "float", "std"]
```
Here only the `integer`, `float` and `rand` features are enabled. If none of the
features are selected, the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) is not required and
thus not enabled. In that case, only the [ Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html) trait and the traits that
are in the

[module are provided by the crate.](https://docs.rs/ops/index.html)

`ops`[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-integer*crate- *num-traits*crate- *num-integer*crate
- `num-complex`, disabled by default. This adds conversion methods to and from complex floats as provided by the- *num-complex*crate- *num-complex*crate
- `nightly-float`, disabled by default. This requires the nightly compiler, and implements some operations with the experimental- `f16`- `f128`
- `borsh`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support using the- *borsh*crate

[17](https://docs.rs#17)/*!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)# Arbitrary-precision numbers
[19](https://docs.rs#19)
[20](https://docs.rs#20)Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and
[21](https://docs.rs#21)correct rounding:
[22](https://docs.rs#22)
[23](https://docs.rs#23)  * [`Integer`] is a bignum integer with arbitrary precision,
[24](https://docs.rs#24)  * [`Rational`] is a bignum rational number with arbitrary precision,
[25](https://docs.rs#25)  * [`Float`] is a multi-precision floating-point number with correct rounding,
[26](https://docs.rs#26)    and
[27](https://docs.rs#27)  * [`Complex`] is a multi-precision complex number with correct rounding.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)
[29](https://docs.rs#29)Rug is a high-level interface to the following [GNU] libraries:
[30](https://docs.rs#30)
[31](https://docs.rs#31)  * [GMP] for integers and rational numbers,
[32](https://docs.rs#32)  * [MPFR] for floating-point numbers, and
[33](https://docs.rs#33)  * [MPC] for complex numbers.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)
[35](https://docs.rs#35)Rug is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms
[36](https://docs.rs#36)of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published by the Free Software
[37](https://docs.rs#37)Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later
[38](https://docs.rs#38)version. See the full text of the [GNU LGPL] and [GNU GPL] for details.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)
[40](https://docs.rs#40)You are also free to use the examples in this documentation without any
[41](https://docs.rs#41)restrictions; the examples are in the public domain.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)
[43](https://docs.rs#43)## Quick example
[44](https://docs.rs#44)
[45](https://docs.rs#45)```rust
[46](https://docs.rs#46)# #[cfg(feature = "integer")] {
[47](https://docs.rs#47)use rug::{Assign, Integer};
[48](https://docs.rs#48)let mut int = Integer::new();
[49](https://docs.rs#49)assert_eq!(int, 0);
[50](https://docs.rs#50)int.assign(14);
[51](https://docs.rs#51)assert_eq!(int, 14);
[52](https://docs.rs#52)
[53](https://docs.rs#53)let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
[54](https://docs.rs#54)int.assign(Integer::parse(decimal).unwrap());
[55](https://docs.rs#55)assert!(int > 100_000_000);
[56](https://docs.rs#56)
[57](https://docs.rs#57)let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
[58](https://docs.rs#58)int.assign(Integer::parse_radix(hex_160, 16).unwrap());
[59](https://docs.rs#59)assert_eq!(int.significant_bits(), 160);
[60](https://docs.rs#60)int = (int >> 128) - 1;
[61](https://docs.rs#61)assert_eq!(int, 0xfffe_ffff_u32);
[62](https://docs.rs#62)# }
[63](https://docs.rs#63)```
[64](https://docs.rs#64)
[65](https://docs.rs#65)  * <code>[Integer]::[new][Integer::new]</code> creates a new [`Integer`]
[66](https://docs.rs#66)    intialized to zero.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)  * To assign values to Rug types, we use the [`Assign`] trait and its method
[68](https://docs.rs#68)    [`Assign::assign`]. We do not use the [assignment operator `=`][assignment]
[69](https://docs.rs#69)    as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.
[71](https://docs.rs#71)  * Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to fit in a
[72](https://docs.rs#72)    primitive type. To assign such a number to the large types, we use strings
[73](https://docs.rs#73)    rather than primitives; in the example this is done using
[74](https://docs.rs#74)    <code>[Integer]::[parse][Integer::parse]</code> and
[75](https://docs.rs#75)    <code>[Integer]::[parse\_radix][Integer::parse_radix]</code>.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)  * We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types using the
[77](https://docs.rs#77)    normal comparison operators, for example `int > 100_000_000`.
[78](https://docs.rs#78)  * Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and primitive types
[79](https://docs.rs#79)    on either side of the operator, for example `int >> 128`.
[80](https://docs.rs#80)
[81](https://docs.rs#81)## Using with primitive types
[82](https://docs.rs#82)
[83](https://docs.rs#83)With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two values of
[84](https://docs.rs#84)the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive types, conversion to
[85](https://docs.rs#85)and from Rug types can be expensive, so the arithmetic operators are overloaded
[86](https://docs.rs#86)to work on many combinations of Rug types and primitives. The following are
[87](https://docs.rs#87)provided:
[88](https://docs.rs#88)
[89](https://docs.rs#89) 1. Where they make sense, all arithmetic operators are overloaded to work with
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    Rug types and the primitives [`i8`], [`i16`], [`i32`], [`i64`], [`i128`],
[91](https://docs.rs#91)    [`u8`], [`u16`], [`u32`], [`u64`], [`u128`], [`f32`] and [`f64`].
[92](https://docs.rs#92) 2. Where they make sense, conversions using the [`From`] trait and assignments
[93](https://docs.rs#93)    using the [`Assign`] trait are supported for all the primitives in 1 above
[94](https://docs.rs#94)    as well as [`bool`], [`isize`] and [`usize`].
[95](https://docs.rs#95) 3. Comparisons between Rug types and all the numeric primitives listed in 1 and
[96](https://docs.rs#96)    2 above are supported.
[97](https://docs.rs#97) 4. For [`Rational`] numbers, conversions and comparisons are also supported for
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    tuples containing two integer primitives: the first is the numerator and the
[99](https://docs.rs#99)    second is the denominator which must not be zero. The two primitives do not
[100](https://docs.rs#100)    need to be of the same type.
[101](https://docs.rs#101) 5. For [`Complex`] numbers, conversions and comparisons are also supported for
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    tuples containing two primitives: the first is the real part and the second
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    is the imaginary part. The two primitives do not need to be of the same
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    type.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)
[106](https://docs.rs#106)## Operators
[107](https://docs.rs#107)
[108](https://docs.rs#108)Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug
[109](https://docs.rs#109)types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug
[110](https://docs.rs#110)type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)For example
[112](https://docs.rs#112)
[113](https://docs.rs#113)```rust
[114](https://docs.rs#114)# #[cfg(feature = "integer")] {
[115](https://docs.rs#115)use rug::Integer;
[116](https://docs.rs#116)let a = Integer::from(10);
[117](https://docs.rs#117)let b = 5 - a;
[118](https://docs.rs#118)assert_eq!(b, 5 - 10);
[119](https://docs.rs#119)# }
[120](https://docs.rs#120)```
[121](https://docs.rs#121)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned [`Integer`].
[123](https://docs.rs#123)
[124](https://docs.rs#124)If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references
[125](https://docs.rs#125)instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an
[126](https://docs.rs#126)incomplete-computation value. For example
[127](https://docs.rs#127)
[128](https://docs.rs#128)```rust
[129](https://docs.rs#129)# #[cfg(feature = "integer")] {
[130](https://docs.rs#130)use rug::Integer;
[131](https://docs.rs#131)let (a, b) = (Integer::from(10), Integer::from(20));
[132](https://docs.rs#132)let incomplete = &a - &b;
[133](https://docs.rs#133)// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
[134](https://docs.rs#134)let sub = Integer::from(incomplete);
[135](https://docs.rs#135)assert_eq!(sub, -10);
[136](https://docs.rs#136)# }
[137](https://docs.rs#137)```
[138](https://docs.rs#138)
[139](https://docs.rs#139)Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
[140](https://docs.rs#140)still needs to be converted or assigned into an [`Integer`]. This is covered in
[141](https://docs.rs#141)more detail in the [*Incomplete-computation values*] section.
[142](https://docs.rs#142)
[143](https://docs.rs#143)### Shifting operations
[144](https://docs.rs#144)
[145](https://docs.rs#145)The left shift `<<` and right shift `>>` operators support shifting by negative
[146](https://docs.rs#146)values, for example `a << 5` is equivalent to `a >> -5`.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)
[148](https://docs.rs#148)The shifting operators are also supported for the [`Float`] and [`Complex`]
[149](https://docs.rs#149)number types, where they are equivalent to multiplication or division by a power
[150](https://docs.rs#150)of two. Only the exponent of the value is affected; the mantissa is unchanged.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)### Exponentiation
[153](https://docs.rs#153)
[154](https://docs.rs#154)Exponentiation (raising to a power) does not have a dedicated operator in Rust.
[155](https://docs.rs#155)In order to perform exponentiation of Rug types, the [`Pow`][ops::Pow] trait has
[156](https://docs.rs#156)to be brought into scope, for example
[157](https://docs.rs#157)
[158](https://docs.rs#158)```rust
[159](https://docs.rs#159)# #[cfg(feature = "integer")] {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)use rug::ops::Pow;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)use rug::Integer;
[162](https://docs.rs#162)let base = Integer::from(10);
[163](https://docs.rs#163)let power = base.pow(5);
[164](https://docs.rs#164)assert_eq!(power, 100_000);
[165](https://docs.rs#165)# }
[166](https://docs.rs#166)```
[167](https://docs.rs#167)
[168](https://docs.rs#168)### Compound assignments to right-hand-side operands
[169](https://docs.rs#169)
[170](https://docs.rs#170)Traits are provided for compound assignment to right-hand-side operands. This
[171](https://docs.rs#171)can be useful for non-commutative operations like subtraction. The names of the
[172](https://docs.rs#172)traits and their methods are similar to Rust compound assignment traits, with
[173](https://docs.rs#173)the suffix “`Assign`” replaced with “`From`”. For example the counterpart to
[174](https://docs.rs#174)[`SubAssign`][core::ops::SubAssign] is [`SubFrom`][ops::SubFrom]:
[175](https://docs.rs#175)
[176](https://docs.rs#176)```rust
[177](https://docs.rs#177)# #[cfg(feature = "integer")] {
[178](https://docs.rs#178)use rug::ops::SubFrom;
[179](https://docs.rs#179)use rug::Integer;
[180](https://docs.rs#180)let mut rhs = Integer::from(10);
[181](https://docs.rs#181)// set rhs = 100 - rhs
[182](https://docs.rs#182)rhs.sub_from(100);
[183](https://docs.rs#183)assert_eq!(rhs, 90);
[184](https://docs.rs#184)# }
[185](https://docs.rs#185)```
[186](https://docs.rs#186)
[187](https://docs.rs#187)## Incomplete-computation values
[188](https://docs.rs#188)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)There are two main reasons why operations like `&a - &b` do not perform a
[190](https://docs.rs#190)complete computation and return a Rug type:
[191](https://docs.rs#191)
[192](https://docs.rs#192) 1. Sometimes we need to assign the result to an object that already exists.
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    Since Rug types require memory allocations, this can help reduce the number
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    of allocations. (While the allocations might not affect performance
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    noticeably for computationally intensive functions, they can have a much
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    more significant effect on faster functions like addition.)
[197](https://docs.rs#197) 2. For the [`Float`] and [`Complex`] number types, we need to know the
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    precision when we create a value, and the operation itself does not convey
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    information about what precision is desired for the result.
[200](https://docs.rs#200)
[201](https://docs.rs#201)There are two things that can be done with incomplete-computation values:
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203) 1. Assign them to an existing object without unnecessary allocations. This is
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    usually achieved using the [`Assign`] trait or a similar method, for example
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    <code>int.[assign][Assign::assign]\(incomplete)</code> and
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    <code>float.[assign\_round][ops::AssignRound::assign_round]\(incomplete, [Round][float::Round]::[Up][float::Round::Up])</code>.
[207](https://docs.rs#207) 2. Convert them to the final value using the [`Complete`] trait, the [`From`]
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    trait or a similar method. For example incomplete integers can be completed
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    using <code>incomplete.[complete][Complete::complete]\()</code> or
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    <code>[Integer]::[from][From::from]\(incomplete)</code>. Incomplete
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    floating-point numbers can be completed using
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    <code>incomplete.[complete][ops::CompleteRound::complete]\(53)</code> or
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    <code>[Float]::[with_val][Float::with_val]\(53, incomplete)</code> since the
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    precision has to be specified.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)Let us consider a couple of examples.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)
[218](https://docs.rs#218)```rust
[219](https://docs.rs#219)# #[cfg(feature = "integer")] {
[220](https://docs.rs#220)use rug::{Assign, Integer};
[221](https://docs.rs#221)let mut buffer = Integer::new();
[222](https://docs.rs#222)// ... buffer can be used and reused ...
[223](https://docs.rs#223)let (a, b) = (Integer::from(10), Integer::from(20));
[224](https://docs.rs#224)let incomplete = &a - &b;
[225](https://docs.rs#225)buffer.assign(incomplete);
[226](https://docs.rs#226)assert_eq!(buffer, -10);
[227](https://docs.rs#227)# }
[228](https://docs.rs#228)```
[229](https://docs.rs#229)
[230](https://docs.rs#230)Here the assignment from `incomplete` into `buffer` does not require an
[231](https://docs.rs#231)allocation unless the result does not fit in the current capacity of `buffer`.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)If `&a - &b` returned an [`Integer`] instead, then an allocation would take
[233](https://docs.rs#233)place even if it is not necessary.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)
[235](https://docs.rs#235)```rust
[236](https://docs.rs#236)# #[cfg(feature = "float")] {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)use rug::float::Constant;
[238](https://docs.rs#238)use rug::Float;
[239](https://docs.rs#239)// x has a precision of 10 bits
[240](https://docs.rs#240)let x = Float::with_val(10, 180);
[241](https://docs.rs#241)// y has a precision of 50 bits
[242](https://docs.rs#242)let y = Float::with_val(50, Constant::Pi);
[243](https://docs.rs#243)let incomplete = &x / &y;
[244](https://docs.rs#244)// z has a precision of 45 bits
[245](https://docs.rs#245)let z = Float::with_val(45, incomplete);
[246](https://docs.rs#246)assert!(57.295 < z && z < 57.296);
[247](https://docs.rs#247)# }
[248](https://docs.rs#248)```
[249](https://docs.rs#249)
[250](https://docs.rs#250)The precision to use for the result depends on the requirements of the algorithm
[251](https://docs.rs#251)being implemented. Here `z` is created with a precision of 45.
[252](https://docs.rs#252)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)Many operations can return incomplete-computation values, for example
[254](https://docs.rs#254)
[255](https://docs.rs#255)  * unary operators applied to references, for example `-&int`
[256](https://docs.rs#256)  * binary operators applied to two references, for example `&int1 + &int2`
[257](https://docs.rs#257)  * binary operators applied to a primitive and a reference, for example `&int *
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    10`
[259](https://docs.rs#259)  * methods that take a reference, for example
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    <code>int.[abs\_ref][Integer::abs_ref]\()</code>
[261](https://docs.rs#261)  * methods that take two references, for example
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    <code>int1.[gcd\_ref][Integer::gcd_ref]\(\&int2)</code>
[263](https://docs.rs#263)  * string parsing, for example
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    <code>[Integer]::[parse][Integer::parse]\(\"12\")</code>
[265](https://docs.rs#265)
[266](https://docs.rs#266)These operations return objects that can be stored in temporary variables like
[267](https://docs.rs#267)`incomplete` in the last few code examples. However, the names of the types are
[268](https://docs.rs#268)not public, and consequently, the incomplete-computation values cannot be for
[269](https://docs.rs#269)example stored in a struct. If you need to store the value in a struct, complete
[270](https://docs.rs#270)it to its final type and value.
[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)## Using Rug
[273](https://docs.rs#273)
[274](https://docs.rs#274)Rug is available on [crates.io][rug crate]. To use Rug in your crate, add it as
[275](https://docs.rs#275)a dependency inside [*Cargo.toml*]:
[276](https://docs.rs#276)
[277](https://docs.rs#277)```toml
[278](https://docs.rs#278)[dependencies]
[279](https://docs.rs#279)rug = "1.30"
[280](https://docs.rs#280)```
[281](https://docs.rs#281)
[282](https://docs.rs#282)Rug requires rustc version 1.85.0 or later.
[283](https://docs.rs#283)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)Rug also depends on the [GMP], [MPFR] and [MPC] libraries through the low-level
[285](https://docs.rs#285)FFI bindings in the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate][sys crate], which needs some setup to
[286](https://docs.rs#286)build; the [gmp-mpfr-sys documentation][sys] has some details on usage under
[287](https://docs.rs#287)[GNU/Linux][sys gnu], [macOS][sys mac] and [Windows][sys win].
[288](https://docs.rs#288)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)## Optional features
[290](https://docs.rs#290)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)The Rug crate has six optional features:
[292](https://docs.rs#292)
[293](https://docs.rs#293) 1. `integer`, enabled by default. Required for the [`Integer`] type and its
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    supporting features.
[295](https://docs.rs#295) 2. `rational`, enabled by default. Required for the [`Rational`] number type
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    and its supporting features. This feature requires the `integer` feature.
[297](https://docs.rs#297) 3. `float`, enabled by default. Required for the [`Float`] type and its
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    supporting features.
[299](https://docs.rs#299) 4. `complex`, enabled by default. Required for the [`Complex`] number type and
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    its supporting features. This feature requires the `float` feature.
[301](https://docs.rs#301) 5. `rand`, enabled by default. Required for the [`RandState`][rand::RandState]
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    type and its supporting features. This feature requires the `integer`
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    feature.
[304](https://docs.rs#304) 6. `std`, enabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    `no_std`, such as methods that return [`String`].
[306](https://docs.rs#306) 7. `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    [`Integer`], [`Rational`], [`Float`] and [`Complex`] number types, providing
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    that they are enabled. This feature requires the `std` feature and the
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    [serde crate].
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)The first six optional features are enabled by default; to use features
[312](https://docs.rs#312)selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [*Cargo.toml*]:
[313](https://docs.rs#313)
[314](https://docs.rs#314)```toml
[315](https://docs.rs#315)[dependencies.rug]
[316](https://docs.rs#316)version = "1.30"
[317](https://docs.rs#317)default-features = false
[318](https://docs.rs#318)features = ["integer", "float", "std"]
[319](https://docs.rs#319)```
[320](https://docs.rs#320)
[321](https://docs.rs#321)Here only the `integer`, `float` and `rand` features are enabled. If none of the
[322](https://docs.rs#322)features are selected, the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate][sys crate] is not required and
[323](https://docs.rs#323)thus not enabled. In that case, only the [`Assign`] trait and the traits that
[324](https://docs.rs#324)are in the [`ops`] module are provided by the crate.
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)## Experimental optional features
[327](https://docs.rs#327)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features
[329](https://docs.rs#329)are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor
[330](https://docs.rs#330)version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be
[331](https://docs.rs#331)updated to an incompatible newer version.
[332](https://docs.rs#332)
[333](https://docs.rs#333) 1. `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    [*num-traits* crate] and the [*num-integer* crate]. (The plan is to promote
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    this to an optional feature once the [*num-traits* crate] and the
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    [*num-integer* crate] reach version 1.0.0.)
[337](https://docs.rs#337) 2. `num-complex`, disabled by default. This adds conversion methods to and from
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    complex floats as provided by the [*num-complex* crate]. (The plan is to
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    promote this to an optional feature once the [*num-complex* crate] reaces
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    version 1.0.0.)
[341](https://docs.rs#341) 3. `nightly-float`, disabled by default. This requires the nightly compiler,
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    and implements some operations with the experimental [`f16`] and [`f128`]
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    primitives. (The plan is to always implement the operations and remove this
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    experimental feature once the primitives are stabilized.)
[345](https://docs.rs#345) 4. `borsh`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support using the
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    [*borsh* crate]. (The plan is to promote this to an optional feature.)
[347](https://docs.rs#347)
