[473](https://docs.rs#473)/**
[474](https://docs.rs#474)Assigns to a number from another value.
[475](https://docs.rs#475)
[476](https://docs.rs#476)# Examples
[477](https://docs.rs#477)
[478](https://docs.rs#478)Implementing the trait:
[479](https://docs.rs#479)
[480](https://docs.rs#480)```rust
[481](https://docs.rs#481)use rug::Assign;
[482](https://docs.rs#482)struct I(i32);
[483](https://docs.rs#483)impl Assign<i16> for I {
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    fn assign(&mut self, rhs: i16) {
[485](https://docs.rs#485)        self.0 = rhs.into();
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    }
[487](https://docs.rs#487)}
[488](https://docs.rs#488)let mut i = I(0);
[489](https://docs.rs#489)i.assign(42_i16);
[490](https://docs.rs#490)assert_eq!(i.0, 42);
[491](https://docs.rs#491)```
[492](https://docs.rs#492)
[493](https://docs.rs#493)Performing an assignment operation using the trait:
[494](https://docs.rs#494)
[495](https://docs.rs#495)```rust
[496](https://docs.rs#496)# #[cfg(feature = "integer")] {
[497](https://docs.rs#497)use rug::{Assign, Integer};
[498](https://docs.rs#498)let mut i = Integer::from(15);
[499](https://docs.rs#499)assert_eq!(i, 15);
[500](https://docs.rs#500)i.assign(23);
[501](https://docs.rs#501)assert_eq!(i, 23);
[502](https://docs.rs#502)# }
[503](https://docs.rs#503)```
[504](https://docs.rs#504)*/

[506](https://docs.rs#506)    /// Peforms the assignement.
[507](https://docs.rs#507)    fn assign(&mut self, src: Src);
[508](https://docs.rs#508)}

[510](https://docs.rs#510)/**
[511](https://docs.rs#511)Completes an [incomplete-computation value][icv].
[512](https://docs.rs#512)
[513](https://docs.rs#513)# Examples
[514](https://docs.rs#514)
[515](https://docs.rs#515)Implementing the trait:
[516](https://docs.rs#516)
[517](https://docs.rs#517)```rust
[518](https://docs.rs#518)# #[cfg(feature = "integer")] {
[519](https://docs.rs#519)use rug::{Complete, Integer};
[520](https://docs.rs#520)struct LazyPow4<'a>(&'a Integer);
[521](https://docs.rs#521)impl Complete for LazyPow4<'_> {
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    type Completed = Integer;
[523](https://docs.rs#523)    fn complete(self) -> Integer {
[524](https://docs.rs#524)        self.0.clone().square().square()
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    }
[526](https://docs.rs#526)}
[527](https://docs.rs#527)
[528](https://docs.rs#528)assert_eq!(LazyPow4(&Integer::from(3)).complete(), 3i32.pow(4));
[529](https://docs.rs#529)# }
[530](https://docs.rs#530)```
[531](https://docs.rs#531)
[532](https://docs.rs#532)Completing an [incomplete-computation value][icv]:
[533](https://docs.rs#533)
[534](https://docs.rs#534)```rust
[535](https://docs.rs#535)# #[cfg(feature = "integer")] {
[536](https://docs.rs#536)use rug::{Complete, Integer};
[537](https://docs.rs#537)let incomplete = Integer::fibonacci(12);
[538](https://docs.rs#538)let complete = incomplete.complete();
[539](https://docs.rs#539)assert_eq!(complete, 144);
[540](https://docs.rs#540)# }
[541](https://docs.rs#541)```
[542](https://docs.rs#542)
[543](https://docs.rs#543)[icv]: crate#incomplete-computation-values
[544](https://docs.rs#544)*/
[545](https://docs.rs#545)pub trait Complete {
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    /// The type of the completed operation.
[547](https://docs.rs#547)    type Completed;
[548](https://docs.rs#548)
[549](https://docs.rs#549)    /// Completes the operation.
[550](https://docs.rs#550)    fn complete(self) -> Self::Completed;
[551](https://docs.rs#551)
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    /// Completes the operation and stores the result in a target.
[553](https://docs.rs#553)    ///
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    /// # Examples
[555](https://docs.rs#555)    ///
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    /// ```rust
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    /// # #[cfg(feature = "integer")] {
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    /// use rug::{Complete, Integer};
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    /// let mut complete = Integer::new();
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    /// Integer::fibonacci(12).complete_into(&mut complete);
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    /// assert_eq!(complete, 144);
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    /// # }
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    /// ```
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    #[inline]
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    fn complete_into<T>(self, target: &mut T)
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    where
[567](https://docs.rs#567)        Self: Sized,
[568](https://docs.rs#568)        T: Assign<Self>,
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    {
[570](https://docs.rs#570)        target.assign(self);
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    }
[572](https://docs.rs#572)}

[607](https://docs.rs#607)mod static_assertions {
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp::{LIMB_BITS, NAIL_BITS, NUMB_BITS, limb_t};
[609](https://docs.rs#609)
[610](https://docs.rs#610)    static_assert!(NAIL_BITS == 0);
[611](https://docs.rs#611)    static_assert!(NUMB_BITS == LIMB_BITS);
[612](https://docs.rs#612)    static_assert!(cfg!(target_pointer_width = "32") ^ cfg!(target_pointer_width = "64"));
[613](https://docs.rs#613)    static_assert!(cfg!(gmp_limb_bits_32) ^ cfg!(gmp_limb_bits_64));
[614](https://docs.rs#614)    #[cfg(gmp_limb_bits_64)]
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    static_assert!(NUMB_BITS == 64);
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    #[cfg(gmp_limb_bits_32)]
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    static_assert!(NUMB_BITS == 32);

# Integer in rug - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/1.30.0/rug/struct.Integer.html

`pub struct Integer { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An arbitrary-precision integer.

Standard arithmetic operations, bitwise operations and comparisons are
supported. In standard arithmetic operations such as addition, you can mix
`Integer` and primitive integer types; the result will be an `Integer`.

Internally the integer is not stored using a two’s-complement representation, however, for bitwise operations and shifts, the functionality is the same as if the representation was using two’s complement.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
// Create an integer initialized as zero.
let mut int = Integer::new();
assert_eq!(int, 0);
assert_eq!(int.to_u32(), Some(0));
int.assign(-14);
assert_eq!(int, -14);
assert_eq!(int.to_u32(), None);
assert_eq!(int.to_i32(), Some(-14));
```
Arithmetic operations with mixed arbitrary and primitive types are allowed. Note
that in the following example, there is only one allocation. The `Integer`
instance is moved into the shift operation so that the result can be stored in
the same instance, then that result is similarly consumed by the addition
operation.

```
use rug::Integer;
let mut a = Integer::from(0xc);
a = (a << 80) + 0xffee;
assert_eq!(a.to_string_radix(16), "c0000000000000000ffee");
//                                 ↑   ↑   ↑   ↑   ↑   ↑
//                                80  64  48  32  16   0
```
Bitwise operations on `Integer` values behave as if the value uses a
two’s-complement representation.

```
use rug::Integer;
let mut i = Integer::from(1);
i = i << 1000;
// i is now 1000000... (1000 zeros)
assert_eq!(i.significant_bits(), 1001);
assert_eq!(i.find_one(0), Some(1000));
i -= 1;
// i is now 111111... (1000 ones)
assert_eq!(i.count_ones(), Some(1000));
let a = Integer::from(0xf00d);
// -1 is all ones in two’s complement
let all_ones_xor_a = Integer::from(-1 ^ &a);
// a is unchanged as we borrowed it
let complement_a = !a;
// now a has been moved, so this would cause an error:
// assert!(a > 0);
assert_eq!(all_ones_xor_a, complement_a);
assert_eq!(complement_a, -0xf00e);
assert_eq!(format!("{:x}", complement_a), "-f00e");
```
To initialize a large `Integer` that does not fit in a primitive type, you can
parse a string.

```
use rug::Integer;
let s1 = "123456789012345678901234567890";
let i1 = s1.parse::<Integer>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(i1.significant_bits(), 97);
let s2 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
let i2 = Integer::from_str_radix(s2, 16).unwrap();
assert_eq!(i2.significant_bits(), 160);
assert_eq!(i2.count_ones(), Some(80));
```
Operations on two borrowed `Integer` values result in an [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) that has to be assigned to a new `Integer` value.

```
use rug::Integer;
let a = Integer::from(10);
let b = Integer::from(3);
let a_b_ref = &a + &b;
let a_b = Integer::from(a_b_ref);
assert_eq!(a_b, 13);
```
As a special case, when an [incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) is obtained from
multiplying two `Integer` references, it can be added to or subtracted from
another `Integer` (or reference). This can be useful for multiply-accumulate
operations.

```
use rug::Integer;
let mut acc = Integer::from(100);
let m1 = Integer::from(3);
let m2 = Integer::from(7);
// 100 + 3 × 7 = 121
acc += &m1 * &m2;
assert_eq!(acc, 121);
let other = Integer::from(2000);
// Do not consume any values here:
// 2000 - 3 × 7 = 1979
let sub = Integer::from(&other - &m1 * &m2);
assert_eq!(sub, 1979);
```
The `Integer` type supports various functions. Most methods have three versions:

- The first method consumes the operand.
- The second method has a “`_mut`” suffix and mutates the operand.
- The third method has a “`_ref`” suffix and borrows the operand. The returned item is an[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)that can be assigned to an`Integer`.

```
use rug::Integer;
// 1. consume the operand
let a = Integer::from(-15);
let abs_a = a.abs();
assert_eq!(abs_a, 15);
// 2. mutate the operand
let mut b = Integer::from(-16);
b.abs_mut();
assert_eq!(b, 16);
// 3. borrow the operand
let c = Integer::from(-17);
let r = c.abs_ref();
let abs_c = Integer::from(r);
assert_eq!(abs_c, 17);
// c was not consumed
assert_eq!(c, -17);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Reserves capacity for at least `additional` more bits in the
[ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

If the integer already has enough excess capacity, this function does nothing.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
// 0x2000_0000 needs 30 bits.
let mut i = Integer::from(0x2000_0000);
assert_eq!(i.significant_bits(), 30);
i.reserve(290);
let capacity = i.capacity();
assert!(capacity >= 320);
i.reserve(0);
assert_eq!(i.capacity(), capacity);
i.reserve(291);
assert!(i.capacity() >= 321);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#363-365)#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#363-365)

#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

Shrinks the capacity of the [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) as much as possible.

The capacity can still be larger than the number of significant bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
// let i be 100 bits wide
let mut i = Integer::from_str_radix("fffff12345678901234567890", 16)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(i.significant_bits(), 100);
assert!(i.capacity() >= 100);
i >>= 80;
i.shrink_to_fit();
assert!(i.capacity() >= 20);
```
Shrinks the capacity of the [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) with a lower bound in bits.

The capacity will remain at least as large as both the current number of siginificant bits and the supplied value.

If the current capacity is less than the lower limit, this method has no effect.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
// let i be 100 bits wide
let mut i = Integer::from_str_radix("fffff12345678901234567890", 16)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(i.significant_bits(), 100);
assert!(i.capacity() >= 100);
i >>= 80;
i.shrink_to(50);
assert!(i.capacity() >= 50);
i.shrink_to(0);
assert!(i.capacity() >= 20);
```
Creates an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) from an initialized

[GMP integer](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.mpz_t.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The function must *not*be used to create a constant`Integer``Integer`*copied*on use, leading to undefined behavior when they are dropped.
- The value must be initialized as a valid `mpz_t`
- The `mpz_t`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::Integer;
let i = unsafe {
    let mut z = MaybeUninit::uninit();
    gmp::mpz_init_set_ui(z.as_mut_ptr(), 15);
    let z = z.assume_init();
    // z is initialized and unique
    Integer::from_raw(z)
};
assert_eq!(i, 15);
// since i is an Integer now, deallocation is automatic
```
This can be used to create a static [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) using

[to initialize the raw value. See the](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/fn.MPZ_ROINIT_N.html)

`MPZ_ROINIT_N`[GMP documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/C/GMP/constant.Integer_Functions.html#index-MPZ_005fROINIT_005fN)for details.

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp::{limb_t, mpz_t};
use rug::Integer;
const LIMBS: [limb_t; 2] = [123, 456];
const MPZ: mpz_t =
    unsafe { gmp::MPZ_ROINIT_N(LIMBS.as_ptr().cast_mut(), -2) };
// Must *not* be const, otherwise it would lead to undefined
// behavior on use, as it would create a copy that is dropped.
static I: Integer = unsafe { Integer::from_raw(MPZ) };
let check = -((Integer::from(LIMBS[1]) << gmp::NUMB_BITS) + LIMBS[0]);
assert_eq!(I, check);
```
Converts an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) into a

[GMP integer](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.mpz_t.html).

The returned object should be freed to avoid memory leaks.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(15);
let mut z = i.into_raw();
unsafe {
    let u = gmp::mpz_get_ui(&z);
    assert_eq!(u, 15);
    // free object to prevent memory leak
    gmp::mpz_clear(&mut z);
}
```
Returns a pointer to the inner [GMP integer](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.mpz_t.html).

The returned pointer will be valid for as long as `self` is valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(15);
let z_ptr = i.as_raw();
unsafe {
    let u = gmp::mpz_get_ui(z_ptr);
    assert_eq!(u, 15);
}
// i is still valid
assert_eq!(i, 15);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#620-634)#### pub unsafe fn [assign_digits_unaligned](https://docs.rs#method.assign_digits_unaligned)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(
    &mut self,

    order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html),

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#620-634)

#### pub unsafe fn [assign_digits_unaligned](https://docs.rs#method.assign_digits_unaligned)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(
    &mut self,
    src: [*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html),
)

Assigns from digits of type `T` in a memory area, where `T` can be any
[unsigned integer primitive type](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html).

The memory area is addressed using a pointer and a length. The `len`
parameter is the number of digits, *not* the number of bytes.

There are no data alignment restrictions on `src`, any address is
allowed.

The resulting value cannot be negative.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

To avoid undefined behavior, `src` must be [valid](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ptr/index.html#safety) for reading `len`
digits, that is `len` × `size_of::<T>()` bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
// hex bytes: [ fe dc ba 98 87 87 87 87 76 54 32 10 ]
let digits = [
    0xfedc_ba98u32.to_be(),
    0x8787_8787u32.to_be(),
    0x7654_3210u32.to_be(),
];
let ptr = digits.as_ptr();
let mut i = Integer::new();
unsafe {
    let unaligned = (ptr.cast::<u8>()).offset(2).cast::<u32>();
    i.assign_digits_unaligned(unaligned, 2, Order::MsfBe);
}
assert_eq!(i, 0xba98_8787_8787_7654u64);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#686-705)#### pub fn [to_digits](https://docs.rs#method.to_digits)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(&self, order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html)) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#686-705)

#### pub fn [to_digits](https://docs.rs#method.to_digits)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(&self, order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html)) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<T>

Converts the absolute value to a [ Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html) of digits of type

`T`, where
`T` can be any [unsigned integer primitive type](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html).

The [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) type also has the

[method, which can be used to borrow the digits without copying them. This does come with some more constraints compared to](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.as_limbs)

`as_limbs``to_digits`:- The digit width is not optional and depends on the implementation:
`limb_t``u64``u32`
- The order is not optional and is least significant digit first, with
each digit in the target’s endianness, equivalent to
[Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html)::[Lsf](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html#variant.Lsf)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(0x1234_5678_9abc_def0u64);
let digits = i.to_digits::<u32>(Order::MsfBe);
assert_eq!(digits, [0x1234_5678u32.to_be(), 0x9abc_def0u32.to_be()]);
let zero = Integer::new();
let digits_zero = zero.to_digits::<u32>(Order::MsfBe);
assert!(digits_zero.is_empty());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#732-737)#### pub fn [write_digits](https://docs.rs#method.write_digits)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(&self, digits: &mut [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#732-737)

#### pub fn [write_digits](https://docs.rs#method.write_digits)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(&self, digits: &mut [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html))

Writes the absolute value into a [slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html) of digits of type `T`, where
`T` can be any [unsigned integer primitive type](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html).

The slice must be large enough to hold the digits; the minimum size can
be obtained using the [ significant_digits](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.significant_digits) method.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the slice does not have sufficient capacity.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-19)Examples

```
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(0x1234_5678_9abc_def0u64);

```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#814-851)#### pub unsafe fn [write_digits_unaligned](https://docs.rs#method.write_digits_unaligned)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(
    &self,
    dst: [*mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html),
)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#814-851)

#### pub unsafe fn [write_digits_unaligned](https://docs.rs#method.write_digits_unaligned)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(
    &self,
    dst: [*mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html),
)

Writes the absolute value into a memory area of digits of type `T`,
where `T` can be any [unsigned integer primitive
type](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html).

The memory area is addressed using a pointer and a length. The `len`
parameter is the number of digits, *not* the number of bytes.

The length must be large enough to hold the digits; the minimum length
can be obtained using the [ significant_digits](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.significant_digits) method.

There are no data alignment restrictions on `dst`, any address is
allowed.

The memory locations can be uninitialized before this method is called;
this method sets all `len` elements, padding with zeros if the length is
larger than required.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-2)Safety

To avoid undefined behavior, `dst` must be [valid](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ptr/index.html#safety) for writing `len`
digits, that is `len` × `size_of::<T>()` bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

Panics if the length is less than the number of digits.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-20)Examples

```
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(0xfedc_ba98_7654_3210u64);
let mut digits = [0xffff_ffffu32; 4];
let ptr = digits.as_mut_ptr();
unsafe {
    let unaligned = (ptr.cast::<u8>()).offset(2).cast::<u32>();
    i.write_digits_unaligned(unaligned, 3, Order::MsfBe);
}
assert_eq!(
    digits,
    [
        0xffff_0000u32.to_be(),
        0x0000_fedcu32.to_be(),
        0xba98_7654u32.to_be(),
        0x3210_ffffu32.to_be(),
    ]
);
```
The following example shows how to write into uninitialized memory. In
practice, the following code could be replaced by a call to the safe
method [ to_digits](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.to_digits).

```
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(0x1234_5678_9abc_def0u64);
let len = i.significant_digits::<u32>();
assert_eq!(len, 2);
// The following code is equivalent to:
//     let digits = i.to_digits::<u32>(Order::MsfBe);
let mut digits = Vec::<u32>::with_capacity(len);
let ptr = digits.as_mut_ptr();
unsafe {
    i.write_digits_unaligned(ptr, len, Order::MsfBe);
    digits.set_len(len);
}
assert_eq!(digits, [0x1234_5678u32.to_be(), 0x9abc_def0u32.to_be()]);
```
Extracts a [slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html) of [limbs](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/type.limb_t.html) used to store the value.

The [slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html) contains the absolute value of `self`, with the least
significant limb first.

The [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) type also implements

[AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[limb_t](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/type.limb_t.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)>[§](https://docs.rs#examples-21)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
assert!(Integer::new().as_limbs().is_empty());
assert_eq!(Integer::from(13).as_limbs(), &[13]);
assert_eq!(Integer::from(-23).as_limbs(), &[23]);
```
`int.as_limbs()` is like a borrowing non-copy version of
`int.`.[to_digits](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.to_digits)::<[limb_t]>([Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html)::[Lsf](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html#variant.Lsf))

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp::limb_t;
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
let int = Integer::from(0x1234_5678_9abc_def0u64);
// no copying for int_slice, which is borrowing int
let int_slice = int.as_limbs();
// digits is a copy and does not borrow int
let digits = int.to_digits::<limb_t>(Order::Lsf);
// no copying for digits_slice, which is borrowing digits
let digits_slice = &digits[..];
assert_eq!(int_slice, digits_slice);
```

[if it is](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)

`f32`[finite](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html#method.is_finite), rounding towards zero.

This conversion can also be performed using
`value.`.[checked_as](https://docs.rs/az/1.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/az/trait.CheckedAs.html#tymethod.checked_as)::<[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)>()

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-22)Examples

```

```

Parses a decimal string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

The string can start with an optional minus or plus sign. ASCII whitespace is ignored everywhere in the string. Underscores anywhere except before the first digit are ignored as well.

```

#### pub fn [parse_radix](https://docs.rs#method.parse_radix)<S: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>>(

Parses a string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

The string can start with an optional minus or plus sign. ASCII whitespace is ignored everywhere in the string. Underscores anywhere except before the first digit are ignored as well.

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

```

let invalid = Integer::parse_radix("123", 3);
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#1064-1079)#### pub unsafe fn [assign_bytes_radix_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.assign_bytes_radix_unchecked)(
    &mut self,
    bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
    radix: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html),
    is_negative: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#1064-1079)

#### pub unsafe fn [assign_bytes_radix_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.assign_bytes_radix_unchecked)(
    &mut self,
    bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
    radix: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html),
    is_negative: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
)

Assigns from bytes in the given radix.

The radix must be between 2 and 256 inclusive.

Each byte must be a value from 0 to `radix - 1`, not an ASCII character.
The bytes must be ordered most-significant byte first.

If `is_negative` is [ true](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html), the returned value is negative (unless it is 0).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-3)Safety

The caller must ensure that

- 2 ≤ `radix`≤ 256
- all bytes are in the range 0 ≤ *x*<`radix`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-27)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
let bytes = &[0, 3, 9, 2];
let radix = 10;
let neg = true;
let mut i = Integer::new();
// SAFETY: radix and bytes are in the required ranges
unsafe {
    i.assign_bytes_radix_unchecked(bytes, radix, neg);
}
assert_eq!(i, -392);
```

Converts to an [ f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), rounding towards zero.

This conversion can also be performed using

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-52)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
let min = Integer::from_f32(f32::MIN).unwrap();
let min_minus_one = min - 1u32;
// min_minus_one is truncated to f32::MIN
assert_eq!(min_minus_one.to_f32(), f32::MIN);
let times_two = min_minus_one * 2u32;
// times_two is too small
assert_eq!(times_two.to_f32(), f32::NEG_INFINITY);
```
Converts to an [ f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html), rounding towards zero.

This conversion can also be performed using

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-53)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
// An `f64` has 53 bits of precision.
let exact = 0x1f_ffff_ffff_ffff_u64;
let i = Integer::from(exact);
assert_eq!(i.to_f64(), exact as f64);
// large has 56 ones
let large = 0xff_ffff_ffff_ffff_u64;
// trunc has 53 ones followed by 3 zeros
let trunc = 0xff_ffff_ffff_fff8_u64;
let j = Integer::from(large);
assert_eq!(j.to_f64() as u64, trunc);
let max = Integer::from_f64(f64::MAX).unwrap();
let max_plus_one = max + 1u32;
// max_plus_one is truncated to f64::MAX
assert_eq!(max_plus_one.to_f64(), f64::MAX);
let times_two = max_plus_one * 2u32;
// times_two is too large
assert_eq!(times_two.to_f64(), f64::INFINITY);
```

Returns a string representation of the number for the specified `radix`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-4)Panics

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-56)Examples

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let mut i = Integer::new();
assert_eq!(i.to_string_radix(10), "0");
i.assign(-10);
assert_eq!(i.to_string_radix(16), "-a");
i.assign(0x1234cdef);
assert_eq!(i.to_string_radix(4), "102031030313233");
i.assign(Integer::parse_radix("123456789aAbBcCdDeEfF", 16).unwrap());
assert_eq!(i.to_string_radix(16), "123456789aabbccddeeff");
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#1919-1927)#### pub const fn [as_neg](https://docs.rs#method.as_neg)(&self) -> [BorrowInteger](https://docs.rs/integer/struct.BorrowInteger.html)<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#1919-1927)

#### pub const fn [as_neg](https://docs.rs#method.as_neg)(&self) -> [BorrowInteger](https://docs.rs/integer/struct.BorrowInteger.html)<'_>

Borrows a negated copy of the [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

The returned object implements [Deref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html)<[Target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html#associatedtype.Target) = [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)>

This method performs a shallow copy and negates it, and negation does not change the allocated data.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-59)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(42);
let neg_i = i.as_neg();
assert_eq!(*neg_i, -42);
// methods taking &self can be used on the returned object
let reneg_i = neg_i.as_neg();
assert_eq!(*reneg_i, 42);
assert_eq!(*reneg_i, i);
```

#### pub fn [is_congruent](https://docs.rs#method.is_congruent)(&self, c: &Self, divisor: &Self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns [ true](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) if the number is congruent to

*c*mod

*divisor*, that is, if there exists a

*q*such that

`self` =
*c*+

*q*×

*divisor*. Unlike other division functions,

`divisor` can be zero.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-70)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
let n = Integer::from(105);
let divisor = Integer::from(10);
assert!(n.is_congruent(&Integer::from(5), &divisor));
assert!(n.is_congruent(&Integer::from(25), &divisor));
assert!(!n.is_congruent(&Integer::from(7), &divisor));
// n is congruent to itself if divisor is 0
assert!(n.is_congruent(&n, &Integer::from(0)));
```

#### pub fn [signed_bits](https://docs.rs#method.signed_bits)(&self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

Returns the number of bits required to represent the value using a two’s-complement representation.

For non-negative numbers, this method returns one more than
the [ significant_bits](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.significant_bits) method, since an extra zero is needed
before the most significant bit.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-79)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
assert_eq!(Integer::from(-5).signed_bits(), 4); // “1011”
assert_eq!(Integer::from(-4).signed_bits(), 3); //  “100”
assert_eq!(Integer::from(-3).signed_bits(), 3); //  “101”
assert_eq!(Integer::from(-2).signed_bits(), 2); //   “10”
assert_eq!(Integer::from(-1).signed_bits(), 1); //    “1”
assert_eq!(Integer::from(0).signed_bits(), 1);  //    “0”
assert_eq!(Integer::from(1).signed_bits(), 2);  //   “01”
assert_eq!(Integer::from(2).signed_bits(), 3);  //  “010”
assert_eq!(Integer::from(3).signed_bits(), 3);  //  “011”
assert_eq!(Integer::from(4).signed_bits(), 4);  // “0100”
```

#### pub fn [keep_signed_bits](https://docs.rs#method.keep_signed_bits)(self, n: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> Self

Keeps the *n* least significant bits only, producing a negative
result if the *n*th least significant bit is one.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-103)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;

assert_eq!(i_keep_8, -1);
let j = Integer::from(15 << 8 | 15);
let j_keep_8 = j.keep_signed_bits(8);
assert_eq!(j_keep_8, 15);
```

#### pub fn [div_rem_round](https://docs.rs#method.div_rem_round)(self, divisor: Self) -> (Self, Self)

Performs a division producing both the quotient and remainder, with the quotient rounded to the nearest integer.

When the quotient before rounding lies exactly between two integers, it is rounded away from zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-17)Panics

Panics if `divisor` is zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-122)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
// 23 / -10 → -2 rem 3
let (q, rem) = Integer::from(23).div_rem_round((-10).into());
assert!(q == -2 && rem == 3);
// 25 / 10 → 3 rem -5
let (q, rem) = Integer::from(25).div_rem_round(10.into());
assert!(q == 3 && rem == -5);
// -27 / 10 → -3 rem 3
let (q, rem) = Integer::from(-27).div_rem_round(10.into());
assert!(q == -3 && rem == 3);
```

Finds the inverse modulo `modulo` and returns [ Ok(inverse)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok) if it
exists, or

[if the inverse does not exist.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)

`Err(unchanged)`The inverse exists if the modulo is not zero, and `self` and the modulo
are co-prime, that is their GCD is 1.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-136)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
let n = Integer::from(2);
// Modulo 4, 2 has no inverse: there is no i such that 2 × i = 1.
let inv_mod_4 = match n.invert(&Integer::from(4)) {
    Ok(_) => unreachable!(),
    Err(unchanged) => unchanged,
};
// no inverse exists, so value is unchanged
assert_eq!(inv_mod_4, 2);
let n = inv_mod_4;
// Modulo 5, the inverse of 2 is 3, as 2 × 3 = 1.
let inv_mod_5 = match n.invert(&Integer::from(5)) {
    Ok(inverse) => inverse,
    Err(_) => unreachable!(),
};
assert_eq!(inv_mod_5, 3);
```

Raises a number to the power of `exponent` modulo `modulo` and returns
[ Ok(power)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok) if an answer exists, or

[if it does not.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)

`Err(unchanged)`If the exponent is negative, then the number must have an inverse for an answer to exist.

When the exponent is positive and the modulo is not zero, an answer always exists.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-139)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
// 7 ^ 5 = 16807
let n = Integer::from(7);
let e = Integer::from(5);
let m = Integer::from(1000);
let power = match n.pow_mod(&e, &m) {
    Ok(power) => power,
    Err(_) => unreachable!(),
};
assert_eq!(power, 807);
```
When the exponent is negative, an answer exists if an inverse exists.

```
use rug::Integer;
// 7 × 143 modulo 1000 = 1, so 7 has an inverse 143.
// 7 ^ -5 modulo 1000 = 143 ^ 5 modulo 1000 = 943.
let n = Integer::from(7);
let e = Integer::from(-5);
let m = Integer::from(1000);
let power = match n.pow_mod(&e, &m) {
    Ok(power) => power,
    Err(_) => unreachable!(),
};
assert_eq!(power, 943);
```

#### pub fn [secure_pow_mod](https://docs.rs#method.secure_pow_mod)(self, exponent: &Self, modulo: &Self) -> Self

Raises a number to the power of `exponent` modulo `modulo`, with
resilience to side-channel attacks.

The exponent must be greater than zero, and the modulo must be odd.

This method is intended for cryptographic purposes where resilience to side-channel attacks is desired. The function is designed to take the same time and use the same cache access patterns for same-sized arguments, assuming that the arguments are placed at the same position and the machine state is identical when starting.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-27)Panics

Panics if `exponent` ≤ 0 or if `modulo` is even.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-142)Examples

let m = Integer::from(13);

```

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-152)Examples

```
use rug::{Assign, Complete, Integer};
let i = Integer::from(1004);
let mut root = Integer::new();
let mut rem = Integer::new();
// 1004 = 10^3 + 5
(&mut root, &mut rem).assign(i.root_rem_ref(3));
assert_eq!(root, 10);
assert_eq!(rem, 4);

let (other_root, other_rem) = i.root_rem_ref(6).complete();
assert_eq!(other_root, 3);
assert_eq!(other_rem, 275);

#### pub fn [is_probably_prime](https://docs.rs#method.is_probably_prime)(&self, reps: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [IsPrime](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.IsPrime.html)

Determines wheter a number is prime.

This function uses some trial divisions, a Baille-PSW probable prime
test, then `reps` − 24 Miller-Rabin probabilistic
primality tests.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-162)Examples

```
use rug::integer::IsPrime;
use rug::Integer;

assert_eq!(no.is_probably_prime(30), IsPrime::No);
let yes = Integer::from(817_504_243);
assert_eq!(yes.is_probably_prime(30), IsPrime::Yes);
// 16_412_292_043_871_650_369 is actually a prime.
let probably = Integer::from(16_412_292_043_871_650_369_u64);
assert_eq!(probably.is_probably_prime(30), IsPrime::Probably);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#4867-4870)#### pub fn [extended_gcd](https://docs.rs#method.extended_gcd)(self, other: Self, rop: Self) -> (Self, Self, Self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#4867-4870)

#### pub fn [extended_gcd](https://docs.rs#method.extended_gcd)(self, other: Self, rop: Self) -> (Self, Self, Self)

Finds the greatest common divisor (GCD) of the two inputs (`self` and
`other`), and two coefficients to obtain the GCD from the two inputs.

The GCD is always positive except when both inputs are zero. If the
inputs are *a* and *b*, then the GCD is *g* and the
coefficients are *s* and *t* such that

*a* × *s* + *b* × *t* = *g*

The values *s* and *t* are chosen such that normally,
|*s*| < |*b*| / (2*g*) and
|*t*| < |*a*| / (2*g*), and these
relations define *s* and *t* uniquely. There are a few
exceptional cases:

- If |*a*| = |*b*|, then*s*= 0,*t*= sgn(*b*).
- Otherwise, if *b*= 0 or |*b*| = 2*g*, then*s*= sgn(*a*), and if*a*= 0 or |*a*| = 2*g*, then*t*= sgn(*b*).

The initial value of `rop` is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-175)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
let a = Integer::from(4);
let b = Integer::from(6);
let (g, s, t) = a.extended_gcd(b, Integer::new());
assert_eq!(g, 2);
assert_eq!(s, -1);
assert_eq!(t, 1);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#4913-4915)#### pub fn [extended_gcd_mut](https://docs.rs#method.extended_gcd_mut)(&mut self, other: &mut Self, rop: &mut Self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#4913-4915)

#### pub fn [extended_gcd_mut](https://docs.rs#method.extended_gcd_mut)(&mut self, other: &mut Self, rop: &mut Self)

Finds the greatest common divisor (GCD) of the two inputs (`self` and
`other`), and two coefficients to obtain the GCD from the two inputs.

The GCD is stored in `self`, and the two coefficients are stored in
`other` and `rop`.

The GCD is always positive except when both inputs are zero. If the
inputs are *a* and *b*, then the GCD is *g* and the
coefficients are *s* and *t* such that

*a* × *s* + *b* × *t* = *g*

The values *s* and *t* are chosen such that normally,
|*s*| < |*b*| / (2*g*) and
|*t*| < |*a*| / (2*g*), and these
relations define *s* and *t* uniquely. There are a few
exceptional cases:

- If |*a*| = |*b*|, then*s*= 0,*t*= sgn(*b*).
- Otherwise, if *b*= 0 or |*b*| = 2*g*, then*s*= sgn(*a*), and if*a*= 0 or |*a*| = 2*g*, then*t*= sgn(*b*).

The initial value of `rop` is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-176)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
let mut a_g = Integer::from(4);
let mut b_s = Integer::from(6);
let mut t = Integer::new();
a_g.extended_gcd_mut(&mut b_s, &mut t);
assert_eq!(a_g, 2);
assert_eq!(b_s, -1);
assert_eq!(t, 1);
```

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-177)Examples

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let a = Integer::from(4);
let b = Integer::from(6);
let r = a.extended_gcd_ref(&b);
let mut g = Integer::new();
let mut s = Integer::new();
let mut t = Integer::new();
(&mut g, &mut s, &mut t).assign(r);
assert_eq!(a, 4);
assert_eq!(b, 6);
assert_eq!(g, 2);
assert_eq!(s, -1);
assert_eq!(t, 1);
```
In the case that only one of the two coefficients is required, this can be achieved as follows:

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let a = Integer::from(4);
let b = Integer::from(6);
// no t required
let (mut g1, mut s1) = (Integer::new(), Integer::new());
(&mut g1, &mut s1).assign(a.extended_gcd_ref(&b));
assert_eq!(g1, 2);
assert_eq!(s1, -1);
// no s required
let (mut g2, mut t2) = (Integer::new(), Integer::new());
(&mut g2, &mut t2).assign(b.extended_gcd_ref(&a));
assert_eq!(g2, 2);
assert_eq!(t2, 1);
```
Finds the least common multiple.

The result is always positive except when one or both inputs are zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-178)Examples

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let a = Integer::from(10);
let mut b = Integer::from(25);
// lcm of 10, 25 is 50
let lcm1 = a.lcm(&b);
assert_eq!(lcm1, 50);
b.assign(0);
// lcm of 50, 0 is 0
let lcm2 = lcm1.lcm(&b);
assert_eq!(lcm2, 0);
```

# Rational in rug - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/1.30.0/rug/struct.Rational.html

`pub struct Rational { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An arbitrary-precision rational number.

A `Rational` number is made up of a numerator [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) and denominator

[. After](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)

`Integer``Rational` number functions, the number is always in
canonical form, that is the denominator is always greater than zero, and there
are no common factors. Zero is stored as 0/1.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use rug::Rational;
let r = Rational::from((-12, 15));
let recip = Rational::from(r.recip_ref());
assert_eq!(recip, Rational::from((-5, 4)));
assert_eq!(recip, -1.25);
// The numerator and denominator are stored in canonical form.
let (num, den) = r.into_numer_denom();
assert_eq!(num, -4);
assert_eq!(den, 5);
```
When comparing `Rational` numbers, it is sometimes convenient to compare to a
pair of primitive integers, like in the comparison to `Rational::from((-5, 4))`
in the example above. `Rational::from((-5, 4))` requires memory allocation,
which can be an expensive operation. To avoid this allocation, when both the
numerator and denominator fit in a primitive integer, we can use
[ MiniRational](https://docs.rs/rational/struct.MiniRational.html) instead, which does not require heap memory allocation.

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
let r = Rational::from((-12, 15));
let recip = Rational::from(r.recip_ref());
assert_eq!(recip, MiniRational::from((-5, 4)));
```
The `Rational` number type supports various functions. Most methods have three
versions:

- The first method consumes the operand.
- The second method has a “`_mut`” suffix and mutates the operand.
- The third method has a “`_ref`” suffix and borrows the operand. The returned item is an[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)that can be assigned to a`Rational`number.

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
// 1. consume the operand
let a = Rational::from((-15, 2));
let abs_a = a.abs();
assert_eq!(abs_a, MiniRational::from((15, 2)));
// 2. mutate the operand
let mut b = Rational::from((-17, 2));
b.abs_mut();
assert_eq!(b, MiniRational::from((17, 2)));
// 3. borrow the operand
let c = Rational::from((-19, 2));
let r = c.abs_ref();
let abs_c = Rational::from(r);
assert_eq!(abs_c, MiniRational::from((19, 2)));
// c was not consumed
assert_eq!(c, MiniRational::from((-19, 2)));
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) number from an initialized

[GMP rational number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.mpq_t.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The function must *not*be used to create a constant`Rational``Rational`*copied*on use, leading to undefined behavior when they are dropped.
- The value must be initialized as a valid `mpq_t`
- The `mpq_t`
- The numerator and denominator must be in canonical form, as the rest
of the library assumes that they are. Most GMP functions leave the
rational number in canonical form, but assignment functions do not.
Check the [GMP documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/C/GMP/constant.Rational_Number_Functions.html#index-Rational-number-functions)for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
let r = unsafe {
    let mut q = MaybeUninit::uninit();
    gmp::mpq_init(q.as_mut_ptr());
    let mut q = q.assume_init();
    gmp::mpq_set_si(&mut q, -145, 10);
    gmp::mpq_canonicalize(&mut q);
    // q is initialized and unique
    Rational::from_raw(q)
};
assert_eq!(r, MiniRational::from((-145, 10)));
// since r is a Rational now, deallocation is automatic
```
This can be used to create a static [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) number using

[to initialize the raw numerator and denominator values. See the](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/fn.MPZ_ROINIT_N.html)

`MPZ_ROINIT_N`[GMP documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/C/GMP/constant.Integer_Functions.html#index-MPZ_005fROINIT_005fN)for details.

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp::{limb_t, mpq_t};
use rug::{Integer, Rational};
const NUMER_LIMBS: [limb_t; 2] = [0, 5];
const DENOM_LIMBS: [limb_t; 1] = [3];
const MPQ: mpq_t = unsafe {
    mpq_t {
        num: gmp::MPZ_ROINIT_N(NUMER_LIMBS.as_ptr().cast_mut(), -2),
        den: gmp::MPZ_ROINIT_N(DENOM_LIMBS.as_ptr().cast_mut(), 1),
    }
};
// Must *not* be const, otherwise it would lead to undefined
// behavior on use, as it would create a copy that is dropped.
static R: Rational = unsafe { Rational::from_raw(MPQ) };
let numer_check =
    -((Integer::from(NUMER_LIMBS[1]) << gmp::NUMB_BITS) + NUMER_LIMBS[0]);
let denom_check = Integer::from(DENOM_LIMBS[0]);
assert_eq!(*R.numer(), numer_check);
assert_eq!(*R.denom(), denom_check);
let check = Rational::from((&numer_check, &denom_check));
assert_eq!(R, check);
assert_eq!(*R.numer(), *check.numer());
assert_eq!(*R.denom(), *check.denom());
```
Converts a [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) number into a

[GMP rational number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.mpq_t.html).

The returned object should be freed to avoid memory leaks.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::Rational;
let r = Rational::from((-145, 10));
let mut q = r.into_raw();
unsafe {
    let d = gmp::mpq_get_d(&q);
    assert_eq!(d, -14.5);
    // free object to prevent memory leak
    gmp::mpq_clear(&mut q);
}
```
Returns a pointer to the inner [GMP rational number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.mpq_t.html).

The returned pointer will be valid for as long as `self` is valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
let r = Rational::from((-145, 10));
let q_ptr = r.as_raw();
unsafe {
    let d = gmp::mpq_get_d(q_ptr);
    assert_eq!(d, -14.5);
}
// r is still valid
assert_eq!(r, MiniRational::from((-145, 10)));
```

use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;

    gmp::mpq_inv(q_ptr, q_ptr);

Creates a [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) number from an

[if it is](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)

`f32`[finite](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html#method.is_finite), losing no precision.

This conversion can also be performed using

- [Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html)::- [try_from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.TryFrom.html#tymethod.try_from)(value)

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;

// -17.125 can be stored exactly as f32
let r = Rational::from_f32(-17.125).unwrap();
assert_eq!(r, MiniRational::from((-17125, 1000)));
let inf = Rational::from_f32(f32::INFINITY);
assert!(inf.is_none());
```

#### pub fn [from_str_radix](https://docs.rs#method.from_str_radix)(src: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), radix: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, [ParseRationalError](https://docs.rs/rational/struct.ParseRationalError.html)>

Parses a [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) number.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```

use rug::Rational;

```
Parses a decimal string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html)
number.

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

The string must contain a numerator, and may contain a denominator; the
numerator and denominator are separated with a “`/`”. The numerator can
start with an optional minus or plus sign.

ASCII whitespace is ignored everywhere in the string. Underscores are
ignored anywhere except before the first digit of the numerator and
between the “`/`” and the the first digit of the denominator.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::{Complete, Rational};
assert_eq!(
    Rational::parse("-12/23").unwrap().complete(),
    MiniRational::from((-12, 23))
);
assert_eq!(
    Rational::parse("+ 12 / 23").unwrap().complete(),
    MiniRational::from((12, 23))
);
let invalid = Rational::parse("12/");
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```

Parses a string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html)
number.

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

The string must contain a numerator, and may contain a denominator; the
numerator and denominator are separated with a “`/`”. The numerator can
start with an optional minus or plus sign.

ASCII whitespace is ignored everywhere in the string. Underscores are
ignored anywhere except before the first digit of the numerator and
between the “`/`” and the the first digit of the denominator.

If parsing is already done by an external function, the unsafe low-level
[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[assign_bytes_radix_unchecked](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.assign_bytes_radix_unchecked)[ mutate_numer_denom](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html#method.mutate_numer_denom) method.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::{Complete, Rational};
let valid1 = Rational::parse_radix("12/23", 4);
assert_eq!(
    valid1.unwrap().complete(),
    MiniRational::from((2 + 4 * 1, 3 + 4 * 2))
);
let valid2 = Rational::parse_radix("12 / yz", 36);
assert_eq!(
    valid2.unwrap().complete(),
    MiniRational::from((2 + 36 * 1, 35 + 36 * 34))
);
let invalid = Rational::parse_radix("12/23", 3);
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```
If parsing is done externally, low-level code can be used.

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
let num_bytes = &[1, 2];
let den_bytes = &[2, 3];
let radix = 10;
let neg = true;
let mut r = Rational::new();
// SAFETY: radix and the bytes are in the required ranges
r.mutate_numer_denom(|num, den| unsafe {
    num.assign_bytes_radix_unchecked(num_bytes, radix, neg);
    den.assign_bytes_radix_unchecked(den_bytes, radix, false);
});
// -12/23
assert_eq!(r, MiniRational::from((-12, 23)));
```
Converts to an [ f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), rounding towards zero.

This conversion can also be performed using

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
let min = Rational::from_f32(f32::MIN).unwrap();
let minus_small = min - MiniRational::from((7, 2)).borrow_excl();
// minus_small is truncated to f32::MIN
assert_eq!(minus_small.to_f32(), f32::MIN);
let times_three_two = minus_small * MiniRational::from((3, 2)).borrow_excl();
// times_three_two is too small
assert_eq!(times_three_two.to_f32(), f32::NEG_INFINITY);
```
Converts to an [ f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html), rounding towards zero.

This conversion can also be performed using

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
// An `f64` has 53 bits of precision.
let exact = 0x1f_1234_5678_9aff_u64;
let den = 0x1000_u64;
let r = Rational::from((exact, den));
assert_eq!(r.to_f64(), exact as f64 / den as f64);
// large has 56 ones
let large = 0xff_1234_5678_9aff_u64;
// trunc has 53 ones followed by 3 zeros
let trunc = 0xff_1234_5678_9af8_u64;
let j = Rational::from((large, den));
assert_eq!(j.to_f64(), trunc as f64 / den as f64);
let max = Rational::from_f64(f64::MAX).unwrap();
let plus_small = max + MiniRational::from((7, 2)).borrow_excl();
// plus_small is truncated to f64::MAX
assert_eq!(plus_small.to_f64(), f64::MAX);
let times_three_two = plus_small * MiniRational::from((3, 2)).borrow_excl();
// times_three_two is too large
assert_eq!(times_three_two.to_f64(), f64::INFINITY);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rational/big.rs.html#766-776)#### pub unsafe fn [from_canonical](https://docs.rs#method.from_canonical)<Num, Den>(num: Num, den: Den) -> Self

#### pub unsafe fn [from_canonical](https://docs.rs#method.from_canonical)<Num, Den>(num: Num, den: Den) -> Self

Creates a new [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) number from a numerator and denominator
without canonicalizing aftwerwards.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

This function is unsafe because it does not canonicalize the
[ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) number. The caller must ensure that the numerator and
denominator are in canonical form, as the rest of the library assumes
that they are.

There are a few methods that can be called on [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) numbers that
are not in canonical form:

- `numer`- `denom`
- assignment methods, which overwrite the previous value and leave the number in canonical form
- `mutate_numer_denom`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-19)Examples

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
// -3/5 is in canonical form
let r = unsafe { Rational::from_canonical(-3, 5) };
assert_eq!(r, MiniRational::from((-3, 5)));
```

There are a few methods that can be called on [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) numbers that

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rational/big.rs.html#900-917)#### pub fn [mutate_numer_denom](https://docs.rs#method.mutate_numer_denom)<F>(&mut self, func: F)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rational/big.rs.html#900-917)

#### pub fn [mutate_numer_denom](https://docs.rs#method.mutate_numer_denom)<F>(&mut self, func: F)

Calls a function with mutable references to the numerator and denominator, then canonicalizes the number.

The denominator must not be zero when the function returns.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-3)Panics

Panics if the denominator is zero when the function returns.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-23)Examples

```
use rug::Rational;
let mut r = Rational::from((3, 5));
r.mutate_numer_denom(|num, den| {
    // change r from 3/5 to 4/8, which is equal to 1/2
    *num += 1;
    *den += 3;
});
assert_eq!(*r.numer(), 1);
assert_eq!(*r.denom(), 2);
```
This method does not check that the numerator and denominator are in
canonical form before calling `func`. This means that this method can be
used to canonicalize the number after some unsafe methods that do not
leave the number in cononical form.

```
use rug::Rational;
let mut r = Rational::from((3, 5));
unsafe {
    // leave r in non-canonical form
    *r.as_mut_numer_denom_no_canonicalization().0 += 1;
    *r.as_mut_numer_denom_no_canonicalization().1 -= 13;
}
// At this point, r is still not canonical: 4 / -8
assert_eq!(*r.numer(), 4);
assert_eq!(*r.denom(), -8);
r.mutate_numer_denom(|_, _| {});
// Now r is in canonical form: -1 / 2
assert_eq!(*r.numer(), -1);
assert_eq!(*r.denom(), 2);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rational/big.rs.html#979-983)#### pub unsafe fn [as_mut_numer_denom_no_canonicalization](https://docs.rs#method.as_mut_numer_denom_no_canonicalization)(
    &mut self,
) -> (&mut [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html), &mut [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rational/big.rs.html#979-983)

#### pub unsafe fn [as_mut_numer_denom_no_canonicalization](https://docs.rs#method.as_mut_numer_denom_no_canonicalization)(
    &mut self,
) -> (&mut [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html), &mut [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html))

Borrows the numerator and denominator mutably without canonicalizing aftwerwards.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-3)Safety

This function is unsafe because it does not canonicalize the
[ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) number when the borrow ends. The caller must ensure that
the numerator and denominator are left in canonical form, as the rest of
the library assumes that they are.

There are a few methods that can be called on [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) numbers that
are not in canonical form:

- `numer`- `denom`
- assignment methods, which overwrite the previous value and leave the number in canonical form
- `mutate_numer_denom`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-24)Examples

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
let mut r = Rational::from((3, 5));
{
    let (num, den) = unsafe { r.as_mut_numer_denom_no_canonicalization() };
    // Add one to r by adding den to num. Since num and den
    // are relatively prime, r remains in canonical form.
    *num += &*den;
}
assert_eq!(r, MiniRational::from((8, 5)));
```
This method can also be used to group some operations before canonicalization. This is usually not beneficial, as early canonicalization usually means subsequent arithmetic operations have less work to do.

```
use rug::Rational;
let mut r = Rational::from((3, 5));
unsafe {
    // first operation: add 1 to numerator
    *r.as_mut_numer_denom_no_canonicalization().0 += 1;
    // second operation: subtract 13 from denominator
    *r.as_mut_numer_denom_no_canonicalization().1 -= 13;
}
// At this point, r is still not canonical: 4 / -8
assert_eq!(*r.numer(), 4);
assert_eq!(*r.denom(), -8);
r.mutate_numer_denom(|_, _| {});
// Now r is in canonical form: -1 / 2
assert_eq!(*r.numer(), -1);
assert_eq!(*r.denom(), 2);
```

Compares the absolute values.

Adds a list of [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) values.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html)
- [From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)<Src> for- [Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html)

Clamps the value within the specified bounds.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-44)Examples

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
let min = MiniRational::from((-3, 2));
let max = MiniRational::from((3, 2));
let min_borrow = &*min.borrow();
let max_borrow = &*max.borrow();
let too_small = Rational::from((-5, 2));
let clamped1 = too_small.clamp(min_borrow, max_borrow);
assert_eq!(clamped1, MiniRational::from((-3, 2)));
let in_range = Rational::from((1, 2));
let clamped2 = in_range.clamp(min_borrow, max_borrow);
assert_eq!(clamped2, MiniRational::from((1, 2)));
```

This method never reallocates or copies the heap data. It simply swaps the allocated data of the numerator and denominator and makes sure the denominator is stored as positive.

#### pub fn [fract_round](https://docs.rs#method.fract_round)(self, round: [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)) -> (Self, [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html))

Computes the fractional and rounded parts of the number.

The fractional part is positive when the number is rounded down and negative when the number is rounded up. When the number lies exactly between two integers, it is rounded away from zero.

The initial value of `round` is ignored.

let (fract2, round2) = r2.fract_round(Integer::new());
assert_eq!(fract2, MiniRational::from((-3, 10)));

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rational/big.rs.html#2580-2582)

#### pub fn [square_ref](https://docs.rs#method.square_ref)(&self) -> MulIncomplete<'_>

Computes the square.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

`r.square_ref()` produces the exact same result as `&r * &r`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-87)Examples

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::{Complete, Rational};
let r = Rational::from((-13, 2));
assert_eq!(r.square_ref().complete(), MiniRational::from((169, 4)));
```

# Float in rug - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/1.30.0/rug/struct.Float.html

`pub struct Float { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A multi-precision floating-point number with arbitrarily large precision and correct rounding

The precision has to be set during construction. The rounding method of the required operations can be specified, and the direction of the rounding is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::ops::DivAssignRound;
use rug::Float;
// A precision of 32 significant bits is specified here.
// (The primitive `f32` has a precision of 24 and
// `f64` has a precision of 53.)
let mut two_thirds_down = Float::with_val(32, 2.0);
let dir = two_thirds_down.div_assign_round(3.0, Round::Down);
// since we rounded down, direction is Ordering::Less
assert_eq!(dir, Ordering::Less);
let mut two_thirds_up = Float::with_val(32, 2.0);
let dir = two_thirds_up.div_assign_round(3.0, Round::Up);
// since we rounded up, direction is Ordering::Greater
assert_eq!(dir, Ordering::Greater);
let diff_expected = 2.0_f64.powi(-32);
let diff = two_thirds_up - two_thirds_down;
assert_eq!(diff, diff_expected);
```
Operations on two borrowed `Float` numbers result in an [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) that has to be assigned to a new `Float` value.

```
use rug::Float;
let a = Float::with_val(53, 10.5);
let b = Float::with_val(53, -1.25);
let a_b_ref = &a + &b;
let a_b = Float::with_val(53, a_b_ref);
assert_eq!(a_b, 9.25);
```
As a special case, when an [incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) is obtained from
multiplying two `Float` references, it can be added to or subtracted from
another `Float` (or reference). This will result in a fused multiply-accumulate
operation, with only one rounding operation taking place.

```
use rug::Float;
// Use only 4 bits of precision for demonstration purposes.
// 24 in binary is 11000.
let a = Float::with_val(4, 24);
// 1.5 in binary is 1.1.
let mul1 = Float::with_val(4, 1.5);
// -13 in binary is -1101.
let mul2 = Float::with_val(4, -13);
// 24 + 1.5 × -13 = 4.5
let add = Float::with_val(4, &a + &mul1 * &mul2);
assert_eq!(add, 4.5);
// 24 - 1.5 × -13 = 43.5, rounded to 44 using four bits of precision.
let sub = a - &mul1 * &mul2;
assert_eq!(sub, 44);
// With separate addition and multiplication:
let a = Float::with_val(4, 24);
// No borrows, so multiplication is computed immediately.
// 1.5 × -13 = -19.5 (binary -10011.1), rounded to -20.
let separate_add = a + mul1 * mul2;
assert_eq!(separate_add, 4);
```
The [incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) obtained from multiplying two `Float`
references can also be added to or subtracted from another such
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values), so that two muliplications and an addition
are fused with only one rounding operation taking place.

```
use rug::Float;
let a = Float::with_val(53, 24);
let b = Float::with_val(53, 1.5);
let c = Float::with_val(53, 12);
let d = Float::with_val(53, 2);
// 24 × 1.5 + 12 × 2 = 60
let add = Float::with_val(53, &a * &b + &c * &d);
assert_eq!(add, 60);
// 24 × 1.5 - 12 × 2 = 12
let sub = Float::with_val(53, &a * &b - &c * &d);
assert_eq!(sub, 12);
```
The `Float` type supports various functions. Most methods have four versions:

- The first method consumes the operand and rounds the returned `Float`to the[nearest](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html#variant.Nearest)representable value.
- The second method has a “`_mut`” suffix, mutates the operand and rounds it the nearest representable value.
- The third method has a “`_round`” suffix, mutates the operand, applies the specified[rounding method](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html), and returns the rounding direction:
- The fourth method has a “`_ref`” suffix and borrows the operand. The returned item is an[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)that can be assigned to a`Float`; the rounding method is selected during the assignment.

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Float;
let expected = 0.9490_f64;
// 1. consume the operand, round to nearest
let a = Float::with_val(53, 1.25);
let sin_a = a.sin();
assert!((sin_a - expected).abs() < 0.0001);
// 2. mutate the operand, round to nearest
let mut b = Float::with_val(53, 1.25);
b.sin_mut();
assert!((b - expected).abs() < 0.0001);
// 3. mutate the operand, apply specified rounding
let mut c = Float::with_val(4, 1.25);
// using 4 significant bits, 0.9490 is rounded down to 0.9375
let dir = c.sin_round(Round::Nearest);
assert_eq!(c, 0.9375);
assert_eq!(dir, Ordering::Less);
// 4. borrow the operand
let d = Float::with_val(53, 1.25);
let r = d.sin_ref();
let sin_d = Float::with_val(53, r);
assert!((sin_d - expected).abs() < 0.0001);
// d was not consumed
assert_eq!(d, 1.25);
```
The following example is a translation of the [MPFR sample](https://www.mpfr.org/sample.html) found on the MPFR
website. The program computes a lower bound on 1 + 1/1! + 1/2! + … + 1/100!
using 200-bit precision. The program writes:

`Sum is 2.7182818284590452353602874713526624977572470936999595749669131`

```
use rug::float;
use rug::float::{FreeCache, Round};
use rug::ops::{AddAssignRound, AssignRound, MulAssignRound};
use rug::Float;
let mut t = Float::with_val(200, 1.0);
let mut s = Float::with_val(200, 1.0);
let mut u = Float::new(200);
for i in 1..=100_u32 {
    // multiply t by i in place, round towards +∞
    t.mul_assign_round(i, Round::Up);
    // set u to 1/t, round towards -∞
    u.assign_round(t.recip_ref(), Round::Down);
    // increase s by u in place, round towards -∞
    s.add_assign_round(&u, Round::Down);
}
// `None` means the number of printed digits depends on the precision
let sr = s.to_string_radix_round(10, None, Round::Down);
println!("Sum is {}", sr);
float::free_cache(FreeCache::All);
```

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Float;
let (f1, dir) = Float::with_val_round(4, 3.3, Round::Nearest);
// 3.3 with precision 4 is rounded down to 3.25
assert_eq!(f1.prec(), 4);
assert_eq!(f1, 3.25);
assert_eq!(dir, Ordering::Less);
let (f2, dir) = Float::with_val_round(4, 3.3, Round::Up);
// 3.3 rounded up to 3.5
assert_eq!(f2.prec(), 4);
assert_eq!(f2, 3.5);
assert_eq!(dir, Ordering::Greater);
```

use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Float;
let (f1, dir) = Float::with_val_round_64(4, 3.3, Round::Nearest);
// 3.3 with precision 4 is rounded down to 3.25
assert_eq!(f1.prec(), 4);
assert_eq!(f1, 3.25);
assert_eq!(dir, Ordering::Less);
let (f2, dir) = Float::with_val_round_64(4, 3.3, Round::Up);
// 3.3 rounded up to 3.5
assert_eq!(f2.prec(), 4);
assert_eq!(f2, 3.5);
assert_eq!(dir, Ordering::Greater);
```

Creates a [ Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html) from an initialized

[MPFR floating-point number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpfr/struct.mpfr_t.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The function must *not*be used to create a constant`Float``Float`*copied*on use, leading to undefined behavior when they are dropped.
- The value must be initialized as a valid `mpfr_t`
- The `mpfr_t`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr::rnd_t;
use rug::Float;
let f = unsafe {
    let mut m = MaybeUninit::uninit();
    mpfr::init2(m.as_mut_ptr(), 53);
    let mut m = m.assume_init();
    mpfr::set_d(&mut m, -14.5, rnd_t::RNDN);
    // m is initialized and unique
    Float::from_raw(m)
};
assert_eq!(f, -14.5);
// since f is a Float now, deallocation is automatic
```
This can be used to create a static [ Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html). See

[and the](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpfr/struct.mpfr_t.html)

`mpfr_t`[MPFR documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/C/MPFR/constant.MPFR_Interface.html#Internals)for details.

```
use core::ptr::NonNull;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp::limb_t;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr::{mpfr_t, prec_t};
use rug::Float;
const LIMBS: [limb_t; 2] = [5, 1 << (limb_t::BITS - 1)];
const LIMBS_PTR: *const [limb_t; 2] = &LIMBS;
const MANTISSA_DIGITS: u32 = limb_t::BITS * 2;
const MPFR: mpfr_t = mpfr_t {
    prec: MANTISSA_DIGITS as prec_t,
    sign: -1,
    exp: 1,
    d: unsafe { NonNull::new_unchecked(LIMBS_PTR.cast_mut().cast()) },
};
// Must *not* be const, otherwise it would lead to undefined
// behavior on use, as it would create a copy that is dropped.
static F: Float = unsafe { Float::from_raw(MPFR) };
let lsig = Float::with_val(MANTISSA_DIGITS, 5) >> (MANTISSA_DIGITS - 1);
let msig = 1u32;
let check = -(lsig + msig);
assert_eq!(F, check);
```
Converts a [ Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html) into an

[MPFR floating-point number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpfr/struct.mpfr_t.html).

The returned object should be freed to avoid memory leaks.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr::rnd_t;
use rug::Float;
let f = Float::with_val(53, -14.5);
let mut m = f.into_raw();
unsafe {
    let d = mpfr::get_d(&m, rnd_t::RNDN);
    assert_eq!(d, -14.5);
    // free object to prevent memory leak
    mpfr::clear(&mut m);
}
```
Returns a pointer to the inner [MPFR floating-point number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpfr/struct.mpfr_t.html).

The returned pointer will be valid for as long as `self` is valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr::rnd_t;
use rug::Float;
let f = Float::with_val(53, -14.5);
let m_ptr = f.as_raw();
unsafe {
    let d = mpfr::get_d(m_ptr, rnd_t::RNDN);
    assert_eq!(d, -14.5);
}
// f is still valid
assert_eq!(f, -14.5);
```

Parses a decimal string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html).

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)> for Src

The string can start with an optional minus or plus sign and must then
have one or more significant digits with an optional decimal point. This
can optionally be followed by an exponent; the exponent can start with a
separator “`e`”, “`E`” or “`@`”, and is followed by an optional minus or
plus sign and by one or more decimal digits.

Alternatively, the string can indicate the special values infinity or
NaN. Infinity can be represented as `"inf"`, `"infinity"`, `"@inf@"` or
`"@infinity@"`,and NaN can be represented as `"nan"` or `"@nan@"`. All
of these special representations are case insensitive. The NaN
representation may also include a possibly-empty string of ASCII
letters, digits and underscores enclosed in brackets, for example
`"nan(char_sequence_1)"`.

ASCII whitespace is ignored everywhere in the string except in the
substrings specified above for special values; for example `" @inf@ "`
is accepted but `"@ inf @"` is not. Underscores are ignored anywhere in
digit strings except before the first digit and between the exponent
separator and the first digit of the exponent.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```
use rug::Float;
let valid = Float::parse("12.25e-4");
let f = Float::with_val(53, valid.unwrap());
assert_eq!(f, 12.25e-4);
let invalid = Float::parse(".e-4");
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```

) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<ParseIncomplete, [ParseFloatError](https://docs.rs/float/struct.ParseFloatError.html)>

Parses a string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html).

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)> for Src

The string can start with an optional minus or plus sign and must then
have one or more significant digits with an optional point. This can
optionally be followed by an exponent; the exponent can start with a
separator “`e`” or “`E`” if the radix ≤ 10, or “`@`” for any radix, and
is followed by an optional minus or plus sign and by one or more decimal
digits.

Alternatively, the string can indicate the special values infinity or
NaN. If the radix ≤ 10, infinity can be represented as `"inf"` or
`"infinity"`, and NaN can be represented as `"nan"`. For any radix,
infinity can also be represented as `"@inf@"` or `"@infinity@"`, and NaN
can be represented as `"@nan@"`. All of these special representations
are case insensitive. The NaN representation may also include a
possibly-empty string of ASCII letters, digits and underscores enclosed
in brackets, for example `"nan(char_sequence_1)"`.

ASCII whitespace is ignored everywhere in the string except in the
substrings specified above for special values; for example `" @inf@ "`
is accepted but `"@ inf @"` is not. Underscores are ignored anywhere in
digit strings except before the first digit and between the exponent
separator and the first digit of the exponent.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-10)Panics

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
use rug::Float;
let valid1 = Float::parse_radix("12.23e-4", 4);
let f1 = Float::with_val(53, valid1.unwrap());
assert_eq!(f1, (2.0 + 4.0 * 1.0 + 0.25 * (2.0 + 0.25 * 3.0)) / 256.0);
let valid2 = Float::parse_radix("12.yz@2", 36);
let f2 = Float::with_val(53, valid2.unwrap());
assert_eq!(f2, 35 + 36 * (34 + 36 * (2 + 36 * 1)));
let invalid = Float::parse_radix("ffe-2", 16);
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```
