## Quick example

```
use ;
let mut int = new;
assert_eq!;
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign;
assert!;
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
int =  - 1;
assert_eq!;
```
- [Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html)::- [new](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.new)creates a new- `Integer`
- To assign values to Rug types, we use the `Assign``Assign::assign`[assignment operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#assignment-expressions)as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.`=`
- Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to fit in a
primitive type. To assign such a number to the large types, we use strings
rather than primitives; in the example this is done using
[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)and[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse_radix](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse_radix).
- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types using the
normal comparison operators, for example `int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and primitive types
on either side of the operator, for example `int >> 128`.

## Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two values of
the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive types, conversion to
and from Rug types can be expensive, so the arithmetic operators are overloaded
to work on many combinations of Rug types and primitives. More details are
available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/index.html#using-with-primitive-types).

## Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```
use Integer;
let a = from;
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```
use Integer;
let  = ;
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = from;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html). This is covered in
more detail in the documentation’s

[section.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*More details on operators are available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/index.html#operators).

## Using Rug

Rug is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/rug). To use Rug in your crate, add it as
a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.19"
```
Rug requires rustc version 1.65.0 or later.

Rug also depends on the [GMP](https://gmplib.org/), [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/) and [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/) libraries through the low-level
FFI bindings in the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys), which needs some setup to
build; the [gmp-mpfr-sys documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.5/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html) has some details on usage under
[GNU/Linux](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.5/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-gnulinux), [macOS](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.5/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-macos) and [Windows](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.5/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-windows).

## Optional features

The Rug crate has six optional features:

- `integer`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Integer`
- `rational`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Rational`- `integer`feature.
- `float`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Float`
- `complex`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Complex`- `float`feature.
- `rand`, enabled by default. Required for the- `RandState`- `integer`feature.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the- `Integer`- `Rational`- `Float`- `Complex`- [serde crate](https://crates.io/crates/serde).

The first five optional features are enabled by default; to use features
selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.19"
 = false
 = ["integer", "float", "rand"]
```
Here only the `integer`, `float` and `rand` features are enabled. If none of the
features are selected, the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) is not required and
thus not enabled. In that case, only the [ Assign](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/trait.Assign.html) trait and the traits that
are in the

[module are provided by the crate.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/ops/index.html)

`ops`## Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-integer*crate

# rug 1.19.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rug/1.19.0

# Arbitrary-precision numbers

Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and correct rounding:

- `Integer`
- `Rational`
- `Float`
- `Complex`

Rug is a high-level interface to the following [GNU](https://www.gnu.org/) libraries:

- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)for integers and rational numbers,
- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)for floating-point numbers, and
- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/)for complex numbers.

Rug is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms
of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published by the Free Software
Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later
version. See the full text of the [GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and [GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

## Quick example

```
use ;
let mut int = new;
assert_eq!;
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign;
assert!;
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
int =  - 1;
assert_eq!;
```
- [Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html)::- [new](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.new)creates a new- `Integer`
- To assign values to Rug types, we use the `Assign``Assign::assign`[assignment operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#assignment-expressions)as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.`=`
- Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to fit in a
primitive type. To assign such a number to the large types, we use strings
rather than primitives; in the example this is done using
[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)and[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse_radix](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse_radix).
- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types using the
normal comparison operators, for example `int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and primitive types
on either side of the operator, for example `int >> 128`.

## Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two values of
the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive types, conversion to
and from Rug types can be expensive, so the arithmetic operators are overloaded
to work on many combinations of Rug types and primitives. More details are
available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/index.html#using-with-primitive-types).

## Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```
use Integer;
let a = from;
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```
use Integer;
let  = ;
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = from;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/struct.Integer.html). This is covered in
more detail in the documentation’s

[section.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*More details on operators are available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/index.html#operators).

```
[]
 = "1.19"
```
Rug requires rustc version 1.65.0 or later.

Rug also depends on the [GMP](https://gmplib.org/), [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/) and [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/) libraries through the low-level
FFI bindings in the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys), which needs some setup to
build; the [gmp-mpfr-sys documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.5/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html) has some details on usage under
[GNU/Linux](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.5/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-gnulinux), [macOS](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.5/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-macos) and [Windows](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.5/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-windows).

## Optional features

The Rug crate has six optional features:

- `integer`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Integer`
- `rational`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Rational`- `integer`feature.
- `float`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Float`
- `complex`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Complex`- `float`feature.
- `rand`, enabled by default. Required for the- `RandState`- `integer`feature.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the- `Integer`- `Rational`- `Float`- `Complex`- [serde crate](https://crates.io/crates/serde).

The first five optional features are enabled by default; to use features
selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.19"
 = false
 = ["integer", "float", "rand"]
```
Here only the `integer`, `float` and `rand` features are enabled. If none of the
features are selected, the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) is not required and
thus not enabled. In that case, only the [ Assign](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/trait.Assign.html) trait and the traits that
are in the

[module are provided by the crate.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.19/rug/ops/index.html)

# rug 1.18.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rug/1.18.0

# Arbitrary-precision numbers

Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and correct rounding:

- `Integer`
- `Rational`
- `Float`
- `Complex`

Rug is a high-level interface to the following [GNU](https://www.gnu.org/) libraries:

- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)for integers and rational numbers,
- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)for floating-point numbers, and
- [MPC](http://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/)for complex numbers.

Rug is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms
of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published by the Free Software
Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later
version. See the full text of the [GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and [GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

## What’s new

### Version 1.18.0 news (2022-11-17)

- For the `Integer``gcd_cofactors``gcd_cofactors_mut``gcd_cofactors_ref``extended_gcd``extended_gcd_mut``extended_gcd_ref`
- All error types now implement `Clone``Copy``PartialEq``Eq`
- The `IntegerExt64`

### Other releases

Details on other releases can be found in [ RELEASES.md](https://gitlab.com/tspiteri/rug/blob/master/RELEASES.md).

## Quick example

```
use ;
let mut int = new;
assert_eq!;
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign;
assert!;
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
int =  - 1;
assert_eq!;
```
- [Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/struct.Integer.html)::- [new](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.new)creates a new- `Integer`
- To assign values to Rug types, we use the `Assign``Assign::assign`[assignment operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#assignment-expressions)as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.`=`
- Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to fit in a
primitive type. To assign such a number to the large types, we use strings
rather than primitives; in the example this is done using
[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)and[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse_radix](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse_radix).
- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types using the
normal comparison operators, for example `int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and primitive types
on either side of the operator, for example `int >> 128`.

## Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two values of
the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive types, conversion to
and from Rug types can be expensive, so the arithmetic operators are overloaded
to work on many combinations of Rug types and primitives. More details are
available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/index.html#using-with-primitive-types).

## Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```
use Integer;
let a = from;
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```
use Integer;
let  = ;
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = from;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/struct.Integer.html). This is covered in
more detail in the documentation’s

[section.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*More details on operators are available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/index.html#operators).

## Using Rug

Rug is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/rug). To use Rug in your crate, add it as
a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.18"
```
Rug requires rustc version 1.37.0 or later.

Rug also depends on the [GMP](https://gmplib.org/), [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/) and [MPC](http://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/) libraries through the low-level
FFI bindings in the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys), which needs some setup to
build; the [gmp-mpfr-sys documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html) has some details on usage under
[GNU/Linux](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-gnulinux), [macOS](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-macos) and [Windows](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-windows).

## Optional features

The Rug crate has six optional features:

- `integer`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Integer`
- `rational`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Rational`- `integer`feature.
- `float`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Float`

- `rand`, enabled by default. Required for the- `RandState`- `integer`feature.

The first five optional features are enabled by default; to use features
selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.18"
 = false
 = ["integer", "float", "rand"]
```
Here only the `integer`, `float` and `rand` features are enabled. If none of the
features are selected, the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) is not required and
thus not enabled. In that case, only the [ Assign](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/trait.Assign.html) trait and the traits that
are in the

[module are provided by the crate.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.18/rug/ops/index.html)

`ops`## Experimental optional features

# Arbitrary-precision numbers

Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and correct rounding:

- `Integer`
- `Rational`
- `Float`
- `Complex`

Rug is a high-level interface to the following [GNU](https://www.gnu.org/) libraries:

- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)for integers and rational numbers,
- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)for floating-point numbers, and
- [MPC](http://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/)for complex numbers.

Rug is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms
of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published by the Free Software
Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later
version. See the full text of the [GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and [GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

## What’s new

### Version 1.15.0 news (2022-02-03)

- Now `Integer``Rational``Float``Complex``Shl``Shr``ShlAssign``ShrAssign``isize``usize``i32``u32`
- The new experimental feature `num-traits`*num-traits*crate*num-integer*crate[issue 30](https://gitlab.com/tspiteri/rug/-/issues/30)).

### Version 1.14.1 news (2022-01-23)

- Bug fix: [Rational](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.14/rug/struct.Rational.html)::[to_f32](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.14/rug/struct.Rational.html#method.to_f32)was rounding away from zero in some cases when the rational number should be converted to a subnormal number ([issue 36](https://gitlab.com/tspiteri/rug/-/issues/36)).

### Version 1.14.0 news (2021-11-24)

- The [Rational](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.14/rug/struct.Rational.html)::[is_integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.14/rug/struct.Rational.html#method.is_integer)method was added.
- The [Complete](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.14/rug/trait.Complete.html)::[complete_into](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.14/rug/trait.Complete.html#method.complete_into)provided method was added to the`Complete`

## Quick example

```
use ;
let mut int = new;
assert_eq!;
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign;
assert!;
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
int =  - 1;
assert_eq!;
```
- [Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/struct.Integer.html)::- [new](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.new)creates a new- `Integer`
- To assign values to Rug types, we use the `Assign``Assign::assign`[assignment operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#assignment-expressions)as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.`=`
- Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to fit in a
primitive type. To assign such a number to the large types, we use strings
rather than primitives; in the example this is done using
[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)and[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse_radix](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse_radix).
- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types using the
normal comparison operators, for example `int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and primitive types
on either side of the operator, for example `int >> 128`.

## Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two values of
the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive types, conversion to
and from Rug types can be expensive, so the arithmetic operators are overloaded
to work on many combinations of Rug types and primitives. More details are
available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/index.html#using-with-primitive-types).

## Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```
use Integer;
let a = from;
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```
use Integer;
let  = ;
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = from;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/struct.Integer.html). This is covered in
more detail in the documentation’s

[section.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*More details on operators are available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/index.html#operators).

## Using Rug

Rug is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/rug). To use Rug in your crate, add it as
a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.15"
```
Rug requires rustc version 1.37.0 or later.

Rug also depends on the [GMP](https://gmplib.org/), [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/) and [MPC](http://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/) libraries through the low-level
FFI bindings in the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys), which needs some setup to
build; the [gmp-mpfr-sys documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html) has some details on usage under
[GNU/Linux](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-gnulinux), [macOS](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-macos) and [Windows](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-windows).

## Optional features

The Rug crate has six optional features:

- `integer`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Integer`
- `rational`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Rational`- `integer`feature.
- `float`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Float`
- `complex`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Complex`- `float`feature.
- `rand`, enabled by default. Required for the- `RandState`- `integer`feature.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the- `Integer`- `Rational`- `Float`- `Complex`- [serde crate](https://crates.io/crates/serde).

The first five optional features are enabled by default; to use features
selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.15"
 = false
 = ["integer", "float", "rand"]
```
Here only the `integer`, `float` and `rand` features are enabled. If none of the
features are selected, the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) is not required and
thus not enabled. In that case, only the [ Assign](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/trait.Assign.html) trait and the traits that
are in the

[module are provided by the crate.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.15/rug/ops/index.html)

`ops`## Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-integer*crate

## Quick example

```
use ;
let mut int = new;
assert_eq!;
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign;
assert!;
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
int =  - 1;
assert_eq!;
```
- [Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/struct.Integer.html)::- [new](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.new)creates a new- `Integer`
- To assign values to Rug types, we use the `Assign``Assign::assign`[assignment operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#assignment-expressions)as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.`=`
- Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to fit in a
primitive type. To assign such a number to the large types, we use strings
rather than primitives; in the example this is done using
[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)and[Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/struct.Integer.html)::[parse_radix](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/struct.Integer.html#method.parse_radix).
- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types using the
normal comparison operators, for example `int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and primitive types
on either side of the operator, for example `int >> 128`.

## Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two values of
the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive types, conversion to
and from Rug types can be expensive, so the arithmetic operators are overloaded
to work on many combinations of Rug types and primitives. More details are
available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/index.html#using-with-primitive-types).

## Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```
use Integer;
let a = from;
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```
use Integer;
let  = ;
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = from;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/struct.Integer.html). This is covered in
more detail in the documentation’s

[section.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*More details on operators are available in the [documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/index.html#operators).

## Using Rug

Rug is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/rug). To use Rug in your crate, add it as
a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.13"
```
Rug requires rustc version 1.37.0 or later.

Rug also depends on the [GMP](https://gmplib.org/), [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/) and [MPC](http://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/) libraries through the low-level
FFI bindings in the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys), which needs some setup to
build; the [gmp-mpfr-sys documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html) has some details on usage under
[GNU/Linux](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-gnulinux), [macOS](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-macos) and [Windows](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.4/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-windows).

## Optional features

The Rug crate has six optional features:

- `integer`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Integer`
- `rational`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Rational`- `integer`feature.
- `float`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Float`
- `complex`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Complex`- `float`feature.
- `rand`, enabled by default. Required for the- `RandState`- `integer`feature.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the- `Integer`- `Rational`- `Float`- `Complex`- [serde crate](https://crates.io/crates/serde).

The first five optional features are enabled by default; to use features
selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.13"
 = false
 = ["integer", "float", "rand"]
```
Here only the `integer`, `float` and `rand` features are enabled. If none of the
features are selected, the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) is not required and
thus not enabled. In that case, only the [ Assign](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/trait.Assign.html) trait and the traits that
are in the

[module are provided by the crate.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.13/rug/ops/index.html)

`ops`

# Arbitrary-precision numbers

Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and correct rounding:

- `Integer`
- `Rational`
- `Float`
- `Complex`

- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)for integers and rational numbers,
- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)for floating-point numbers, and
- [MPC](http://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/)for complex numbers.

- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types
using the normal comparison operators, for example
`int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and
primitive types on either side of the operator, for example
`int >> 128`.

## Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two
values of the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive
types, conversion to and from Rug types can be expensive, so the
arithmetic operators are overloaded to work on many combinations of
Rug types and primitives. More details are available in the
[documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.5/rug/index.html#using-with-primitive-types).

## Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```

let a = from;
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned
[ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.5/rug/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```

let  = ;

// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = from;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final
value. It still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.5/rug/struct.Integer.html).
This is covered in more detail in the documentation’s

[section.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.5/rug/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*More details on operators are available in the
[documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.5/rug/index.html#operators).

# Arbitrary-precision numbers

Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and correct rounding:

- `Integer`
- `Rational`
- `Float`
- `Complex`

Rug is a high-level interface to the following [GNU](https://www.gnu.org/) libraries:

- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)for integers and rational numbers,
- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)for floating-point numbers, and
- [MPC](http://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/)for complex numbers.

Rug is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under
the terms of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published by the
Free Software Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your
option) any later version. See the full text of the [GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and
[GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

## Quick example

```
use ;
let mut int = new;
assert_eq!;
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign;
assert!;
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
int =  - 1;
assert_eq!;
```
- `Integer::new()`- `Integer`
- To assign values to Rug types, we use the `Assign``assign`[assignment operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#assignment-expressions)as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.`=`
- Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to
fit in a primitive type. To assign such a number to the large
types, we use strings rather than primitives; in the example this
is done using `Integer::parse``Integer::parse_radix`
- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types
using the normal comparison operators, for example
`int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and
primitive types on either side of the operator, for example
`int >> 128`.

## Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two
values of the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive
types, conversion to and from Rug types can be expensive, so the
arithmetic operators are overloaded to work on many combinations of
Rug types and primitives. The following are provided:

- Where they make sense, all arithmetic operators are overloaded to
work with Rug types and the primitives `i32``u32``f32``f64`
- Where they make sense, conversions using the `From``Assign``i8``i16``i64``i128``isize``u8``u16``u64``u128``usize`
- Comparisons between Rug types and all the primitives listed in 1 and 2 above are supported.
- For `Rational`
- For `Complex`

## Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```
use Integer;
let a = from;
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned
[ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.4/rug/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```
use Integer;
let  = ;
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = from;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final
value. It still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.4/rug/struct.Integer.html).
This is covered in more detail in the

[section.](https://docs.rs#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*### Shifting operations

The left shift `<<` and right shift `>>` operators support shifting by
negative values, for example `a << 5` is equivalent to `a >> -5`.

The shifting operators are also supported for the [ Float](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.4/rug/struct.Float.html) and

[number types, where they are equivalent to multiplication or division by a power of two. Only the exponent of the value is affected; the mantissa is unchanged.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.4/rug/struct.Complex.html)

`Complex`### Exponentiation

Exponentiation (raising to a power) does not have a dedicated operator
in Rust. In order to perform exponentiation of Rug types, the [ Pow](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.4/rug/ops/trait.Pow.html)
trait has to be brought into scope, for example

```
use Pow;
use Integer;
let base = from;
let power = base.pow;
assert_eq!;
```
### Compound assignments to right-hand-side operands

Traits are provided for compound assignment to right-hand-side
operands. This can be useful for non-commutative operations like
subtraction. The names of the traits and their methods are similar to
Rust compound assignment traits, with the suffix “`Assign`” replaced
with “`From`”. For example the counterpart to [ SubAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ops/trait.SubAssign.html) is

[:](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.4/rug/ops/trait.SubFrom.html)

`SubFrom````
use SubFrom;
use Integer;
let mut rhs = from;
// set rhs = 100 − rhs
rhs.sub_from;
assert_eq!;
```
## Incomplete-computation values

There are two main reasons why operations like `&a - &b` do not
perform a complete computation and return a Rug type:

- Sometimes we need to assign the result to an object that already exists. Since Rug types require memory allocations, this can help reduce the number of allocations. (While the allocations might not affect performance noticeably for computationally intensive functions, they can have a much more significant effect on faster functions like addition.)
- For the `Float``Complex`

There are two things that can be done with incomplete-computation values:

- Assign them to an existing object without unnecessary allocations.
This is usually achieved using the `Assign``int.assign(incomplete)``float.assign_round(incomplete, Round::Up)`
- Convert them to the final value using the `From``Integer::from(incomplete)``Float::with_val(53, incomplete)`

Let us consider a couple of examples.

```
use ;
let mut buffer = new;
// ... buffer can be used and reused ...
let  = ;
let incomplete = &a - &b;
buffer.assign;
assert_eq!;
```
Here the assignment from `incomplete` into `buffer` does not require
an allocation unless the result does not fit in the current capacity
of `buffer`. If `&a - &b` returned an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.4/rug/struct.Integer.html) instead, then an
allocation would take place even if it is not necessary.

```
use Constant;
use Float;
// x has a precision of 10 bits
let x = with_val;
// y has a precision of 50 bits
let y = with_val;
let incomplete = &x / &y;
// z has a precision of 45 bits
let z = with_val;
assert!;
```
The precision to use for the result depends on the requirements of the
algorithm being implemented. Here `z` is created with a precision
of 45.

Many operations can return incomplete-computation values:

- unary operators applied to references, for example `-&int`;
- binary operators applied to two references, for example
`&int1 + &int2`;
- binary operators applied to a primitive and a reference, for
example `&int * 10`;
- methods that take a reference, for example
`int.abs_ref()`
- methods that take two references, for example
`int1.gcd_ref(&int2)`
- string parsing, for example
`Integer::parse("12")`
- and more.

These operations return objects that can be stored in temporary
variables like `incomplete` in the last few examples. However, the
names of the types are not public, and consequently, the
incomplete-computation values cannot be for example stored in a
struct. If you need to store the value in a struct, convert it to its
final type and value.

# Arbitrary-precision numbers

Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and correct rounding. Its main features are

- bignum [integers](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/struct.Integer.html)with arbitrary precision,
- bignum [rational numbers](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/struct.Rational.html)with arbitrary precision,
- multi-precision [floating-point numbers](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/struct.Float.html)with correct rounding, and
- multi-precision [complex numbers](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/struct.Complex.html)with correct rounding.

This crate is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it
under the terms of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published
by the Free Software Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or
(at your option) any later version. See the full text of the
[GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and [GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

## Quick example

```
use ;
let mut int = new;
assert_eq!;
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign;
assert!;
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign;
assert_eq!;
int =  - 1;
assert_eq!;
```
- `Integer::new()`- `Integer`
- To assign values to Rug types, we use the `Assign``assign`[assignment operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#assignment-expressions)as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.`=`
- Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to
fit in a primitive type. To assign such a number to the large types,
we use strings rather than primitives; in the example this is done
using `Integer::parse``Integer::parse_radix`
- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types
using the normal comparison operators, for example
`int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and
primitive types on either side of the operator, for example
`int >> 128`.

## Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two
values of the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive
types, conversion to and from Rug types can be expensive, so the
arithmetic operators are overloaded to work on many combinations of
Rug types and primitives. The following are provided:

- Where they make sense, all arithmetic operators are overloaded to
work with Rug types and the primitives `i32``u32``f32``f64`
- Where they make sense, conversions using the `From``Assign``i8``i16``i64``isize``u8``u16``u64``usize`
- Comparisons between Rug types and all the primitives listed in 1 and 2 above are supported.
- For `Rational`
- For `Complex`

## Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```
use Integer;
let a = from;
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned
[ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```
use Integer;
let  = ;
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = from;
assert_eq!;
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final
value. It still needs to be converted or assigned into an
[ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/struct.Integer.html). This is covered in more detail in the

[section.](https://docs.rs#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*### Shifting operations

The left shift `<<` and right shift `>>` operators support shifting by
negative values, for example `a << 5` is equivalent to `a >> -5`.

The shifting operators are also supported for the [ Float](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/struct.Float.html)
and

[types, where they are equivalent to multiplication or division by a power of two. Only the exponent of the value is affected; the mantissa is unchanged.](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/struct.Complex.html)

`Complex`### Exponentiation

Exponentiation (raising to a power) does not have a dedicated operator
in Rust. In order to perform exponentiation of Rug types, the
[ Pow](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/ops/trait.Pow.html) trait has to be brought into scope, for example

```
use Integer;
use Pow;
let base = from;
let power = base.pow;
assert_eq!;
```
### Compound assignments to right-hand-side operands

Traits are provided for compound assignment to right-hand-side
operands. This can be useful for non-commutative operations like
subtraction. The names of the traits and their methods are similar
to Rust compound assignment traits, with the suffix `Assign`
replaced with `From`. For example the counterpart to
[ SubAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.SubAssign.html) is

[:](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubFrom.html)

`SubFrom````
use Integer;
use SubFrom;
let mut rhs = from;
// set rhs = 100 - rhs
rhs.sub_from;
assert_eq!;
```
## Incomplete-computation values

There are two main reasons why operations like `&a - &b` do not
perform a complete computation and return a Rug type:

- Sometimes we need to assign the result to an object that already exists. Since Rug types require memory allocations, this can help reduce the number of allocations. (While the allocations might not affect performance noticeably for computationally intensive functions, they can have a much more significant effect on faster functions like addition.)
- For the `Float``Complex`

There are two things that can be done with incomplete-computation values:

- Assign them to an existing object without unnecessary allocations.
This is usually achieved using the `Assign``int.assign(incomplete)``float.assign_round(incomplete, Round::Up)`
- Convert them to the final value using the `From``Integer::from(incomplete)``Float::with_val(53, incomplete)`

Let us consider a couple of examples.

```
use ;
let mut buffer = new;
// ... buffer can be used and reused ...
let  = ;
let incomplete = &a - &b;
buffer.assign;
assert_eq!;
```
Here the assignment from `incomplete` into `buffer` does not require
an allocation unless the result does not fit in the current capacity
of `buffer`. If `&a - &b` returned an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/struct.Integer.html) instead,
then an allocation would take place even if it is not necessary.

```
use Float;
use Constant;
// x has a precision of 10 bits
let x = with_val;
// y has a precision of 50 bits
let y = with_val;
let incomplete = &x / &y;
// z has a precision of 45 bits
let z = with_val;
assert!;
```
The precision to use for the result depends on the requirements of the
algorithm being implemented. Here `z` is created with a precision of
45.

Many operations can return incomplete computation values:

- unary operators applied to references, for example `-&int`;
- binary operators applied to two references, for example
`&int1 + &int2`;
- binary operators applied to a primitive and a reference, for example
`&int * 10`;
- methods that take a reference, for example
`int.abs_ref()`
- methods that take two references, for example
`int1.gcd_ref(&int2)`
- string parsing, for example `Integer::parse("12")`
- and more.

These operations return objects that can be stored in temporary
variables like `incomplete` in the last few examples. However, the
names of the types are not public, and consequently, the
incomplete-computation values cannot be for example stored in a
struct. If you need to store the value in a struct, convert it to its
final type and value.

## Using Rug

Rug is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/rug). To use Rug in your crate,
add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
You also need to declare it by adding this to your crate root (usually
*lib.rs* or *main.rs*):

```
extern crate rug;
```
Rug requires rustc version 1.18.0 or later.

Rug also depends on the low-level bindings in the
[gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) which needs some setup to build; the
[gmp-mpfr-sys documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/%5E1.1/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html) has some details on usage under
[GNU/Linux](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/%5E1.1/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-gnulinux), [macOS](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/%5E1.1/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-macos) and [Windows](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/%5E1.1/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-windows).

## Optional features

The Rug crate has six optional features:

- `integer`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Integer`
- `rational`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Rational`- `integer`feature.
- `float`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Float`
- `complex`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Complex`- `float`feature.
- `rand`, enabled by default. Required for the- `RandState`- `integer`feature.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the- `Integer`- `Rational`- `Float`- `Complex`- [serde crate](https://crates.io/crates/serde).

The first five optional features are enabled by default; to use
features selectively, you can add the dependency like this to
[ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.0"
 = false
 = ["integer", "float", "rand"]
```
Here only the `integer`, `float` and `rand` features are enabled. If
none of the features are selected, the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/%5E1.1/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html) is
not required and thus not enabled. In that case, only the
[ Assign](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/trait.Assign.html) trait and some

[other traits](https://docs.rs/rug/~1.0/rug/ops/index.html)are provided by the crate.

# rug 0.9.3 - Docs.rs

# Arbitrary-precision numbers

The `rug` crate provides integers and floating-point numbers with
arbitrary precision and correct rounding. Its main features are:

- big [integers](https://docs.rs/rug/0.9.3/rug/struct.Integer.html)with arbitrary precision,
- big [rational numbers](https://docs.rs/rug/0.9.3/rug/struct.Rational.html)with arbitrary precision,
- multi-precision [floating-point numbers](https://docs.rs/rug/0.9.3/rug/struct.Float.html)with correct rounding, and
- multi-precision [complex numbers](https://docs.rs/rug/0.9.3/rug/struct.Complex.html)with correct rounding.

This crate is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it
under the terms of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published
by the Free Software Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or
(at your option) any later version. See the full text of the
[GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and [GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

[Documentation](https://docs.rs/rug/0.9.3/rug/index.html) for this crate is available. This crate depends
on the low-level bindings in the [ gmp-mpfr-sys](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) crate, which
provides Rust FFI bindings for:

- the [GNU Multiple Precision Arithmetic Library](https://gmplib.org/)(GMP),
- the [GNU MPFR Library](http://www.mpfr.org/), a library for multiple-precision floating-point computations, and
- [GNU MPC](http://www.multiprecision.org/), a library for the arithmetic of complex numbers with arbitrarily high precision.

It can be helpful to refer to the documentation of the [GMP](https://tspiteri.gitlab.io/gmp-mpfr-sys/gmp/index.html),
[MPFR](https://tspiteri.gitlab.io/gmp-mpfr-sys/mpfr/index.html) and [MPC](https://tspiteri.gitlab.io/gmp-mpfr-sys/mpc/index.html) libraries.

## Examples

```
extern crate rug;
use ;
```
## Usage

This crate requires rustc version 1.18.0 or later.

To use `rug` in your crate, add `extern crate rug;` to the crate root
and add `rug` as a dependency in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.9.3"
```
The `rug` crate depends on the low-level bindings in the
[ gmp-mpfr-sys](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) crate. This should be transparent on GNU/Linux
and macOS, but may need some work on Windows. See the

[documentation for some details.](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/%5E1.1.0/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html)

`gmp-mpfr-sys`### Optional features

The `rug` crate has six optional features:

- `integer`, enabled by default.
- `rational`, enabled by default. This feature requires the- `integer`feature.
- `float`, enabled by default.
- `complex`, enabled by default. This feature requires the- `float`feature.
- `rand`, enabled by default. This feature requires the- `integer`feature.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the- `Integer`,- `Rational`,- `Float`and- `Complex`types, providing that they are enabled.

The first five optional features are enabled by default; to disable
them add this to `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.9.3"
 = false
```
If none of the first five optional features are selected, the
[ gmp-mpfr-sys](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) crate is not required and thus not enabled.

To use features selectively, you can add this to `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.9.3"
 = false
# Pick which features to use
 = ["integer", "float", "rand"]
```

# Integer in rug - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/struct.Integer.html

`pub struct Integer { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An arbitrary-precision integer.

Standard arithmetic operations, bitwise operations and comparisons are
supported. In standard arithmetic operations such as addition, you can mix
`Integer` and primitive integer types; the result will be an `Integer`.

Internally the integer is not stored using a two’s-complement representation, however, for bitwise operations and shifts, the functionality is the same as if the representation was using two’s complement.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
// Create an integer initialized as zero.
let mut int = Integer::new();
assert_eq!(int, 0);
assert_eq!(int.to_u32(), Some(0));
int.assign(-14);
assert_eq!(int, -14);
assert_eq!(int.to_u32(), None);
assert_eq!(int.to_i32(), Some(-14));
```
Arithmetic operations with mixed arbitrary and primitive types are allowed. Note
that in the following example, there is only one allocation. The `Integer`
instance is moved into the shift operation so that the result can be stored in
the same instance, then that result is similarly consumed by the addition
operation.

```
use rug::Integer;
let mut a = Integer::from(0xc);
a = (a << 80) + 0xffee;
assert_eq!(a.to_string_radix(16), "c0000000000000000ffee");
//                                 ↑   ↑   ↑   ↑   ↑   ↑
//                                80  64  48  32  16   0
```
Bitwise operations on `Integer` values behave as if the value uses a
two’s-complement representation.

```
use rug::Integer;
let mut i = Integer::from(1);
i = i << 1000;
// i is now 1000000... (1000 zeros)
assert_eq!(i.significant_bits(), 1001);
assert_eq!(i.find_one(0), Some(1000));
i -= 1;
// i is now 111111... (1000 ones)
assert_eq!(i.count_ones(), Some(1000));
let a = Integer::from(0xf00d);
// -1 is all ones in two’s complement
let all_ones_xor_a = Integer::from(-1 ^ &a);
// a is unchanged as we borrowed it
let complement_a = !a;
// now a has been moved, so this would cause an error:
// assert!(a > 0);
assert_eq!(all_ones_xor_a, complement_a);
assert_eq!(complement_a, -0xf00e);
assert_eq!(format!("{:x}", complement_a), "-f00e");
```
To initialize a large `Integer` that does not fit in a primitive type, you can
parse a string.

```
use rug::Integer;
let s1 = "123456789012345678901234567890";
let i1 = s1.parse::<Integer>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(i1.significant_bits(), 97);
let s2 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
let i2 = Integer::from_str_radix(s2, 16).unwrap();
assert_eq!(i2.significant_bits(), 160);
assert_eq!(i2.count_ones(), Some(80));
```
Operations on two borrowed `Integer` values result in an [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) that has to be assigned to a new `Integer` value.

```
use rug::Integer;
let a = Integer::from(10);
let b = Integer::from(3);
let a_b_ref = &a + &b;
let a_b = Integer::from(a_b_ref);
assert_eq!(a_b, 13);
```
As a special case, when an [incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) is obtained from
multiplying two `Integer` references, it can be added to or subtracted from
another `Integer` (or reference). This can be useful for multiply-accumulate
operations.

```
use rug::Integer;
let mut acc = Integer::from(100);
let m1 = Integer::from(3);
let m2 = Integer::from(7);
// 100 + 3 × 7 = 121
acc += &m1 * &m2;
assert_eq!(acc, 121);
let other = Integer::from(2000);
// Do not consume any values here:
// 2000 - 3 × 7 = 1979
let sub = Integer::from(&other - &m1 * &m2);
assert_eq!(sub, 1979);
```
The `Integer` type supports various functions. Most methods have three versions:

- The first method consumes the operand.
- The second method has a “`_mut`” suffix and mutates the operand.
- The third method has a “`_ref`” suffix and borrows the operand. The returned item is an[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)that can be assigned to an`Integer`.

```
use rug::Integer;
// 1. consume the operand
let a = Integer::from(-15);
let abs_a = a.abs();
assert_eq!(abs_a, 15);
// 2. mutate the operand
let mut b = Integer::from(-16);
b.abs_mut();
assert_eq!(b, 16);
// 3. borrow the operand
let c = Integer::from(-17);
let r = c.abs_ref();
let abs_c = Integer::from(r);
assert_eq!(abs_c, 17);
// c was not consumed
assert_eq!(c, -17);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Reserves capacity for at least `additional` more bits in the
[ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

If the integer already has enough excess capacity, this function does nothing.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
// 0x2000_0000 needs 30 bits.
let mut i = Integer::from(0x2000_0000);
assert_eq!(i.significant_bits(), 30);
i.reserve(290);
let capacity = i.capacity();
assert!(capacity >= 320);
i.reserve(0);
assert_eq!(i.capacity(), capacity);
i.reserve(291);
assert!(i.capacity() >= 321);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#363-365)#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#363-365)

#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://docs.rs#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

Shrinks the capacity of the [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) as much as possible.

The capacity can still be larger than the number of significant bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
// let i be 100 bits wide
let mut i = Integer::from_str_radix("fffff12345678901234567890", 16)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(i.significant_bits(), 100);
assert!(i.capacity() >= 100);
i >>= 80;
i.shrink_to_fit();
assert!(i.capacity() >= 20);
```
Shrinks the capacity of the [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) with a lower bound in bits.

The capacity will remain at least as large as both the current number of siginificant bits and the supplied value.

If the current capacity is less than the lower limit, this method has no effect.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
// let i be 100 bits wide
let mut i = Integer::from_str_radix("fffff12345678901234567890", 16)
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(i.significant_bits(), 100);
assert!(i.capacity() >= 100);
i >>= 80;
i.shrink_to(50);
assert!(i.capacity() >= 50);
i.shrink_to(0);
assert!(i.capacity() >= 20);
```
Creates an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) from an initialized

[GMP integer](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.mpz_t.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The function must *not*be used to create a constant`Integer``Integer`*copied*on use, leading to undefined behavior when they are dropped.
- The value must be initialized as a valid `mpz_t`
- The `mpz_t`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::Integer;
let i = unsafe {
    let mut z = MaybeUninit::uninit();
    gmp::mpz_init_set_ui(z.as_mut_ptr(), 15);
    let z = z.assume_init();
    // z is initialized and unique
    Integer::from_raw(z)
};
assert_eq!(i, 15);
// since i is an Integer now, deallocation is automatic
```
This can be used to create a static [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) using

[to initialize the raw value. See the](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/fn.MPZ_ROINIT_N.html)

`MPZ_ROINIT_N`[GMP documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/C/GMP/constant.Integer_Functions.html#index-MPZ_005fROINIT_005fN)for details.

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp::{limb_t, mpz_t};
use rug::Integer;
const LIMBS: [limb_t; 2] = [123, 456];
const MPZ: mpz_t =
    unsafe { gmp::MPZ_ROINIT_N(LIMBS.as_ptr().cast_mut(), -2) };
// Must *not* be const, otherwise it would lead to undefined
// behavior on use, as it would create a copy that is dropped.
static I: Integer = unsafe { Integer::from_raw(MPZ) };
let check = -((Integer::from(LIMBS[1]) << gmp::NUMB_BITS) + LIMBS[0]);
assert_eq!(I, check);
```
Converts an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) into a

[GMP integer](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.mpz_t.html).

The returned object should be freed to avoid memory leaks.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(15);
let mut z = i.into_raw();
unsafe {
    let u = gmp::mpz_get_ui(&z);
    assert_eq!(u, 15);
    // free object to prevent memory leak
    gmp::mpz_clear(&mut z);
}
```
Returns a pointer to the inner [GMP integer](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.mpz_t.html).

The returned pointer will be valid for as long as `self` is valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(15);
let z_ptr = i.as_raw();
unsafe {
    let u = gmp::mpz_get_ui(z_ptr);
    assert_eq!(u, 15);
}
// i is still valid
assert_eq!(i, 15);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#620-634)#### pub unsafe fn [assign_digits_unaligned](https://docs.rs#method.assign_digits_unaligned)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#620-634)

#### pub unsafe fn [assign_digits_unaligned](https://docs.rs#method.assign_digits_unaligned)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(
    &mut self,
    src: [*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html),
)

Assigns from digits of type `T` in a memory area, where `T` can be any
[unsigned integer primitive type](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html).

The memory area is addressed using a pointer and a length. The `len`
parameter is the number of digits, *not* the number of bytes.

There are no data alignment restrictions on `src`, any address is
allowed.

The resulting value cannot be negative.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

To avoid undefined behavior, `src` must be [valid](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ptr/index.html#safety) for reading `len`
digits, that is `len` × `size_of::<T>()` bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
// hex bytes: [ fe dc ba 98 87 87 87 87 76 54 32 10 ]
let digits = [
    0xfedc_ba98u32.to_be(),
    0x8787_8787u32.to_be(),
    0x7654_3210u32.to_be(),
];
let ptr = digits.as_ptr();
let mut i = Integer::new();
unsafe {
    let unaligned = (ptr.cast::<u8>()).offset(2).cast::<u32>();
    i.assign_digits_unaligned(unaligned, 2, Order::MsfBe);
}
assert_eq!(i, 0xba98_8787_8787_7654u64);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#686-705)#### pub fn [to_digits](https://docs.rs#method.to_digits)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(&self, order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html)) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<T>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#686-705)

#### pub fn [to_digits](https://docs.rs#method.to_digits)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(&self, order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html)) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<T>

Converts the absolute value to a [ Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html) of digits of type

`T`, where
`T` can be any [unsigned integer primitive type](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html).

The [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) type also has the

[method, which can be used to borrow the digits without copying them. This does come with some more constraints compared to](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.as_limbs)

`as_limbs``to_digits`:- The digit width is not optional and depends on the implementation:
`limb_t``u64``u32`
- The order is not optional and is least significant digit first, with
each digit in the target’s endianness, equivalent to
[Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html)::[Lsf](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html#variant.Lsf)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(0x1234_5678_9abc_def0u64);
let digits = i.to_digits::<u32>(Order::MsfBe);
assert_eq!(digits, [0x1234_5678u32.to_be(), 0x9abc_def0u32.to_be()]);
let zero = Integer::new();
let digits_zero = zero.to_digits::<u32>(Order::MsfBe);
assert!(digits_zero.is_empty());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#732-737)#### pub fn [write_digits](https://docs.rs#method.write_digits)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(&self, digits: &mut [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#732-737)

#### pub fn [write_digits](https://docs.rs#method.write_digits)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(&self, digits: &mut [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html))

Writes the absolute value into a [slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html) of digits of type `T`, where
`T` can be any [unsigned integer primitive type](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html).

The slice must be large enough to hold the digits; the minimum size can
be obtained using the [ significant_digits](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.significant_digits) method.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the slice does not have sufficient capacity.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-19)Examples

```
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(0x1234_5678_9abc_def0u64);

```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#814-851)#### pub unsafe fn [write_digits_unaligned](https://docs.rs#method.write_digits_unaligned)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(
    &self,
    dst: [*mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html),
)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#814-851)

#### pub unsafe fn [write_digits_unaligned](https://docs.rs#method.write_digits_unaligned)<T: [UnsignedPrimitive](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html)>(
    &self,
    dst: [*mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    order: [Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html),
)

Writes the absolute value into a memory area of digits of type `T`,
where `T` can be any [unsigned integer primitive
type](https://docs.rs/integer/trait.UnsignedPrimitive.html).

The memory area is addressed using a pointer and a length. The `len`
parameter is the number of digits, *not* the number of bytes.

The length must be large enough to hold the digits; the minimum length
can be obtained using the [ significant_digits](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.significant_digits) method.

There are no data alignment restrictions on `dst`, any address is
allowed.

The memory locations can be uninitialized before this method is called;
this method sets all `len` elements, padding with zeros if the length is
larger than required.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-2)Safety

To avoid undefined behavior, `dst` must be [valid](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ptr/index.html#safety) for writing `len`
digits, that is `len` × `size_of::<T>()` bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

Panics if the length is less than the number of digits.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-20)Examples

```
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(0xfedc_ba98_7654_3210u64);
let mut digits = [0xffff_ffffu32; 4];
let ptr = digits.as_mut_ptr();
unsafe {
    let unaligned = (ptr.cast::<u8>()).offset(2).cast::<u32>();
    i.write_digits_unaligned(unaligned, 3, Order::MsfBe);
}
assert_eq!(
    digits,
    [
        0xffff_0000u32.to_be(),
        0x0000_fedcu32.to_be(),
        0xba98_7654u32.to_be(),
        0x3210_ffffu32.to_be(),
    ]
);
```
The following example shows how to write into uninitialized memory. In
practice, the following code could be replaced by a call to the safe
method [ to_digits](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.to_digits).

```
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
let i = Integer::from(0x1234_5678_9abc_def0u64);
let len = i.significant_digits::<u32>();
assert_eq!(len, 2);
// The following code is equivalent to:
//     let digits = i.to_digits::<u32>(Order::MsfBe);
let mut digits = Vec::<u32>::with_capacity(len);
let ptr = digits.as_mut_ptr();
unsafe {
    i.write_digits_unaligned(ptr, len, Order::MsfBe);
    digits.set_len(len);
}
assert_eq!(digits, [0x1234_5678u32.to_be(), 0x9abc_def0u32.to_be()]);
```
Extracts a [slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html) of [limbs](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/type.limb_t.html) used to store the value.

The [slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html) contains the absolute value of `self`, with the least
significant limb first.

The [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) type also implements

[AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[limb_t](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/type.limb_t.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)>[§](https://docs.rs#examples-21)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
assert!(Integer::new().as_limbs().is_empty());
assert_eq!(Integer::from(13).as_limbs(), &[13]);
assert_eq!(Integer::from(-23).as_limbs(), &[23]);
```
`int.as_limbs()` is like a borrowing non-copy version of
`int.`.[to_digits](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.to_digits)::<[limb_t]>([Order](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html)::[Lsf](https://docs.rs/integer/enum.Order.html#variant.Lsf))

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp::limb_t;
use rug::integer::Order;
use rug::Integer;
let int = Integer::from(0x1234_5678_9abc_def0u64);
// no copying for int_slice, which is borrowing int
let int_slice = int.as_limbs();
// digits is a copy and does not borrow int
let digits = int.to_digits::<limb_t>(Order::Lsf);
// no copying for digits_slice, which is borrowing digits
let digits_slice = &digits[..];
assert_eq!(int_slice, digits_slice);
```

[if it is](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)

`f32`[finite](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html#method.is_finite), rounding towards zero.

This conversion can also be performed using
`value.`.[checked_as](https://docs.rs/az/1.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/az/trait.CheckedAs.html#tymethod.checked_as)::<[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)>()

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-22)Examples

```

```

Parses a decimal string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

The string can start with an optional minus or plus sign. ASCII whitespace is ignored everywhere in the string. Underscores anywhere except before the first digit are ignored as well.

```

#### pub fn [parse_radix](https://docs.rs#method.parse_radix)<S: [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>>(

Parses a string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

The string can start with an optional minus or plus sign. ASCII whitespace is ignored everywhere in the string. Underscores anywhere except before the first digit are ignored as well.

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

```

let invalid = Integer::parse_radix("123", 3);
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#1064-1079)#### pub unsafe fn [assign_bytes_radix_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.assign_bytes_radix_unchecked)(
    &mut self,
    bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
    radix: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html),
    is_negative: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/big.rs.html#1064-1079)

#### pub unsafe fn [assign_bytes_radix_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.assign_bytes_radix_unchecked)(
    &mut self,
    bytes: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
    radix: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html),
    is_negative: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
)

Assigns from bytes in the given radix.

The radix must be between 2 and 256 inclusive.

Each byte must be a value from 0 to `radix - 1`, not an ASCII character.
The bytes must be ordered most-significant byte first.

If `is_negative` is [ true](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html), the returned value is negative (unless it is 0).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-3)Safety

The caller must ensure that

- 2 ≤ `radix`≤ 256
- all bytes are in the range 0 ≤ *x*<`radix`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-27)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
let bytes = &[0, 3, 9, 2];
let radix = 10;
let neg = true;
let mut i = Integer::new();
// SAFETY: radix and bytes are in the required ranges
unsafe {
    i.assign_bytes_radix_unchecked(bytes, radix, neg);
}
assert_eq!(i, -392);
```

Converts to an [ f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), rounding towards zero.

This conversion can also be performed using

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-52)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
let min = Integer::from_f32(f32::MIN).unwrap();
let min_minus_one = min - 1u32;
// min_minus_one is truncated to f32::MIN
assert_eq!(min_minus_one.to_f32(), f32::MIN);
let times_two = min_minus_one * 2u32;
// times_two is too small
assert_eq!(times_two.to_f32(), f32::NEG_INFINITY);
```
Converts to an [ f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html), rounding towards zero.

This conversion can also be performed using

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-53)Examples

```
use rug::Integer;
// An `f64` has 53 bits of precision.
let exact = 0x1f_ffff_ffff_ffff_u64;
let i = Integer::from(exact);
assert_eq!(i.to_f64(), exact as f64);
// large has 56 ones
let large = 0xff_ffff_ffff_ffff_u64;
// trunc has 53 ones followed by 3 zeros
let trunc = 0xff_ffff_ffff_fff8_u64;
let j = Integer::from(large);
assert_eq!(j.to_f64() as u64, trunc);
let max = Integer::from_f64(f64::MAX).unwrap();
let max_plus_one = max + 1u32;
// max_plus_one is truncated to f64::MAX
assert_eq!(max_plus_one.to_f64(), f64::MAX);
let times_two = max_plus_one * 2u32;
// times_two is too large
assert_eq!(times_two.to_f64(), f64::INFINITY);
```
