let min = -1.5;
let max = 1.5;
let mut too_small = Float::with_val(53, -2.5);
too_small.clamp_mut(&min, &max);
assert_eq!(too_small, -1.5);
let mut in_range = Float::with_val(53, 0.5);
in_range.clamp_mut(&min, &max);
assert_eq!(in_range, 0.5);
```
Clamps the value within the specified bounds, applying the specified rounding method.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-17)Panics

Panics if the maximum value is less than the minimum value, unless
assigning any of them to `self` produces the same value with the same
rounding direction.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-152)Examples

```

```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/float/big.rs.html#5263-5266)

#### pub fn [positive_diff](https://docs.rs#method.positive_diff)(self, other: &Self) -> Self

Computes the positive difference between `self` and `other`, rounding to
the nearest.

The positive difference is `self` − `other` if `self` > `other`, zero if
`self` ≤ `other`, or NaN if any operand is NaN.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-166)Examples

```
use rug::Float;
let a = Float::with_val(53, 12.5);
let b = Float::with_val(53, 7.3);
let diff1 = a.positive_diff(&b);
assert_eq!(diff1, 5.2);
let diff2 = diff1.positive_diff(&b);
assert_eq!(diff2, 0);
```

Computes the sine and cosine of `self`, applying the specified rounding
method.

The sine is stored in `self` and keeps its precision, while the cosine
is stored in `cos` keeping its precision.

The initial value of `cos` is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-209)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Float;
// Use only 4 bits of precision to show rounding.
let mut sin = Float::with_val(4, 1.25);

// sin(1.25) = 0.9490, using 4 significant bits: 0.9375
// cos(1.25) = 0.3153, using 4 significant bits: 0.3125

    sin.sin_cos_round(&mut cos, Round::Nearest);

assert_eq!(dir_sin, Ordering::Less);
assert_eq!(cos, 0.3125);
assert_eq!(dir_cos, Ordering::Less);
```

#### pub fn [sin_cos_ref](https://docs.rs#method.sin_cos_ref)(&self) -> SinCosIncomplete<'_>

Computes the sine and cosine.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html),- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)&mut- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html), &mut- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html),- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)&mut- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html), &mut- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html),- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-210)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::ops::AssignRound;
use rug::{Assign, Float};
let phase = Float::with_val(53, 1.25);
let (mut sin, mut cos) = (Float::new(53), Float::new(53));
let sin_cos = phase.sin_cos_ref();
(&mut sin, &mut cos).assign(sin_cos);
let expected_sin = 0.9490_f64;
let expected_cos = 0.3153_f64;
assert!((sin - expected_sin).abs() < 0.0001);
assert!((cos - expected_cos).abs() < 0.0001);
// using 4 significant bits: sin = 0.9375
// using 4 significant bits: cos = 0.3125
let (mut sin_4, mut cos_4) = (Float::new(4), Float::new(4));
let sin_cos = phase.sin_cos_ref();
let (dir_sin, dir_cos) = (&mut sin_4, &mut cos_4)
    .assign_round(sin_cos, Round::Nearest);
assert_eq!(sin_4, 0.9375);
assert_eq!(dir_sin, Ordering::Less);
assert_eq!(cos_4, 0.3125);
assert_eq!(dir_cos, Ordering::Less);
```

Computes the arc-tangent2 of `self` and `x` then divides by 2π/*u*,
rounding to the nearest.

For example, if *u* = 360, then this is the arc-tangent
in degrees.

This is similar to the arc-tangent of `self / x`, but has an output
range of *u* rather than *u*/2.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-275)Examples

```
use rug::Float;
let y = Float::with_val(53, 3.0);
let x = Float::with_val(53, -4.0);
let atan2 = y.atan2_u(&x, 360);
let expected = 143.1301_f64;
assert!((atan2 - expected).abs() < 0.0001);
```

```

let expected_cosh = 1.8884_f64;
assert!((sinh - expected_sinh).abs() < 0.0001);
assert!((cosh - expected_cosh).abs() < 0.0001);
```

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)&mut- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html), &mut- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html),- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)&mut- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html), &mut- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html),- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-310)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::ops::AssignRound;
use rug::{Assign, Float};
let phase = Float::with_val(53, 1.25);
let (mut sinh, mut cosh) = (Float::new(53), Float::new(53));
let sinh_cosh = phase.sinh_cosh_ref();
(&mut sinh, &mut cosh).assign(sinh_cosh);
let expected_sinh = 1.6019_f64;
let expected_cosh = 1.8884_f64;
assert!((sinh - expected_sinh).abs() < 0.0001);
assert!((cosh - expected_cosh).abs() < 0.0001);
// using 4 significant bits: sin = 1.625
// using 4 significant bits: cos = 1.875
let (mut sinh_4, mut cosh_4) = (Float::new(4), Float::new(4));
let sinh_cosh = phase.sinh_cosh_ref();
let (dir_sinh, dir_cosh) = (&mut sinh_4, &mut cosh_4)
    .assign_round(sinh_cosh, Round::Nearest);
assert_eq!(sinh_4, 1.625);
assert_eq!(dir_sinh, Ordering::Greater);
assert_eq!(cosh_4, 1.875);
assert_eq!(dir_cosh, Ordering::Less);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/float/big.rs.html#9941-9944)

#### pub fn [ln_abs_gamma](https://docs.rs#method.ln_abs_gamma)(self) -> (Self, [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html))

Computes the logarithm of the absolute value of the gamma function on
`self`, rounding to the nearest.

Returns [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)::[Less](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Less)[Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)::[Greater](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Greater)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-384)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Constant;
use rug::Float;
// gamma of 1/2 is √π
let ln_gamma_64 = Float::with_val(64, Constant::Pi).sqrt().ln();
let f = Float::with_val(53, 0.5);
let (ln_gamma, sign) = f.ln_abs_gamma();
// gamma of 1/2 is positive
assert_eq!(sign, Ordering::Greater);
// check to 53 significant bits
assert_eq!(ln_gamma, Float::with_val(53, &ln_gamma_64));
```
If the gamma function is negative, the sign returned is
[Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)::[Less](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Less)

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Constant;
use rug::Float;
// gamma of -1/2 is -2√π
let abs_gamma_64 = Float::with_val(64, Constant::Pi).sqrt() * 2u32;
let ln_gamma_64 = abs_gamma_64.ln();
let f = Float::with_val(53, -0.5);
let (ln_gamma, sign) = f.ln_abs_gamma();
// gamma of -1/2 is negative
assert_eq!(sign, Ordering::Less);
// check to 53 significant bits
assert_eq!(ln_gamma, Float::with_val(53, &ln_gamma_64));
```

#### pub fn [ln_abs_gamma_round](https://docs.rs#method.ln_abs_gamma_round)(&mut self, round: [Round](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html)) -> ([Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html), [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html))

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-386)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::{Constant, Round};
use rug::Float;

assert_eq!(dir, check_dir);
```

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-387)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Constant;
use rug::{Assign, Float};
let neg1_2 = Float::with_val(53, -0.5);
// gamma of -1/2 is -2√π

let ln_gamma_64 = abs_gamma_64.ln();

// check to 53 significant bits
assert_eq!(f, Float::with_val(53, &ln_gamma_64));
```

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-449)Examples

```

let f2 = Float::with_val(53, 23.75);
let round2 = Float::with_val(53, f2.round_ref());
assert_eq!(round2, 24);
```
Double rounding may happen when assigning to a target with a precision less than the number of significant bits for the truncated integer.

```
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Float;
use rug::ops::AssignRound;
let f = Float::with_val(53, 6.5);
// 6.5 (binary 110.1) is rounded to 7 (binary 111)
let r = f.round_ref();
// use only 2 bits of precision in destination
let mut dst = Float::new(2);
// 7 (binary 111) is rounded to 8 (binary 1000) by
// round-even rule in order to store in 2-bit Float, even
// though 6 (binary 110) is closer to original 6.5).
dst.assign_round(r, Round::Nearest);
assert_eq!(dst, 8);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/float/big.rs.html#11628-11630)#### pub fn [trunc_fract_round](https://docs.rs#method.trunc_fract_round)(
    &mut self,
    fract: &mut Self,
    round: [Round](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html),
) -> ([Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html), [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/float/big.rs.html#11628-11630)

#### pub fn [trunc_fract_round](https://docs.rs#method.trunc_fract_round)(
    &mut self,
    fract: &mut Self,
    round: [Round](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html),
) -> ([Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html), [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html))

Gets the integer and fractional parts of the number, applying the specified rounding method.

The first element of the returned tuple of rounding directions is always
[Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)::[Equal](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Equal)

The integer part is stored in `self` and keeps its precision, while the
fractional part is stored in `fract` keeping its precision.

The initial value of `fract` is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-461)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Float;
// 0.515625 in binary is 0.100001
let mut f1 = Float::with_val(53, -23.515625);
let mut fract1 = Float::new(4);
let dir1 = f1.trunc_fract_round(&mut fract1, Round::Nearest);
assert_eq!(f1, -23);
assert_eq!(fract1, -0.5);
assert_eq!(dir1, (Ordering::Equal, Ordering::Greater));
let mut f2 = Float::with_val(53, 23.515625);
let mut fract2 = Float::new(4);
let dir2 = f2.trunc_fract_round(&mut fract2, Round::Nearest);
assert_eq!(f2, 23);
assert_eq!(fract2, 0.5);
assert_eq!(dir2, (Ordering::Equal, Ordering::Less));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/float/big.rs.html#11705-11707)#### pub fn [random_bits](https://docs.rs#method.random_bits)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomBitsIncomplete<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/float/big.rs.html#11705-11707)

#### pub fn [random_bits](https://docs.rs#method.random_bits)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomBitsIncomplete<'_>

Generates a random number in the range
0 ≤ *x* < 1.

This is equivalent to generating a random integer in the range
0 ≤ *x* < 2 p, where
2

is two raised to the power of the precision, and then dividing the integer by 2

*p*. The smallest non-zero result will thus be 2

*p*−, and will only have one bit set. In the smaller possible results, many bits will be zero, and not all the precision will be used.

*p*There is a corner case where the generated random number is converted to NaN: if the precision is very large, the generated random number could have an exponent less than the allowed minimum exponent, and NaN is used to indicate this. For this to occur in practice, the minimum exponent has to be set to have a very small magnitude using the low-level MPFR interface, or the random number generator has to be designed specifically to trigger this case.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-463)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
use rug::{Assign, Float};
let mut rand = RandState::new();
let mut f = Float::new(2);
f.assign(Float::random_bits(&mut rand));
assert!(f == 0.0 || f == 0.25 || f == 0.5 || f == 0.75);
println!("0.0 ≤ {} < 1.0", f);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/float/big.rs.html#11750-11752)#### pub fn [random_cont](https://docs.rs#method.random_cont)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomContIncomplete<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/float/big.rs.html#11750-11752)

#### pub fn [random_cont](https://docs.rs#method.random_cont)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomContIncomplete<'_>

Generates a random number in the continuous range
0 ≤ *x* < 1.

The result can be rounded up to be equal to one. Unlike the
[ random_bits](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html#method.random_bits) method which generates a discrete
random number at intervals depending on the precision, this method is
equivalent to generating a continuous random number with infinite
precision and then rounding the result. This means that even the smaller
numbers will be using all the available precision bits, and rounding is
performed in all cases, not in some corner case.

Rounding directions for generated random numbers cannot be
[Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)::[Equal](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Equal)

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-464)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
use rug::Float;
let mut rand = RandState::new();
let f = Float::with_val(2, Float::random_cont(&mut rand));
// The significand is either 0b10 or 0b11
assert!(
    f == 1.0
        || f == 0.75
        || f == 0.5
        || f == 0.375
        || f == 0.25
        || f <= 0.1875
);
```

# Complex in rug - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/struct.Complex.html

`pub struct Complex { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A multi-precision complex number with arbitrarily large precision and correct rounding.

The precision has to be set during construction. The rounding method of the required operations can be specified, and the direction of the rounding is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use rug::{Assign, Complex, Float};
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (40, 30));
assert_eq!(format!("{:.3}", c), "(40.0 30.0)");
let mut f = Float::with_val(53, c.abs_ref());
assert_eq!(f, 50);
f.assign(c.arg_ref());
assert_eq!(f, 0.75_f64.atan());
```
Operations on two borrowed `Complex` numbers result in an
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) that has to be assigned to a new `Complex`
number.

```
use rug::Complex;
let a = Complex::with_val(53, (10.5, -11));
let b = Complex::with_val(53, (-1.25, -1.5));
let a_b_ref = &a + &b;
let a_b = Complex::with_val(53, a_b_ref);
assert_eq!(a_b, (9.25, -12.5));
```
As a special case, when an [incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) is obtained from
multiplying two `Complex` number references, it can be added to or subtracted
from another `Complex` number (or reference). This will result in a fused
multiply-accumulate operation, with only one rounding operation taking place.

```
use rug::Complex;
let mut acc = Complex::with_val(53, (1000, 1000));
let m1 = Complex::with_val(53, (10, 0));
let m2 = Complex::with_val(53, (1, -1));
// (1000 + 1000i) - (10 + 0i) × (1 - i) = (990 + 1010i)
acc -= &m1 * &m2;
assert_eq!(acc, (990, 1010));
```
The `Complex` number type supports various functions. Most methods have four
versions:

- The first method consumes the operand and rounds the returned `Complex`number to the[nearest](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html#variant.Nearest)representable value.
- The second method has a “`_mut`” suffix, mutates the operand and rounds it the nearest representable value.
- The third method has a “`_round`” suffix, mutates the operand, applies the specified[rounding method](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html)to the real and imaginary parts, and returns the rounding direction for both:
- The fourth method has a “`_ref`” suffix and borrows the operand. The returned item is an[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)that can be assigned to a`Complex`number; the rounding method is selected during the assignment.

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Complex;
let expected = Complex::with_val(53, (1.2985, 0.6350));
// 1. consume the operand, round to nearest
let a = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
let sin_a = a.sin();
assert!(*(sin_a - &expected).abs().real() < 0.0001);
// 2. mutate the operand, round to nearest
let mut b = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
b.sin_mut();
assert!(*(b - &expected).abs().real() < 0.0001);
// 3. mutate the operand, apply specified rounding
let mut c = Complex::with_val(4, (1, 1));
// using 4 significant bits, 1.2985 is rounded down to 1.25
// and 0.6350 is rounded down to 0.625.
let dir = c.sin_round((Round::Nearest, Round::Nearest));
assert_eq!(c, (1.25, 0.625));
assert_eq!(dir, (Ordering::Less, Ordering::Less));
// 4. borrow the operand
let d = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
let r = d.sin_ref();
let sin_d = Complex::with_val(53, r);
assert!(*(sin_d - &expected).abs().real() < 0.0001);
// d was not consumed
assert_eq!(d, (1, 1));
```

Creates a [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number from an initialized

[MPC complex number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpc/struct.mpc_t.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The function must *not*be used to create a constant`Complex``Complex`*copied*on use, leading to undefined behavior when they are dropped.
- The value must be initialized as a valid `mpc_t`
- The `mpc_t`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpc;
use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use rug::Complex;
let c = unsafe {
    let mut m = MaybeUninit::uninit();
    mpc::init3(m.as_mut_ptr(), 53, 53);
    let mut m = m.assume_init();
    mpc::set_d_d(&mut m, -14.5, 3.25, mpc::RNDNN);
    // m is initialized and unique
    Complex::from_raw(m)
};
assert_eq!(c, (-14.5, 3.25));
// since c is a Complex now, deallocation is automatic
```
This can be used to create a static [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number. See

[,](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpc/struct.mpc_t.html)

`mpc_t`[and the](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpfr/struct.mpfr_t.html)

`mpfr_t`[MPFR documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/C/MPFR/constant.MPFR_Interface.html#Internals)for details.

```
use core::ptr::NonNull;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp::limb_t;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr::{mpfr_t, prec_t};
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpc::mpc_t;
use rug::{Complex, Float};
const LIMBS: [limb_t; 2] = [5, 1 << (limb_t::BITS - 1)];
const LIMBS_PTR: *const [limb_t; 2] = &LIMBS;
const MANTISSA_DIGITS: u32 = limb_t::BITS * 2;
const MPC: mpc_t = mpc_t {
    re: mpfr_t {
        prec: MANTISSA_DIGITS as prec_t,
        sign: -1,
        exp: 1,
        d: unsafe { NonNull::new_unchecked(LIMBS_PTR.cast_mut().cast()) },
    },
    im: mpfr_t {
        prec: MANTISSA_DIGITS as prec_t,
        sign: 1,
        exp: 1,
        d: unsafe { NonNull::new_unchecked(LIMBS_PTR.cast_mut().cast()) },
    },
};
// Must *not* be const, otherwise it would lead to undefined
// behavior on use, as it would create a copy that is dropped.
static C: Complex = unsafe { Complex::from_raw(MPC) };
let lsig = Float::with_val(MANTISSA_DIGITS, 5) >> (MANTISSA_DIGITS - 1);
let msig = 1u32;
let val = lsig + msig;
let check = Complex::from((-val.clone(), val));
assert_eq!(C, check);
```
Converts a [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number into an

[MPC complex number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpc/struct.mpc_t.html).

The returned object should be freed to avoid memory leaks.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpc;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr::rnd_t;
use rug::Complex;
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (-14.5, 3.25));
let mut m = c.into_raw();
unsafe {
    let re_ptr = mpc::realref_const(&m);
    let re = mpfr::get_d(re_ptr, rnd_t::RNDN);
    assert_eq!(re, -14.5);
    let im_ptr = mpc::imagref_const(&m);
    let im = mpfr::get_d(im_ptr, rnd_t::RNDN);
    assert_eq!(im, 3.25);
    // free object to prevent memory leak
    mpc::clear(&mut m);
}
```
Returns a pointer to the inner [MPC complex number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpc/struct.mpc_t.html).

The returned pointer will be valid for as long as `self` is valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpc;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr::rnd_t;
use rug::Complex;
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (-14.5, 3.25));
let m_ptr = c.as_raw();
unsafe {
    let re_ptr = mpc::realref_const(m_ptr);
    let re = mpfr::get_d(re_ptr, rnd_t::RNDN);
    assert_eq!(re, -14.5);
    let im_ptr = mpc::imagref_const(m_ptr);
    let im = mpfr::get_d(im_ptr, rnd_t::RNDN);
    assert_eq!(im, 3.25);
}
// c is still valid
assert_eq!(c, (-14.5, 3.25));
```

Parses a decimal string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number.

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

The string can contain either of the following three:

- One floating-point number that can be parsed by
[Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html#method.parse)
- Two floating-point numbers inside round brackets separated by one comma. ASCII whitespace is treated in the same way as 1 above, and is also allowed around the brackets and the comma.
- Two floating-point numbers inside round brackets separated by ASCII whitespace. Since the real and imaginary parts are separated by whitespace, they themselves cannot contain whitespace. ASCII whitespace is still allowed around the brackets and between the two parts.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let valid1 = Complex::parse("(12.5, -13.5)");
let c1 = Complex::with_val(53, valid1.unwrap());
assert_eq!(c1, (12.5, -13.5));
let valid2 = Complex::parse("(inf 0.0)");
let c2 = Complex::with_val(53, valid2.unwrap());
assert_eq!(c2, (f64::INFINITY, 0.0));
let invalid = Complex::parse("(1 2 3)");
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```

Parses a string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number.

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

The string can contain either of the following three:

- One floating-point number that can be parsed by
[Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)::[parse_radix](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html#method.parse_radix)
- Two floating-point numbers inside round brackets separated by one comma. ASCII whitespace is treated in the same way as 1 above, and is also allowed around the brackets and the comma.
- Two floating-point numbers inside round brackets separated by ASCII whitespace. Since the real and imaginary parts are separated by whitespace, they themselves cannot contain whitespace. ASCII whitespace is still allowed around the brackets and between the two parts.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-10)Panics

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let valid1 = Complex::parse_radix("(12, 1a)", 16);
let c1 = Complex::with_val(53, valid1.unwrap());
assert_eq!(c1, (0x12, 0x1a));
let valid2 = Complex::parse_radix("(@inf@ zz)", 36);
let c2 = Complex::with_val(53, valid2.unwrap());
assert_eq!(c2, (f64::INFINITY, 35 * 36 + 35));
let invalid = Complex::parse_radix("(1 2 3)", 10);
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```

let c = Complex::with_val(200, (val.clone(), val));
let nc = c.to_c128_round((Round::Up, Round::Down));
assert_eq!(nc.re, 1.0 + f128::EPSILON);
assert_eq!(nc.im, 1.0);
```
Returns a string representation of the value for the specified `radix`
rounding to the nearest.

The exponent is encoded in decimal. If the number of digits is not specified, the output string will have enough precision such that reading it again will give the exact same number.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-11)Panics

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-27)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let c1 = Complex::with_val(53, 0);
assert_eq!(c1.to_string_radix(10, None), "(0 0)");
let c2 = Complex::with_val(12, (15, 5));
assert_eq!(c2.to_string_radix(16, None), "(f.000 5.000)");
let c3 = Complex::with_val(53, (10, -4));
assert_eq!(c3.to_string_radix(10, Some(3)), "(10.0 -4.00)");
assert_eq!(c3.to_string_radix(5, Some(3)), "(20.0 -4.00)");
// 2 raised to the power of 80 in hex is 1 followed by 20 zeros
let c4 = Complex::with_val(53, (80f64.exp2(), 0.25));
assert_eq!(c4.to_string_radix(10, Some(3)), "(1.21e24 2.50e-1)");
assert_eq!(c4.to_string_radix(16, Some(3)), "(1.00@20 4.00@-1)");
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#1074-1092)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#1074-1092)

Returns a string representation of the value for the specified `radix`
applying the specified rounding method.

The exponent is encoded in decimal. If the number of digits is not specified, the output string will have enough precision such that reading it again will give the exact same number.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-12)Panics

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-28)Examples

```
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Complex;
let c = Complex::with_val(10, 10.4);
let down = (Round::Down, Round::Down);
let nearest = (Round::Nearest, Round::Nearest);
let up = (Round::Up, Round::Up);
let nd = c.to_string_radix_round(10, None, down);
assert_eq!(nd, "(10.406 0)");
let nu = c.to_string_radix_round(10, None, up);
assert_eq!(nu, "(10.407 0)");
let sd = c.to_string_radix_round(10, Some(2), down);
assert_eq!(sd, "(10 0)");
let sn = c.to_string_radix_round(10, Some(2), nearest);
assert_eq!(sn, "(10 0)");
let su = c.to_string_radix_round(10, Some(2), up);
assert_eq!(su, "(11 0)");
```

Borrows a negated copy of the [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number.

The returned object implements [Deref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html)<[Target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html#associatedtype.Target) = [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)>

This method performs a shallow copy and negates it, and negation does not change the allocated data.

Unlike the other negation methods (the `-` operator,
[Neg](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Neg.html)::[neg](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Neg.html#tymethod.neg)[MPFR NaN flag](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpfr/fn.set_nanflag.html) if a NaN is encountered.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-36)Examples

```

assert_eq!(*neg_c, (-4.2, 2.3));
// methods taking &self can be used on the returned object
let reneg_c = neg_c.as_neg();
assert_eq!(*reneg_c, (4.2, -2.3));
assert_eq!(*reneg_c, c);
```

, rounding towards zero.

Compares the absolute values of `self` and `other`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-43)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::Complex;
let five = Complex::with_val(53, (5, 0));
let five_rotated = Complex::with_val(53, (3, -4));
let greater_than_five = Complex::with_val(53, (-4, -4));
let has_nan = Complex::with_val(53, (5, 0.0 / 0.0));
assert_eq!(five.cmp_abs(&five_rotated), Some(Ordering::Equal));
assert_eq!(five.cmp_abs(&greater_than_five), Some(Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(five.cmp_abs(&has_nan), None);
```
Returns the total ordering between `self` and `other`.

For ordering, the real part has precedence over the imaginary part. Negative zero is ordered as less than positive zero. Negative NaN is ordered as less than negative infinity, while positive NaN is ordered as greater than positive infinity. Comparing two negative NaNs or two positive NaNs produces equality.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-44)Examples

```
use rug::float::Special;
use rug::Complex;
let mut values = vec![
    Complex::with_val(53, (Special::Zero, Special::Zero)),
    Complex::with_val(53, (Special::Zero, Special::NegZero)),
    Complex::with_val(53, (Special::NegZero, Special::Infinity)),
];
values.sort_by(Complex::total_cmp);
// (-0, +∞)
assert!(values[0].real().is_zero() && values[0].real().is_sign_negative());
assert!(values[0].imag().is_infinite() && values[0].imag().is_sign_positive());
// (+0, -0)
assert!(values[1].real().is_zero() && values[1].real().is_sign_positive());
assert!(values[1].imag().is_zero() && values[1].imag().is_sign_negative());
// (+0, +0)
assert!(values[2].real().is_zero() && values[2].real().is_sign_positive());
assert!(values[2].imag().is_zero() && values[2].imag().is_sign_positive());
```
Adds a list of [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) numbers with correct rounding.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AddAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.AddAssign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AddAssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AddAssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [Add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Add.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [Add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Add.html)<- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src
- [SubAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.SubAssign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [SubFrom](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubFrom.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [SubAssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubAssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [SubFromRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubFromRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [Sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Sub.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [Sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Sub.html)<- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-45)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
// Give each value only 4 bits of precision for example purposes.
let values = [
    Complex::with_val(4, (5.0, 1024.0)),
    Complex::with_val(4, (1024.0, 15.0)),
    Complex::with_val(4, (-1024.0, -1024.0)),
    Complex::with_val(4, (-4.5, -16.0)),
];
// The result should still be exact if it fits.
let r1 = Complex::sum(values.iter());
let sum1 = Complex::with_val(4, r1);
assert_eq!(sum1, (0.5, -1.0));
let r2 = Complex::sum(values.iter());
let sum2 = Complex::with_val(4, (1.0, -1.0)) + r2;
assert_eq!(sum2, (1.5, -2.0));
let r3 = Complex::sum(values.iter());
let mut sum3 = Complex::with_val(4, (16, 16));
sum3 += r3;
// (16.5, 15) rounded to (16, 15)
assert_eq!(sum3, (16, 15));
```
Finds the dot product of a list of [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) numbers pairs with
correct rounding.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AddAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.AddAssign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AddAssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AddAssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [Add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Add.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [Add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Add.html)<- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src
- [SubAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.SubAssign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [SubFrom](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubFrom.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [SubAssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubAssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [SubFromRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubFromRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [Sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Sub.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [Sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Sub.html)<- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

This method will produce a result with correct rounding, except for some cases where underflow and/or overflow occur in intermediate products.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-46)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let a = [
    Complex::with_val(53, (5.0, 10.25)),
    Complex::with_val(53, (10.25, 5.0)),
];
let b = [
    Complex::with_val(53, (-2.75, -11.5)),
    Complex::with_val(53, (-4.5, 16.0)),
];
let r = Complex::dot(a.iter().zip(b.iter()));
let dot = Complex::with_val(53, r);
let expected = Complex::with_val(53, &a[0] * &b[0]) + &a[1] * &b[1];
assert_eq!(dot, expected);
let r = Complex::dot(a.iter().zip(b.iter()));
let add_dot = Complex::with_val(53, (1.0, 2.0)) + r;
let add_expected = Complex::with_val(53, (1.0, 2.0)) + &expected;
assert_eq!(add_dot, add_expected);
let r = Complex::dot(a.iter().zip(b.iter()));
let mut add_dot2 = Complex::with_val(53, (1.0, 2.0));
add_dot2 += r;
assert_eq!(add_dot2, add_expected);
```
Multiplies and adds in one fused operation, rounding to the nearest with only one rounding error.

`a.mul_add(&b, &c)` produces a result like `&a * &b + &c`, but `a` is
consumed and the result produced uses its precision.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-47)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let a = Complex::with_val(53, (10, 0));
let b = Complex::with_val(53, (1, -1));
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (1000, 1000));
// (10 + 0i) × (1 - i) + (1000 + 1000i) = (1010 + 990i)
let mul_add = a.mul_add(&b, &c);
assert_eq!(mul_add, (1010, 990));
```

`ans`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-49)Examples

```

Computes a projection onto the Riemann sphere, rounding to the nearest.

If no parts of the number are infinite, the result is unchanged. If any part is infinite, the real part of the result is set to +∞ and the imaginary part of the result is set to 0 with the same sign as the imaginary part of the input.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-55)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let c1 = Complex::with_val(53, (1.5, 2.5));
let proj1 = c1.proj();
assert_eq!(proj1, (1.5, 2.5));
let c2 = Complex::with_val(53, (f64::NAN, f64::NEG_INFINITY));
let proj2 = c2.proj();
assert_eq!(proj2, (f64::INFINITY, 0.0));
// imaginary was negative, so now it is minus zero
assert!(proj2.imag().is_sign_negative());
```

use rug::Complex;

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#2932-2934)#### pub fn [root_of_unity](https://docs.rs#method.root_of_unity)(n: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html), k: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> RootOfUnityIncomplete

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#2932-2934)

#### pub fn [root_of_unity](https://docs.rs#method.root_of_unity)(n: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html), k: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> RootOfUnityIncomplete

Generates a root of unity, rounding to the nearest.

The generated number is the *n*th root of unity raised to the power
*k*, that is its magnitude is 1 and its argument is
2π*k*/*n*.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-101)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let r = Complex::root_of_unity(3, 2);
let c = Complex::with_val(53, r);
let expected = Complex::with_val(53, (-0.5, -0.8660));
assert!(*(c - expected).abs().real() < 0.0001);
```

Computes the sine and cosine of `self`, rounding to the nearest.

The sine keeps the precision of `self` while the cosine keeps the
precision of `cos`.

The initial value of `cos` is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-122)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
let (sin, cos) = c.sin_cos(Complex::new(53));
let expected_sin = Complex::with_val(53, (1.2985, 0.6350));
let expected_cos = Complex::with_val(53, (0.8337, -0.9889));
assert!(*(sin - expected_sin).abs().real() < 0.0001);
assert!(*(cos - expected_cos).abs().real() < 0.0001);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#3375-3377)#### pub fn [sin_cos_mut](https://docs.rs#method.sin_cos_mut)(&mut self, cos: &mut Self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#3375-3377)

#### pub fn [sin_cos_mut](https://docs.rs#method.sin_cos_mut)(&mut self, cos: &mut Self)

Computes the sine and cosine of `self`, rounding to the nearest.

The sine is stored in `self` and keeps its precision, while the cosine
is stored in `cos` keeping its precision.

The initial value of `cos` is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-123)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let mut sin = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
let mut cos = Complex::new(53);
sin.sin_cos_mut(&mut cos);
let expected_sin = Complex::with_val(53, (1.2985, 0.6350));
let expected_cos = Complex::with_val(53, (0.8337, -0.9889));
assert!(*(sin - expected_sin).abs().real() < 0.0001);
assert!(*(cos - expected_cos).abs().real() < 0.0001);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#3408-3410)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#3408-3410)

Computes the sine and cosine of `self`, applying the specified rounding
methods.

The sine is stored in `self` and keeps its precision, while the cosine
is stored in `cos` keeping its precision.

The initial value of `cos` is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-124)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Complex;
// Use only 4 bits of precision to show rounding.
let mut sin = Complex::with_val(4, (1, 1));
let mut cos = Complex::new(4);
// sin(1 + i) = (1.2985 + 0.6350)
// using 4 significant bits: (1.25 + 0.625i)
// cos(1 + i) = (0.8337 - 0.9889i)
// using 4 significant bits: (0.8125 - i)
let (dir_sin, dir_cos) =
    sin.sin_cos_round(&mut cos, (Round::Nearest, Round::Nearest));
assert_eq!(sin, (1.25, 0.625));
assert_eq!(dir_sin, (Ordering::Less, Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(cos, (0.8125, -1));
assert_eq!(dir_cos, (Ordering::Less, Ordering::Less));
```

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)&mut- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html), &mut- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html),- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)&mut- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html), &mut- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html),- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-125)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::ops::AssignRound;
use rug::{Assign, Complex};
let phase = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
let (mut sin, mut cos) = (Complex::new(53), Complex::new(53));
let sin_cos = phase.sin_cos_ref();
(&mut sin, &mut cos).assign(sin_cos);
let expected_sin = Complex::with_val(53, (1.2985, 0.6350));
let expected_cos = Complex::with_val(53, (0.8337, -0.9889));
assert!(*(sin - expected_sin).abs().real() < 0.0001);
assert!(*(cos - expected_cos).abs().real() < 0.0001);
// using 4 significant bits: sin = (1.25 + 0.625i)
// using 4 significant bits: cos = (0.8125 - i)
let (mut sin_4, mut cos_4) = (Complex::new(4), Complex::new(4));
let sin_cos = phase.sin_cos_ref();
let (dir_sin, dir_cos) = (&mut sin_4, &mut cos_4)
    .assign_round(sin_cos, (Round::Nearest, Round::Nearest));
assert_eq!(sin_4, (1.25, 0.625));
assert_eq!(dir_sin, (Ordering::Less, Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(cos_4, (0.8125, -1));
assert_eq!(dir_cos, (Ordering::Less, Ordering::Less));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#4381-4383)#### pub fn [random_bits](https://docs.rs#method.random_bits)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomBitsIncomplete<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#4381-4383)

#### pub fn [random_bits](https://docs.rs#method.random_bits)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomBitsIncomplete<'_>

Generates a random complex number with both the real and imaginary parts
in the range 0 ≤ *x* < 1.

This is equivalent to generating a random integer in the range
0 ≤ *x* < 2 p for each part,
where 2

is two raised to the power of the precision, and then dividing the integer by 2

*p*. The smallest non-zero result will thus be 2

*p*−, and will only have one bit set. In the smaller possible results, many bits will be zero, and not all the precision will be used.

*p*There is a corner case where the generated random number part is converted to NaN: if the precision is very large, the generated random number could have an exponent less than the allowed minimum exponent, and NaN is used to indicate this. For this to occur in practice, the minimum exponent has to be set to have a very small magnitude using the low-level MPFR interface, or the random number generator has to be designed specifically to trigger this case.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-170)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
use rug::{Assign, Complex};
let mut rand = RandState::new();
let mut c = Complex::new(2);
c.assign(Complex::random_bits(&mut rand));
let (re, im) = c.into_real_imag();
assert!(re == 0.0 || re == 0.25 || re == 0.5 || re == 0.75);
assert!(im == 0.0 || im == 0.25 || im == 0.5 || im == 0.75);
println!("0.0 ≤ {} < 1.0", re);
println!("0.0 ≤ {} < 1.0", im);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#4437-4439)#### pub fn [random_cont](https://docs.rs#method.random_cont)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomContIncomplete<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#4437-4439)

#### pub fn [random_cont](https://docs.rs#method.random_cont)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomContIncomplete<'_>

Generates a random complex number with both the real and imaginary parts
in the continous range 0 ≤ *x* < 1, and rounds
to the nearest.

The result parts can be rounded up to be equal to one. Unlike the
[ random_bits](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html#method.random_bits) method which generates a discrete
random number at intervals depending on the precision, this method is
equivalent to generating a continuous random number with infinite
precision and then rounding the result. This means that even the smaller
numbers will be using all the available precision bits, and rounding is
performed in all cases, not in some corner case.

Rounding directions for generated random numbers cannot be
[Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)::[Equal](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Equal)

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-171)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
use rug::Complex;
let mut rand = RandState::new();
let c = Complex::with_val(2, Complex::random_cont(&mut rand));
let (re, im) = c.into_real_imag();
// The significand is either 0b10 or 0b11
assert!(
    re == 1.0
        || re == 0.75
        || re == 0.5
        || re == 0.375
        || re == 0.25
        || re <= 0.1875
);
assert!(
    im == 1.0
        || im == 0.75
        || im == 0.5
        || im == 0.375
        || im == 0.25
        || im <= 0.1875
);
```

# MiniInteger in rug::integer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/integer/struct.MiniInteger.html

`pub struct MiniInteger { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A small integer that does not require any memory allocation.

This can be useful when you have a primitive integer type such as [ u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html) or

[, but need a reference to an](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i8.html)

`i8`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)

`Integer`If there are functions that take a [ u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html) or

[directly instead of an](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)

`i32`[reference, using them can still be faster than using a](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)

`Integer``MiniInteger`; the functions would still need to check for the size of an
[obtained using](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)

`Integer``MiniInteger`.The [ borrow](https://docs.rs/struct.MiniInteger.html#method.borrow) method returns an object that can be coerced to an

[, as it implements](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)

`Integer`[Deref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html)<[Target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html#associatedtype.Target) = [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)>[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use rug::integer::MiniInteger;
use rug::Integer;
// `a` requires a heap allocation
let mut a = Integer::from(250);
// `b` can reside on the stack
let b = MiniInteger::from(-100);
a.lcm_mut(&b.borrow());
assert_eq!(a, 500);
// another computation:
a.lcm_mut(&MiniInteger::from(30).borrow());
assert_eq!(a, 1500);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/mini.rs.html#169-179)#### pub const fn [const_from_bool](https://docs.rs#method.const_from_bool)(val: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/mini.rs.html#169-179)

#### pub const fn [const_from_bool](https://docs.rs#method.const_from_bool)(val: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

Creates a [ MiniInteger](https://docs.rs/struct.MiniInteger.html) from a

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`bool`This is equivalent to `MiniInteger::from(val)`, but can also be used in
constant context. Unless required in constant context, use the [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)
trait instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#planned-deprecation)Planned deprecation

This method will be deprecated when the [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html) trait is usable in
constant context.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use rug::integer::{BorrowInteger, MiniInteger};
use rug::Integer;
const ONE_MINI: MiniInteger = MiniInteger::const_from_bool(true);
const ONE_BORROW: BorrowInteger = ONE_MINI.borrow();
const ONE: &Integer = BorrowInteger::const_deref(&ONE_BORROW);

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/mini.rs.html#629-635)#### pub unsafe fn [as_nonreallocating_integer](https://docs.rs#method.as_nonreallocating_integer)(&mut self) -> &mut [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/mini.rs.html#629-635)

#### pub unsafe fn [as_nonreallocating_integer](https://docs.rs#method.as_nonreallocating_integer)(&mut self) -> &mut [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)

Returns a mutable reference to an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) for simple operations that
do not need to allocate more space for the number.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

It is undefined behavior to perform operations that reallocate the
internal data of the referenced [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) or to swap it with another
number.

Some GMP functions swap the allocations of their target operands; calling such functions with the mutable reference returned by this method can lead to undefined behavior.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use rug::integer::MiniInteger;
use rug::Assign;
let mut i = MiniInteger::from(1u64);
let capacity = i.borrow().capacity();
// another u64 will not require a reallocation
unsafe {
    i.as_nonreallocating_integer().assign(2u64);
}
assert_eq!(*i.borrow(), 2);
assert_eq!(i.borrow().capacity(), capacity);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/mini.rs.html#656-668)#### pub const fn [borrow](https://docs.rs#method.borrow)(&self) -> [BorrowInteger](https://docs.rs/struct.BorrowInteger.html)<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/mini.rs.html#656-668)

#### pub const fn [borrow](https://docs.rs#method.borrow)(&self) -> [BorrowInteger](https://docs.rs/struct.BorrowInteger.html)<'_>

Borrows the integer.

The returned object implements
[Deref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html)<[Target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html#associatedtype.Target) = [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)>

The borrow lasts until the returned object exits scope. Multiple borrows can be taken at the same time.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
use rug::integer::MiniInteger;
use rug::Integer;
let i = MiniInteger::from(-13i32);
let b = i.borrow();
let abs_ref = b.abs_ref();
assert_eq!(Integer::from(abs_ref), 13);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/mini.rs.html#689-692)#### pub fn [borrow_excl](https://docs.rs#method.borrow_excl)(&mut self) -> &[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/integer/mini.rs.html#689-692)

#### pub fn [borrow_excl](https://docs.rs#method.borrow_excl)(&mut self) -> &[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)

Borrows the integer exclusively.

This is similar to the [ borrow](https://docs.rs/struct.MiniInteger.html#method.borrow) method, but it requires
exclusive access to the underlying

[; the returned reference can however be shared. The exclusive access is required to reduce the amount of housekeeping necessary, providing a more efficient operation.](https://docs.rs/struct.MiniInteger.html)

`MiniInteger`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```
use rug::integer::MiniInteger;
use rug::Integer;
let mut i = MiniInteger::from(-13i32);
let b = i.borrow_excl();
let abs_ref = b.abs_ref();
assert_eq!(Integer::from(abs_ref), 13);
```

# MiniRational in rug::rational - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/rational/struct.MiniRational.html

`pub struct MiniRational { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A small rational number that does not require any memory allocation.

This can be useful when you have a numerator and denominator that are primitive
integer-types such as [ i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html) or

[, and you need a reference to a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)

`u8`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html)

`Rational`Although no allocation is required, setting the value of a `MiniRational` does
require some computation, as the numerator and denominator need to be
canonicalized.

The [ borrow](https://docs.rs/struct.MiniRational.html#method.borrow) method returns an object that can be coerced to a

[, as it implements](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html)

`Rational`[Deref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html)<[Target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html#associatedtype.Target) = [Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html)>[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
use rug::Rational;
// `a` requires a heap allocation
let mut a = Rational::from((100, 13));
// `b` can reside on the stack
let b = MiniRational::from((-100, 21));
a /= &*b.borrow();
assert_eq!(*a.numer(), -21);
assert_eq!(*a.denom(), 13);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rational/mini.rs.html#300-315)#### pub unsafe fn [as_nonreallocating_rational](https://docs.rs#method.as_nonreallocating_rational)(&mut self) -> &mut [Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rational/mini.rs.html#300-315)

#### pub unsafe fn [as_nonreallocating_rational](https://docs.rs#method.as_nonreallocating_rational)(&mut self) -> &mut [Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html)

Returns a mutable reference to a [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) number for simple
operations that do not need to allocate more space for the numerator or
denominator.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

It is undefined behavior to perform operations that reallocate the
internal data of the referenced [ Rational](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html) number or to swap it with
another number, although it is allowed to swap the numerator and
denominator allocations, such as in the reciprocal operation

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Rational.html#method.recip_mut)

`recip_mut`Some GMP functions swap the allocations of their target operands; calling such functions with the mutable reference returned by this method can lead to undefined behavior.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use rug::rational::MiniRational;
let mut r = MiniRational::from((-15i32, 47i32));
let (num_capacity, den_capacity) = {
    let b = r.borrow();
    (b.numer().capacity(), b.denom().capacity())
};
// reciprocating this will not require reallocations
unsafe {
    r.as_nonreallocating_rational().recip_mut();
}
let after = r.borrow();
assert_eq!(*after, MiniRational::from((-47, 15)));
assert_eq!(after.numer().capacity(), num_capacity);
assert_eq!(after.denom().capacity(), den_capacity);
```

The returned object implements

# MiniFloat in rug::float - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/float/struct.MiniFloat.html

`pub struct MiniFloat { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A small float that does not require any memory allocation.

This can be useful when you have a primitive number type but need a reference to
a [ Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html). The

`MiniFloat` will have a precision according to the type of the
primitive used to set its value.- `bool`- `MiniFloat`will have the- [minimum possible precision](https://docs.rs/fn.prec_min.html).
- `i8`- `u8`- `MiniFloat`will have eight bits of precision.
- `i16`- `u16`- `MiniFloat`will have 16 bits of precision.
- `i32`- `u32`- `MiniFloat`will have 32 bits of precision.
- `i64`- `u64`- `MiniFloat`will have 64 bits of precision.
- `i128`- `u128`- `MiniFloat`will have 128 bits of precision.
- `isize`- `usize`- `MiniFloat`will have 32 or 64 bits of precision, depending on the platform.
- `f32`- `MiniFloat`will have 24 bits of precision.
- `f64`- `MiniFloat`will have 53 bits of precision.
- `Special`- `MiniFloat`will have the- [minimum possible precision](https://docs.rs/fn.prec_min.html).

The [ borrow](https://docs.rs/struct.MiniFloat.html#method.borrow) method returns an object that can be coerced to a

[, as it implements](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)

`Float`[Deref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html)<[Target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html#associatedtype.Target) = [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)>[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use rug::float::MiniFloat;
use rug::Float;
// `a` requires a heap allocation, has 53-bit precision
let mut a = Float::with_val(53, 250);
// `b` can reside on the stack
let b = MiniFloat::from(-100f64);
a += &*b.borrow();
assert_eq!(a, 150);
// another computation:
a *= &*b.borrow();
assert_eq!(a, -15000);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/float/mini.rs.html#867-873)#### pub unsafe fn [as_nonreallocating_float](https://docs.rs#method.as_nonreallocating_float)(&mut self) -> &mut [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/float/mini.rs.html#867-873)

#### pub unsafe fn [as_nonreallocating_float](https://docs.rs#method.as_nonreallocating_float)(&mut self) -> &mut [Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)

Returns a mutable reference to a [ Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html) for simple operations that do
not need to change the precision of the number.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

It is undefined behavior modify the precision of the referenced

# MiniComplex in rug::complex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/complex/struct.MiniComplex.html

`pub struct MiniComplex { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A small complex number that does not require any memory allocation.

This can be useful when you have real and imaginary numbers that are primitive
integers or floats and you need a reference to a [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html).

The `MiniComplex` will have a precision according to the types of the
primitives used to set its real and imaginary parts. Note that if different
types are used to set the parts, the parts can have different precisions.

- `bool`- [minimum possible precision](https://docs.rs/float/fn.prec_min.html).
- `i8`- `u8`
- `i16`- `u16`
- `i32`- `u32`
- `i64`- `u64`
- `i128`- `u128`
- `isize`- `usize`
- `f32`
- `f64`
- `Special`- [minimum possible precision](https://docs.rs/float/fn.prec_min.html).

The [ borrow](https://docs.rs/struct.MiniComplex.html#method.borrow) method returns an object that can be coerced to a

[, as it implements](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)

`Complex`[Deref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html)<[Target](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html#associatedtype.Target) = [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)>[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use rug::complex::MiniComplex;
use rug::Complex;
// `a` requires a heap allocation
let mut a = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 2));
// `b` can reside on the stack
let b = MiniComplex::from((-10f64, -20.5f64));
a += &*b.borrow();
assert_eq!(*a.real(), -9);
assert_eq!(*a.imag(), -18.5);
```

#### pub const fn [const_from_real](https://docs.rs#method.const_from_real)(real: [MiniFloat](https://docs.rs/float/struct.MiniFloat.html)) -> Self

Creates a [ MiniComplex](https://docs.rs/struct.MiniComplex.html) from a

[real part.](https://docs.rs/float/struct.MiniFloat.html)

`MiniFloat`This is equivalent to `MiniComplex::from(real)`, but can also be used in
constant context. Unless required in constant context, use the [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)
trait instead.

The precision of the imaginary part is set to the precision of the real part.

[§](https://docs.rs#planned-deprecation)Planned deprecation

This method will be deprecated when the [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html) trait is usable in
constant context.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use rug::complex::{BorrowComplex, MiniComplex};
use rug::float::MiniFloat;
use rug::Complex;
const TWO_FLOAT: MiniFloat = MiniFloat::const_from_i8(2i8);
const TWO_MINI: MiniComplex = MiniComplex::const_from_real(TWO_FLOAT);
const TWO_BORROW: BorrowComplex = TWO_MINI.borrow();
const TWO: &Complex = BorrowComplex::const_deref(&TWO_BORROW);
assert_eq!(*TWO, 2);
assert_eq!(TWO.prec(), (i8::BITS, i8::BITS));
```

# az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/az/~1.3/az/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#numeric-casts)Numeric casts

This crate provides casts and checked casts.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-examples)Quick examples

```
use az::{Az, OverflowingAs, WrappingAs};
use core::num::Wrapping;
// Panics on overflow with `debug_assertions`, otherwise wraps
assert_eq!(12i32.az::<u32>(), 12u32);
// Always wraps
let wrapped = 1u32.wrapping_neg();
assert_eq!((-1).wrapping_as::<u32>(), wrapped);
assert_eq!((-1).overflowing_as::<u32>(), (wrapped, true));
// Wrapping can also be obtained using `Wrapping`
assert_eq!((-1).az::<Wrapping<u32>>().0, wrapped);
```
Conversions from floating-point to integers are also supported.
Numbers are rounded towards zero, but the [ Round](https://docs.rs/struct.Round.html) wrapper can be
used to convert floating-point numbers to integers with rounding to
the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

```
use az::{Az, CheckedAs, Round, SaturatingAs};
assert_eq!(15.7.az::<i32>(), 15);
assert_eq!(Round(15.5).az::<i32>(), 16);
assert_eq!(1.5e20.saturating_as::<i32>(), i32::max_value());
assert_eq!(f32::NAN.checked_as::<i32>(), None);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-casts-for-other-types)Implementing casts for other types

To provide casts for another type, you should implement the [ Cast](https://docs.rs/trait.Cast.html) trait and
if necessary the

[,](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedCast.html)

`CheckedCast`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.StrictCast.html)

`StrictCast`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.SaturatingCast.html)

`SaturatingCast`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.WrappingCast.html)

`WrappingCast`[traits. The](https://docs.rs/trait.OverflowingCast.html)

`OverflowingCast`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.Az.html)

`Az`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedAs.html)

`CheckedAs`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.StrictAs.html)

`StrictAs`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.SaturatingAs.html)

`SaturatingAs`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.WrappingAs.html)

`WrappingAs`[traits are already implemented for all types using blanket implementations that make use of the former traits.](https://docs.rs/trait.OverflowingAs.html)

`OverflowingAs`The cast traits can also be implemented for references. This can be
useful for expensive types that are not [ Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html). For example if you
have your own integer type that does not implement

[, you could implement casts like in the following example. (The type](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html)

`Copy``I` could be
an expensive type, for example a bignum integer, but for the example
it is only a wrapped [.)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.i32.html)

`i32````
use az::{Az, Cast};
use core::borrow::Borrow;
struct I(i32);
impl Cast<i64> for &'_ I {
    fn cast(self) -> i64 { self.0.cast() }
}
let owned = I(12);
assert_eq!((&owned).az::<i64>(), 12);
// borrow can be used if chaining is required
assert_eq!(owned.borrow().az::<i64>(), 12);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-az-crate)Using the *az* crate

The *az* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/az). To use it in
your crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
az = "1.3"
```
The crate requires rustc version 1.85.0 or later.

[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `nightly-float`, disabled by default. This requires the nightly compiler, and implements casts for the experimental- `f16`- `f128`

- [checked_](https://docs.rs/fn.checked_cast.html)- cast
- Casts the value, returning `None`
- [overflowing_](https://docs.rs/fn.overflowing_cast.html)- cast
- Overflowing cast.
- [saturating_](https://docs.rs/fn.saturating_cast.html)- cast
- Casts the value, saturating if the value does not fit.
- [strict_](https://docs.rs/fn.strict_cast.html)- cast
- Casts the value, panicking if the value does not fit.
- [unwrapped_](https://docs.rs/fn.unwrapped_cast.html)- cast

# gmp_mpfr_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/~1.7/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-low-level-bindings-for-gmp-mpfr-and-mpc)Rust low-level bindings for GMP, MPFR and MPC

The gmp-mpfr-sys crate provides Rust FFI bindings to the following
[GNU](https://www.gnu.org/) arbitrary-precision libraries:

- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)for integers and rational numbers,
- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)for floating-point numbers, and
- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/)for complex numbers.

The source of the three libraries is included in the package.

The gmp-mpfr-sys crate is free software: you can redistribute it
and/or modify it under the terms of the GNU Lesser General Public
License as published by the Free Software Foundation, either version 3
of the License, or (at your option) any later version. See the full
text of the [GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and [GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-features)Basic features

This crate contains three modules:

- `gmp`- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/).
- `mpfr`- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/).
- `mpc`- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/).

The versions provided by this crate release are [GMP](https://gmplib.org/) version 6.3.0, [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)
version 4.2.2, and [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/) version 1.4.1.

If you want a high-level API, consider using [Rug](https://crates.io/crates/rug), a crate
which provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary
precision and correct rounding:

- `Integer`
- `Rational`
- `Float`
- `Complex`

[§](https://docs.rs#name-prefixes)Name prefixes

Since modules and enumerated types provide namespacing, most prefixes
in the C names are removed. However, when the prefix is not a whole
word it is not removed. For example [ mp_set_memory_functions](https://docs.rs/C/GMP/constant.Custom_Allocation.html#index-mp_005fset_005fmemory_005ffunctions)
becomes

[, but](https://docs.rs/gmp/fn.set_memory_functions.html)

`mpz_init`[not](https://docs.rs/gmp/fn.mpz_init.html)

`gmp::mpz_init``gmp::z_init`, and [in](https://docs.rs/C/MPFR/constant.MPFR_Basics.html#Rounding-Modes)

`MPFR_RNDN`[becomes](https://docs.rs/C/MPFR/constant.MPFR_Basics.html#index-mpfr_005frnd_005ft)

`enum MPFR_RND_T`[not](https://docs.rs/mpfr/enum.rnd_t.html#variant.RNDN)

`mpc::mpc_t`[§](https://docs.rs#undocumented-or-obsolete-functions)Undocumented or obsolete functions

The bindings do not cover undocumented or obsolete functions and macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-gmp-mpfr-sys)Using gmp-mpfr-sys

The gmp-mpfr-sys crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys). To use
gmp-mpfr-sys in your crate, add it as a dependency inside
[ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
gmp-mpfr-sys = "1.7"
```
This crate requires rustc version 1.71.0 or later.

If the C libraries have a major version bump with some deprecated functions removed, but no features are removed in the Rust bindings, then gmp-mpfr-sys will have a minor version bump rather than a major version bump. This allows more compatiblity across crates that use the Rust bindings but do not use the C libraries directly.

If on the other hand a dependent crate makes use of internal
implementation details, or includes a C library that directly uses the
header (*.h*) and library (*.a*) files built using C, it can be a good
idea to depend on version `"~1.7"` instead of version `"1.7"` in order
to ensure backwards compatibility at the C level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

The gmp-mpfr-sys crate has two optional features:

- `mpfr`, enabled by default. Required to include the- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)library.
- `mpc`, enabled by default. Required to include the- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/)library. This feature requires the- `mpfr`feature.

The [GMP](https://gmplib.org/) library is always included.

The two optional features are enabled by default; to use features
selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies.gmp-mpfr-sys]
version = "1.7"
default-features = false
features = ["mpfr"]
```
Here only the `mpfr` feature is selected.

[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump.

Experimental features may also not work on all platforms.

There are three experimental features:

- `use-system-libs`, disabled by default. Using this feature, the system libraries for- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/), and- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)and- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/)if enabled, will be used instead of building them from source. The major versions of the system libraries must be equal to those provided by the crate, and the minor versions of the system libraries must be greater or equal to those provided by the crate. There are no restriction on the patch version.
- `force-cross`, disabled by default. Without this feature, the build will fail if cross compilation is detected, because cross compilation is not tested or supported and can lead to silent failures that are hard to debug, especially if this crate is an indirect dependency. As an exception, cross compiling from x86_64 to i686 does not need this feature. (Compiling on MinGW does not have this exception because MinGW does not support cross compilation from 64-bit to 32-bit.)
- `c-no-tests`, disabled by default. Using this feature will skip testing the C libraries. This is not advised; the risk that the GMP sources are miscompiled is unfortunately quite high. And if they indeed are miscompiled, the tests are very likely to trigger the compiler-introduced bug.

[§](https://docs.rs#metadata)Metadata

The gmp-mpfr-sys crate passes some metadata to its dependents:

- `DEP_GMP_LIMB_BITS`contains the number of bits per limb, which is 32 or 64.
- `DEP_GMP_OUT_DIR`contains the path of a directory that contains two subdirectories: the first subdirectory is named- *lib*and contains the generated library (- *.a*) files, and the second subdirectory is named- *include*and contains the corresponding header (- *.h*) files.
- `DEP_GMP_LIB_DIR`contains the path of the- *lib*subdirectory of the- `DEP_GMP_OUT_DIR`directory.
- `DEP_GMP_INCLUDE_DIR`contains the path of the- *include*subdirectory of the- `DEP_GMP_OUT_DIR`directory.

A dependent crate can use these environment variables in its build script.

[§](https://docs.rs#cross-compilation)Cross compilation

[§](https://docs.rs#caching-the-built-c-libraries)Caching the built C libraries

Building the C libraries can take some time. In order to save compilation time, the built libraries are cached in the user’s cache directory as follows:

- on GNU/Linux: inside `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/gmp-mpfr-sys`or`$HOME/.cache/gmp-mpfr-sys`
- on macOS: inside `$HOME/Library/Caches/gmp-mpfr-sys`
- on Windows: inside `{FOLDERID_LocalAppData}\gmp-mpfr-sys`

To use a different directory, you can set the environment variable
`GMP_MPFR_SYS_CACHE` to the desired cache directory. Setting the
`GMP_MPFR_SYS_CACHE` variable to an empty string or to a single
underscore (`"_"`) will disable caching.
