# Complex in rug - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/~1.29/rug/struct.Complex.html

`pub struct Complex { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A multi-precision complex number with arbitrarily large precision and correct rounding.

The precision has to be set during construction. The rounding method of the required operations can be specified, and the direction of the rounding is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use rug::{Assign, Complex, Float};
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (40, 30));
assert_eq!(format!("{:.3}", c), "(40.0 30.0)");
let mut f = Float::with_val(53, c.abs_ref());
assert_eq!(f, 50);
f.assign(c.arg_ref());
assert_eq!(f, 0.75_f64.atan());
```
Operations on two borrowed `Complex` numbers result in an
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) that has to be assigned to a new `Complex`
number.

```
use rug::Complex;
let a = Complex::with_val(53, (10.5, -11));
let b = Complex::with_val(53, (-1.25, -1.5));
let a_b_ref = &a + &b;
let a_b = Complex::with_val(53, a_b_ref);
assert_eq!(a_b, (9.25, -12.5));
```
As a special case, when an [incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) is obtained from
multiplying two `Complex` number references, it can be added to or subtracted
from another `Complex` number (or reference). This will result in a fused
multiply-accumulate operation, with only one rounding operation taking place.

```
use rug::Complex;
let mut acc = Complex::with_val(53, (1000, 1000));
let m1 = Complex::with_val(53, (10, 0));
let m2 = Complex::with_val(53, (1, -1));
// (1000 + 1000i) - (10 + 0i) × (1 - i) = (990 + 1010i)
acc -= &m1 * &m2;
assert_eq!(acc, (990, 1010));
```
The `Complex` number type supports various functions. Most methods have four
versions:

- The first method consumes the operand and rounds the returned `Complex`number to the[nearest](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html#variant.Nearest)representable value.
- The second method has a “`_mut`” suffix, mutates the operand and rounds it the nearest representable value.
- The third method has a “`_round`” suffix, mutates the operand, applies the specified[rounding method](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html)to the real and imaginary parts, and returns the rounding direction for both:
- The fourth method has a “`_ref`” suffix and borrows the operand. The returned item is an[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values)that can be assigned to a`Complex`number; the rounding method is selected during the assignment.

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Complex;
let expected = Complex::with_val(53, (1.2985, 0.6350));
// 1. consume the operand, round to nearest
let a = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
let sin_a = a.sin();
assert!(*(sin_a - &expected).abs().real() < 0.0001);
// 2. mutate the operand, round to nearest
let mut b = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
b.sin_mut();
assert!(*(b - &expected).abs().real() < 0.0001);
// 3. mutate the operand, apply specified rounding
let mut c = Complex::with_val(4, (1, 1));
// using 4 significant bits, 1.2985 is rounded down to 1.25
// and 0.6350 is rounded down to 0.625.
let dir = c.sin_round((Round::Nearest, Round::Nearest));
assert_eq!(c, (1.25, 0.625));
assert_eq!(dir, (Ordering::Less, Ordering::Less));
// 4. borrow the operand
let d = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
let r = d.sin_ref();
let sin_d = Complex::with_val(53, r);
assert!(*(sin_d - &expected).abs().real() < 0.0001);
// d was not consumed
assert_eq!(d, (1, 1));
```

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The function must *not*be used to create a constant`Complex``Complex`*copied*on use, leading to undefined behavior when they are dropped.
- The value must be initialized as a valid `mpc_t`
- The `mpc_t`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpc;
use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use rug::Complex;
let c = unsafe {
    let mut m = MaybeUninit::uninit();
    mpc::init3(m.as_mut_ptr(), 53, 53);
    let mut m = m.assume_init();
    mpc::set_d_d(&mut m, -14.5, 3.25, mpc::RNDNN);
    // m is initialized and unique
    Complex::from_raw(m)
};
assert_eq!(c, (-14.5, 3.25));
// since c is a Complex now, deallocation is automatic
```
This can be used to create a static [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number. See

[,](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpc/struct.mpc_t.html)

`mpc_t`[and the](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpfr/struct.mpfr_t.html)

`mpfr_t`[MPFR documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/C/MPFR/constant.MPFR_Interface.html#Internals)for details.

```
use core::ptr::NonNull;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp::limb_t;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr::{mpfr_t, prec_t};
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpc::mpc_t;
use rug::{Complex, Float};
const LIMBS: [limb_t; 2] = [5, 1 << (limb_t::BITS - 1)];
const LIMBS_PTR: *const [limb_t; 2] = &LIMBS;
const MANTISSA_DIGITS: u32 = limb_t::BITS * 2;
const MPC: mpc_t = mpc_t {
    re: mpfr_t {
        prec: MANTISSA_DIGITS as prec_t,
        sign: -1,
        exp: 1,
        d: unsafe { NonNull::new_unchecked(LIMBS_PTR.cast_mut().cast()) },
    },
    im: mpfr_t {
        prec: MANTISSA_DIGITS as prec_t,
        sign: 1,
        exp: 1,
        d: unsafe { NonNull::new_unchecked(LIMBS_PTR.cast_mut().cast()) },
    },
};
// Must *not* be const, otherwise it would lead to undefined
// behavior on use, as it would create a copy that is dropped.
static C: Complex = unsafe { Complex::from_raw(MPC) };
let lsig = Float::with_val(MANTISSA_DIGITS, 5) >> (MANTISSA_DIGITS - 1);
let msig = 1u32;
let val = lsig + msig;
let check = Complex::from((-val.clone(), val));
assert_eq!(C, check);
```
Converts a [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number into an

[MPC complex number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpc/struct.mpc_t.html).

The returned object should be freed to avoid memory leaks.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpc;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr::rnd_t;
use rug::Complex;
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (-14.5, 3.25));
let mut m = c.into_raw();
unsafe {
    let re_ptr = mpc::realref_const(&m);
    let re = mpfr::get_d(re_ptr, rnd_t::RNDN);
    assert_eq!(re, -14.5);
    let im_ptr = mpc::imagref_const(&m);
    let im = mpfr::get_d(im_ptr, rnd_t::RNDN);
    assert_eq!(im, 3.25);
    // free object to prevent memory leak
    mpc::clear(&mut m);
}
```
Returns a pointer to the inner [MPC complex number](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/mpc/struct.mpc_t.html).

The returned pointer will be valid for as long as `self` is valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpc;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::mpfr::rnd_t;
use rug::Complex;
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (-14.5, 3.25));
let m_ptr = c.as_raw();
unsafe {
    let re_ptr = mpc::realref_const(m_ptr);
    let re = mpfr::get_d(re_ptr, rnd_t::RNDN);
    assert_eq!(re, -14.5);
    let im_ptr = mpc::imagref_const(m_ptr);
    let im = mpfr::get_d(im_ptr, rnd_t::RNDN);
    assert_eq!(im, 3.25);
}
// c is still valid
assert_eq!(c, (-14.5, 3.25));
```

Parses a decimal string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number.

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

The string can contain either of the following three:

- One floating-point number that can be parsed by
[Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html#method.parse)
- Two floating-point numbers inside round brackets separated by one comma. ASCII whitespace is treated in the same way as 1 above, and is also allowed around the brackets and the comma.
- Two floating-point numbers inside round brackets separated by ASCII whitespace. Since the real and imaginary parts are separated by whitespace, they themselves cannot contain whitespace. ASCII whitespace is still allowed around the brackets and between the two parts.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let valid1 = Complex::parse("(12.5, -13.5)");
let c1 = Complex::with_val(53, valid1.unwrap());
assert_eq!(c1, (12.5, -13.5));
let valid2 = Complex::parse("(inf 0.0)");
let c2 = Complex::with_val(53, valid2.unwrap());
assert_eq!(c2, (f64::INFINITY, 0.0));
let invalid = Complex::parse("(1 2 3)");
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```

Parses a string slice (`&`) or byte slice
([str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)[&[](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)[]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)[ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number.

The following are implemented with the unwrapped returned
[incomplete-computation value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

The string can contain either of the following three:

- One floating-point number that can be parsed by
[Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)::[parse_radix](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html#method.parse_radix)
- Two floating-point numbers inside round brackets separated by one comma. ASCII whitespace is treated in the same way as 1 above, and is also allowed around the brackets and the comma.
- Two floating-point numbers inside round brackets separated by ASCII whitespace. Since the real and imaginary parts are separated by whitespace, they themselves cannot contain whitespace. ASCII whitespace is still allowed around the brackets and between the two parts.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-10)Panics

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let valid1 = Complex::parse_radix("(12, 1a)", 16);
let c1 = Complex::with_val(53, valid1.unwrap());
assert_eq!(c1, (0x12, 0x1a));
let valid2 = Complex::parse_radix("(@inf@ zz)", 36);
let c2 = Complex::with_val(53, valid2.unwrap());
assert_eq!(c2, (f64::INFINITY, 35 * 36 + 35));
let invalid = Complex::parse_radix("(1 2 3)", 10);
assert!(invalid.is_err());
```

Returns a string representation of the value for the specified `radix`
rounding to the nearest.

The exponent is encoded in decimal. If the number of digits is not specified, the output string will have enough precision such that reading it again will give the exact same number.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-11)Panics

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-27)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let c1 = Complex::with_val(53, 0);
assert_eq!(c1.to_string_radix(10, None), "(0 0)");
let c2 = Complex::with_val(12, (15, 5));
assert_eq!(c2.to_string_radix(16, None), "(f.000 5.000)");
let c3 = Complex::with_val(53, (10, -4));
assert_eq!(c3.to_string_radix(10, Some(3)), "(10.0 -4.00)");
assert_eq!(c3.to_string_radix(5, Some(3)), "(20.0 -4.00)");
// 2 raised to the power of 80 in hex is 1 followed by 20 zeros
let c4 = Complex::with_val(53, (80f64.exp2(), 0.25));
assert_eq!(c4.to_string_radix(10, Some(3)), "(1.21e24 2.50e-1)");
assert_eq!(c4.to_string_radix(16, Some(3)), "(1.00@20 4.00@-1)");
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#1074-1092)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#1074-1092)

Returns a string representation of the value for the specified `radix`
applying the specified rounding method.

The exponent is encoded in decimal. If the number of digits is not specified, the output string will have enough precision such that reading it again will give the exact same number.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-12)Panics

Panics if `radix` is less than 2 or greater than 36.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-28)Examples

```
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Complex;
let c = Complex::with_val(10, 10.4);
let down = (Round::Down, Round::Down);
let nearest = (Round::Nearest, Round::Nearest);
let up = (Round::Up, Round::Up);
let nd = c.to_string_radix_round(10, None, down);
assert_eq!(nd, "(10.406 0)");
let nu = c.to_string_radix_round(10, None, up);
assert_eq!(nu, "(10.407 0)");
let sd = c.to_string_radix_round(10, Some(2), down);
assert_eq!(sd, "(10 0)");
let sn = c.to_string_radix_round(10, Some(2), nearest);
assert_eq!(sn, "(10 0)");
let su = c.to_string_radix_round(10, Some(2), up);
assert_eq!(su, "(11 0)");
```

Compares the absolute values of `self` and `other`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-43)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::Complex;
let five = Complex::with_val(53, (5, 0));
let five_rotated = Complex::with_val(53, (3, -4));
let greater_than_five = Complex::with_val(53, (-4, -4));
let has_nan = Complex::with_val(53, (5, 0.0 / 0.0));
assert_eq!(five.cmp_abs(&five_rotated), Some(Ordering::Equal));
assert_eq!(five.cmp_abs(&greater_than_five), Some(Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(five.cmp_abs(&has_nan), None);
```
Returns the total ordering between `self` and `other`.

For ordering, the real part has precedence over the imaginary part. Negative zero is ordered as less than positive zero. Negative NaN is ordered as less than negative infinity, while positive NaN is ordered as greater than positive infinity. Comparing two negative NaNs or two positive NaNs produces equality.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-44)Examples

```
use rug::float::Special;
use rug::Complex;
let mut values = vec![
    Complex::with_val(53, (Special::Zero, Special::Zero)),
    Complex::with_val(53, (Special::Zero, Special::NegZero)),
    Complex::with_val(53, (Special::NegZero, Special::Infinity)),
];
values.sort_by(Complex::total_cmp);
// (-0, +∞)
assert!(values[0].real().is_zero() && values[0].real().is_sign_negative());
assert!(values[0].imag().is_infinite() && values[0].imag().is_sign_positive());
// (+0, -0)
assert!(values[1].real().is_zero() && values[1].real().is_sign_positive());
assert!(values[1].imag().is_zero() && values[1].imag().is_sign_negative());
// (+0, +0)
assert!(values[2].real().is_zero() && values[2].real().is_sign_positive());
assert!(values[2].imag().is_zero() && values[2].imag().is_sign_positive());
```
Adds a list of [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) numbers with correct rounding.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AddAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.AddAssign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AddAssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AddAssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [Add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Add.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [Add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Add.html)<- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src
- [SubAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.SubAssign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [SubFrom](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubFrom.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [SubAssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubAssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [SubFromRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubFromRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [Sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Sub.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [Sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.Sub.html)<- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-45)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
// Give each value only 4 bits of precision for example purposes.
let values = [
    Complex::with_val(4, (5.0, 1024.0)),
    Complex::with_val(4, (1024.0, 15.0)),
    Complex::with_val(4, (-1024.0, -1024.0)),
    Complex::with_val(4, (-4.5, -16.0)),
];
// The result should still be exact if it fits.
let r1 = Complex::sum(values.iter());
let sum1 = Complex::with_val(4, r1);
assert_eq!(sum1, (0.5, -1.0));
let r2 = Complex::sum(values.iter());
let sum2 = Complex::with_val(4, (1.0, -1.0)) + r2;
assert_eq!(sum2, (1.5, -2.0));
let r3 = Complex::sum(values.iter());
let mut sum3 = Complex::with_val(4, (16, 16));
sum3 += r3;
// (16.5, 15) rounded to (16, 15)
assert_eq!(sum3, (16, 15));
```
Finds the dot product of a list of [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) numbers pairs with

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)

- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

This method will produce a result with correct rounding, except for some cases where underflow and/or overflow occur in intermediate products.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-46)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let a = [
    Complex::with_val(53, (5.0, 10.25)),
    Complex::with_val(53, (10.25, 5.0)),
];
let b = [
    Complex::with_val(53, (-2.75, -11.5)),
    Complex::with_val(53, (-4.5, 16.0)),
];
let r = Complex::dot(a.iter().zip(b.iter()));
let dot = Complex::with_val(53, r);
let expected = Complex::with_val(53, &a[0] * &b[0]) + &a[1] * &b[1];
assert_eq!(dot, expected);
let r = Complex::dot(a.iter().zip(b.iter()));
let add_dot = Complex::with_val(53, (1.0, 2.0)) + r;
let add_expected = Complex::with_val(53, (1.0, 2.0)) + &expected;
assert_eq!(add_dot, add_expected);
let r = Complex::dot(a.iter().zip(b.iter()));
let mut add_dot2 = Complex::with_val(53, (1.0, 2.0));
add_dot2 += r;
assert_eq!(add_dot2, add_expected);
```
Multiplies and adds in one fused operation, rounding to the nearest with only one rounding error.

`a.mul_add(&b, &c)` produces a result like `&a * &b + &c`, but `a` is
consumed and the result produced uses its precision.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-47)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let a = Complex::with_val(53, (10, 0));
let b = Complex::with_val(53, (1, -1));
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (1000, 1000));
// (10 + 0i) × (1 - i) + (1000 + 1000i) = (1010 + 990i)
let mul_add = a.mul_add(&b, &c);
assert_eq!(mul_add, (1010, 990));
```

Multiplies and adds in one fused operation, applying the specified rounding method with only one rounding error.

`a.mul_add_round(&b, &c, round)` produces a result like
`ans.assign_round(&a * &b + &c, round)`, but stores the result in `a`
using its precision rather than in another [ Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html) number like

`ans`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-49)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;

use rug::Complex;
let mut a = Complex::with_val(53, (10, 0));
let b = Complex::with_val(53, (1, -1));
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (1000, 1000));
// (10 + 0i) × (1 - i) + (1000 + 1000i) = (1010 + 990i)
let dir = a.mul_add_round(&b, &c, (Round::Nearest, Round::Nearest));
assert_eq!(a, (1010, 990));
assert_eq!(dir, (Ordering::Equal, Ordering::Equal));
```

Computes a projection onto the Riemann sphere, rounding to the nearest.

If no parts of the number are infinite, the result is unchanged. If any part is infinite, the real part of the result is set to +∞ and the imaginary part of the result is set to 0 with the same sign as the imaginary part of the input.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-55)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let c1 = Complex::with_val(53, (1.5, 2.5));
let proj1 = c1.proj();
assert_eq!(proj1, (1.5, 2.5));
let c2 = Complex::with_val(53, (f64::NAN, f64::NEG_INFINITY));
let proj2 = c2.proj();
assert_eq!(proj2, (f64::INFINITY, 0.0));
// imaginary was negative, so now it is minus zero
assert!(proj2.imag().is_sign_negative());
```

Special values are handled like atan2 in IEEE 754-2008.

```
use rug::Complex;
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (40, 30));
let arg = c.arg();
assert_eq!(arg, (0.75_f64.atan(), 0));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#2932-2934)

#### pub fn [root_of_unity](https://docs.rs#method.root_of_unity)(n: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html), k: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> RootOfUnityIncomplete

Generates a root of unity, rounding to the nearest.

The generated number is the *n*th root of unity raised to the power
*k*, that is its magnitude is 1 and its argument is
2π*k*/*n*.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-101)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let r = Complex::root_of_unity(3, 2);
let c = Complex::with_val(53, r);
let expected = Complex::with_val(53, (-0.5, -0.8660));
assert!(*(c - expected).abs().real() < 0.0001);
```

Computes the sine and cosine of `self`, rounding to the nearest.

The sine keeps the precision of `self` while the cosine keeps the
precision of `cos`.

The initial value of `cos` is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-122)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let c = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
let (sin, cos) = c.sin_cos(Complex::new(53));
let expected_sin = Complex::with_val(53, (1.2985, 0.6350));
let expected_cos = Complex::with_val(53, (0.8337, -0.9889));
assert!(*(sin - expected_sin).abs().real() < 0.0001);
assert!(*(cos - expected_cos).abs().real() < 0.0001);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#3375-3377)#### pub fn [sin_cos_mut](https://docs.rs#method.sin_cos_mut)(&mut self, cos: &mut Self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#3375-3377)

#### pub fn [sin_cos_mut](https://docs.rs#method.sin_cos_mut)(&mut self, cos: &mut Self)

Computes the sine and cosine of `self`, rounding to the nearest.

The sine is stored in `self` and keeps its precision, while the cosine
is stored in `cos` keeping its precision.

The initial value of `cos` is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-123)Examples

```
use rug::Complex;
let mut sin = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
let mut cos = Complex::new(53);
sin.sin_cos_mut(&mut cos);
let expected_sin = Complex::with_val(53, (1.2985, 0.6350));
let expected_cos = Complex::with_val(53, (0.8337, -0.9889));
assert!(*(sin - expected_sin).abs().real() < 0.0001);
assert!(*(cos - expected_cos).abs().real() < 0.0001);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#3408-3410)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#3408-3410)

Computes the sine and cosine of `self`, applying the specified rounding
methods.

The sine is stored in `self` and keeps its precision, while the cosine
is stored in `cos` keeping its precision.

The initial value of `cos` is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-124)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::Complex;
// Use only 4 bits of precision to show rounding.
let mut sin = Complex::with_val(4, (1, 1));
let mut cos = Complex::new(4);
// sin(1 + i) = (1.2985 + 0.6350)
// using 4 significant bits: (1.25 + 0.625i)
// cos(1 + i) = (0.8337 - 0.9889i)
// using 4 significant bits: (0.8125 - i)
let (dir_sin, dir_cos) =
    sin.sin_cos_round(&mut cos, (Round::Nearest, Round::Nearest));
assert_eq!(sin, (1.25, 0.625));
assert_eq!(dir_sin, (Ordering::Less, Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(cos, (0.8125, -1));
assert_eq!(dir_cos, (Ordering::Less, Ordering::Less));
```

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)&mut- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html), &mut- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html),- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)&mut- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html), &mut- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [(](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html),- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)- [)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-125)Examples

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use rug::float::Round;
use rug::ops::AssignRound;
use rug::{Assign, Complex};
let phase = Complex::with_val(53, (1, 1));
let (mut sin, mut cos) = (Complex::new(53), Complex::new(53));
let sin_cos = phase.sin_cos_ref();
(&mut sin, &mut cos).assign(sin_cos);
let expected_sin = Complex::with_val(53, (1.2985, 0.6350));
let expected_cos = Complex::with_val(53, (0.8337, -0.9889));
assert!(*(sin - expected_sin).abs().real() < 0.0001);
assert!(*(cos - expected_cos).abs().real() < 0.0001);
// using 4 significant bits: sin = (1.25 + 0.625i)
// using 4 significant bits: cos = (0.8125 - i)
let (mut sin_4, mut cos_4) = (Complex::new(4), Complex::new(4));
let sin_cos = phase.sin_cos_ref();
let (dir_sin, dir_cos) = (&mut sin_4, &mut cos_4)
    .assign_round(sin_cos, (Round::Nearest, Round::Nearest));
assert_eq!(sin_4, (1.25, 0.625));
assert_eq!(dir_sin, (Ordering::Less, Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(cos_4, (0.8125, -1));
assert_eq!(dir_cos, (Ordering::Less, Ordering::Less));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#4381-4383)#### pub fn [random_bits](https://docs.rs#method.random_bits)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomBitsIncomplete<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#4381-4383)

#### pub fn [random_bits](https://docs.rs#method.random_bits)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomBitsIncomplete<'_>

Generates a random complex number with both the real and imaginary parts
in the range 0 ≤ *x* < 1.

This is equivalent to generating a random integer in the range
0 ≤ *x* < 2 p for each part,
where 2

is two raised to the power of the precision, and then dividing the integer by 2

*p*. The smallest non-zero result will thus be 2

*p*−, and will only have one bit set. In the smaller possible results, many bits will be zero, and not all the precision will be used.

*p*There is a corner case where the generated random number part is converted to NaN: if the precision is very large, the generated random number could have an exponent less than the allowed minimum exponent, and NaN is used to indicate this. For this to occur in practice, the minimum exponent has to be set to have a very small magnitude using the low-level MPFR interface, or the random number generator has to be designed specifically to trigger this case.

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-170)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
use rug::{Assign, Complex};
let mut rand = RandState::new();
let mut c = Complex::new(2);
c.assign(Complex::random_bits(&mut rand));
let (re, im) = c.into_real_imag();
assert!(re == 0.0 || re == 0.25 || re == 0.5 || re == 0.75);
assert!(im == 0.0 || im == 0.25 || im == 0.5 || im == 0.75);
println!("0.0 ≤ {} < 1.0", re);
println!("0.0 ≤ {} < 1.0", im);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#4437-4439)#### pub fn [random_cont](https://docs.rs#method.random_cont)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomContIncomplete<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/complex/big.rs.html#4437-4439)

#### pub fn [random_cont](https://docs.rs#method.random_cont)(rng: &mut dyn [MutRandState](https://docs.rs/rand/trait.MutRandState.html)) -> RandomContIncomplete<'_>

Generates a random complex number with both the real and imaginary parts
in the continous range 0 ≤ *x* < 1, and rounds
to the nearest.

The result parts can be rounded up to be equal to one. Unlike the
[ random_bits](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html#method.random_bits) method which generates a discrete
random number at intervals depending on the precision, this method is
equivalent to generating a continuous random number with infinite
precision and then rounding the result. This means that even the smaller
numbers will be using all the available precision bits, and rounding is
performed in all cases, not in some corner case.

Rounding directions for generated random numbers cannot be
[Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)::[Equal](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Equal)

The following are implemented with the returned [incomplete-computation
value](https://docs.rs/index.html#incomplete-computation-values) as `Src`:

- [Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [AssignRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html)<Src> for- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)
- [CompleteRound](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html)<- [Completed](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#associatedtype.Completed)=- [Complex](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)> for Src

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-171)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
use rug::Complex;
let mut rand = RandState::new();
let c = Complex::with_val(2, Complex::random_cont(&mut rand));
let (re, im) = c.into_real_imag();
// The significand is either 0b10 or 0b11
assert!(
    re == 1.0
        || re == 0.75
        || re == 0.5
        || re == 0.375
        || re == 0.25
        || re <= 0.1875
);
assert!(
    im == 1.0
        || im == 0.75
        || im == 0.5
        || im == 0.375
        || im == 0.25
        || im <= 0.1875
);
```

# Assign in rug - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/trait.Assign.html

```
pub trait Assign<Src = Self> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[assign](https://docs.rs#tymethod.assign)(&mut self, src: Src);
}## Expand description

Assigns to a number from another value.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Implementing the trait:

```
use rug::Assign;
struct I(i32);
impl Assign<i16> for I {
    fn assign(&mut self, rhs: i16) {
        self.0 = rhs.into();
    }
}
let mut i = I(0);
i.assign(42_i16);
assert_eq!(i.0, 42);
```
Performing an assignment operation using the trait:

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let mut i = Integer::from(15);
assert_eq!(i, 15);
i.assign(23);
assert_eq!(i, 23);
```

# rug - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rug/~1.30/rug/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-precision-numbers)Arbitrary-precision numbers

Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and correct rounding:

- `Integer`
- `Rational`
- `Float`
- `Complex`

Rug is a high-level interface to the following [GNU](https://www.gnu.org/) libraries:

- [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)for integers and rational numbers,
- [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/)for floating-point numbers, and
- [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/)for complex numbers.

Rug is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms
of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published by the Free Software
Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later
version. See the full text of the [GNU LGPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/lgpl-3.0.en.html) and [GNU GPL](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html) for details.

You are also free to use the examples in this documentation without any restrictions; the examples are in the public domain.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-example)Quick example

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let mut int = Integer::new();
assert_eq!(int, 0);
int.assign(14);
assert_eq!(int, 14);
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign(Integer::parse(decimal).unwrap());
assert!(int > 100_000_000);
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign(Integer::parse_radix(hex_160, 16).unwrap());
assert_eq!(int.significant_bits(), 160);
int = (int >> 128) - 1;
assert_eq!(int, 0xfffe_ffff_u32);
```
- [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::- [new](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.new)- `Integer`
- To assign values to Rug types, we use the `Assign``Assign::assign`[assignment operator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html#assignment-expressions)as that would drop the left-hand-side operand and replace it with a right-hand-side operand of the same type, which is not what we want here.`=`
- Arbitrary precision numbers can hold numbers that are too large to fit in a
primitive type. To assign such a number to the large types, we use strings
rather than primitives; in the example this is done using
[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[parse_radix](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.parse_radix)
- We can compare Rug types to primitive types or to other Rug types using the
normal comparison operators, for example `int > 100_000_000`.
- Most arithmetic operations are supported with Rug types and primitive types
on either side of the operator, for example `int >> 128`.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-with-primitive-types)Using with primitive types

With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two values of
the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive types, conversion to
and from Rug types can be expensive, so the arithmetic operators are overloaded
to work on many combinations of Rug types and primitives. The following are
provided:

- Where they make sense, all arithmetic operators are overloaded to work with
Rug types and the primitives `i8``i16``i32``i64``i128``u8``u16``u32``u64``u128``f32``f64`
- Where they make sense, conversions using the `From``Assign``bool``isize``usize`
- Comparisons between Rug types and all the numeric primitives listed in 1 and 2 above are supported.
- For `Rational`
- For `Complex`

[§](https://docs.rs#operators)Operators

Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type. For example

```
use rug::Integer;
let a = Integer::from(10);
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!(b, 5 - 10);
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html).

If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an incomplete-computation value. For example

```
use rug::Integer;
let (a, b) = (Integer::from(10), Integer::from(20));
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = Integer::from(incomplete);
assert_eq!(sub, -10);
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
still needs to be converted or assigned into an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html). This is covered in
more detail in the

[section.](https://docs.rs#incomplete-computation-values)

*Incomplete-computation values*[§](https://docs.rs#shifting-operations)Shifting operations

The left shift `<<` and right shift `>>` operators support shifting by negative
values, for example `a << 5` is equivalent to `a >> -5`.

The shifting operators are also supported for the [ Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html) and

[number types, where they are equivalent to multiplication or division by a power of two. Only the exponent of the value is affected; the mantissa is unchanged.](https://docs.rs/struct.Complex.html)

`Complex`[§](https://docs.rs#exponentiation)Exponentiation

Exponentiation (raising to a power) does not have a dedicated operator in Rust.
In order to perform exponentiation of Rug types, the [ Pow](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.Pow.html) trait has
to be brought into scope, for example

```
use rug::ops::Pow;
use rug::Integer;
let base = Integer::from(10);
let power = base.pow(5);
assert_eq!(power, 100_000);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compound-assignments-to-right-hand-side-operands)Compound assignments to right-hand-side operands

Traits are provided for compound assignment to right-hand-side operands. This
can be useful for non-commutative operations like subtraction. The names of the
traits and their methods are similar to Rust compound assignment traits, with
the suffix “`Assign`” replaced with “`From`”. For example the counterpart to
[ SubAssign](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/arith/trait.SubAssign.html) is

[:](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.SubFrom.html)

`SubFrom````
use rug::ops::SubFrom;
use rug::Integer;
let mut rhs = Integer::from(10);
// set rhs = 100 - rhs
rhs.sub_from(100);
assert_eq!(rhs, 90);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#incomplete-computation-values)Incomplete-computation values

There are two main reasons why operations like `&a - &b` do not perform a
complete computation and return a Rug type:

- Sometimes we need to assign the result to an object that already exists. Since Rug types require memory allocations, this can help reduce the number of allocations. (While the allocations might not affect performance noticeably for computationally intensive functions, they can have a much more significant effect on faster functions like addition.)
- For the `Float``Complex`

There are two things that can be done with incomplete-computation values:

- Assign them to an existing object without unnecessary allocations. This is
usually achieved using the `Assign``int.`and[assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html#tymethod.assign)(incomplete)`float.`.[assign_round](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.AssignRound.html#tymethod.assign_round)(incomplete,[Round](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html)::[Up](https://docs.rs/float/enum.Round.html#variant.Up))
- Convert them to the final value using the `Complete``From``incomplete.`or[complete](https://docs.rs/trait.Complete.html#tymethod.complete)()[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html#tymethod.from)(incomplete)`incomplete.`or[complete](https://docs.rs/ops/trait.CompleteRound.html#method.complete)(53)[Float](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html)::[with_val](https://docs.rs/struct.Float.html#method.with_val)(53, incomplete)

Let us consider a couple of examples.

```
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let mut buffer = Integer::new();
// ... buffer can be used and reused ...
let (a, b) = (Integer::from(10), Integer::from(20));
let incomplete = &a - &b;
buffer.assign(incomplete);
assert_eq!(buffer, -10);
```
Here the assignment from `incomplete` into `buffer` does not require an
allocation unless the result does not fit in the current capacity of `buffer`.
If `&a - &b` returned an [ Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html) instead, then an allocation would take
place even if it is not necessary.

```
use rug::float::Constant;
use rug::Float;
// x has a precision of 10 bits
let x = Float::with_val(10, 180);
// y has a precision of 50 bits
let y = Float::with_val(50, Constant::Pi);
let incomplete = &x / &y;
// z has a precision of 45 bits
let z = Float::with_val(45, incomplete);
assert!(57.295 < z && z < 57.296);
```
The precision to use for the result depends on the requirements of the algorithm
being implemented. Here `z` is created with a precision of 45.

Many operations can return incomplete-computation values, for example

- unary operators applied to references, for example `-&int`
- binary operators applied to two references, for example `&int1 + &int2`
- binary operators applied to a primitive and a reference, for example `&int * 10`
- methods that take a reference, for example
`int.`[abs_ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.abs_ref)()
- methods that take two references, for example
`int1.`[gcd_ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.gcd_ref)(&int2)
- string parsing, for example
[Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)::[parse](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html#method.parse)("12")

These operations return objects that can be stored in temporary variables like
`incomplete` in the last few code examples. However, the names of the types are
not public, and consequently, the incomplete-computation values cannot be for
example stored in a struct. If you need to store the value in a struct, complete
it to its final type and value.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-rug)Using Rug

Rug is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/rug). To use Rug in your crate, add it as
a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
rug = "1.30"
```
Rug requires rustc version 1.85.0 or later.

Rug also depends on the [GMP](https://gmplib.org/), [MPFR](https://www.mpfr.org/) and [MPC](https://www.multiprecision.org/mpc/) libraries through the low-level
FFI bindings in the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys), which needs some setup to
build; the [gmp-mpfr-sys documentation](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html) has some details on usage under
[GNU/Linux](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-gnulinux), [macOS](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-macos) and [Windows](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/index.html#building-on-windows).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

The Rug crate has six optional features:

- `integer`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Integer`
- `rational`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Rational`- `integer`feature.
- `float`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Float`
- `complex`, enabled by default. Required for the- `Complex`- `float`feature.
- `rand`, enabled by default. Required for the- `RandState`- `integer`feature.
- `std`, enabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`, such as methods that return- `String`
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the- `Integer`- `Rational`- `Float`- `Complex`- `std`feature and the- [serde crate](https://crates.io/crates/serde).

The first six optional features are enabled by default; to use features
selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies.rug]
version = "1.30"
default-features = false
features = ["integer", "float", "std"]
```
Here only the `integer`, `float` and `rand` features are enabled. If none of the
features are selected, the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate](https://crates.io/crates/gmp-mpfr-sys) is not required and
thus not enabled. In that case, only the [ Assign](https://docs.rs/trait.Assign.html) trait and the traits that
are in the

[module are provided by the crate.](https://docs.rs/ops/index.html)

`ops`[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-integer*crate- *num-traits*crate- *num-integer*crate
- `num-complex`, disabled by default. This adds conversion methods to and from complex floats as provided by the- *num-complex*crate- *num-complex*crate
- `nightly-float`, disabled by default. This requires the nightly compiler, and implements some operations with the experimental- `f16`- `f128`
- `borsh`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support using the- *borsh*crate

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new random generator with a compromise between speed and randomness.

Currently this is equivalent to [ new_mersenne_twister](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html#method.new_mersenne_twister).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
let mut rand = RandState::new();
let u = rand.bits(32);
println!("32 random bits: {:032b}", u);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rand.rs.html#152-161)#### pub fn [new_mersenne_twister](https://docs.rs#method.new_mersenne_twister)() -> [RandState](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html)<'static>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rand.rs.html#152-161)

#### pub fn [new_mersenne_twister](https://docs.rs#method.new_mersenne_twister)() -> [RandState](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html)<'static>

Creates a random generator with a Mersenne Twister algorithm.

This algorithm is fast and has good randomness properties.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
let mut rand = RandState::new_mersenne_twister();
let u = rand.bits(32);
println!("32 random bits: {:032b}", u);
```
Creates a new random generator with a linear congruential algorithm
*X* = (*a* × *X* + *c*) mod 2 m.

The low bits of *X* in this algorithm are not very random, so only
the high half of each *X* is actually used, that is the higher
*m*/2 bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
use rug::Integer;
let a = match Integer::from_str_radix("292787ebd3329ad7e7575e2fd", 16) {
    Ok(i) => i,
    Err(_) => unreachable!(),
};
let c = 1;
let m = 100;
let mut rand = RandState::new_linear_congruential(&a, c, m);
let u = rand.bits(32);
println!("32 random bits: {:032b}", u);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rand.rs.html#219-231)#### pub fn [new_linear_congruential_size](https://docs.rs#method.new_linear_congruential_size)(size: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[RandState](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html)<'static>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rand.rs.html#219-231)

#### pub fn [new_linear_congruential_size](https://docs.rs#method.new_linear_congruential_size)(size: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[RandState](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html)<'static>>

Creates a new random generator with a linear congruential algorithm like
the [ new_linear_congruential](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html#method.new_linear_congruential) method.

For the linear congruential algorithm *X* = (*a* × *X* +
*c*) mod 2 m,

*a*,

*c*and

*m*are selected from a table such that at least

*size*bits of each

*X*will be used, that is

*m*/2 ≥

*size*. The table only has values for

*size*≤ 128;

[will be returned if the requested size is larger.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
let mut rand = match RandState::new_linear_congruential_size(100) {
    Some(r) => r,
    None => unreachable!(),
};
let u = rand.bits(32);
println!("32 random bits: {:032b}", u);
```

Creates a new custom random generator.

If the custom random generator is cloned, the implemented trait method
[RandGen](https://docs.rs/trait.RandGen.html)::[boxed_clone](https://docs.rs/trait.RandGen.html#method.boxed_clone)[ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
use rug::rand::{RandGen, RandState};
use rug::Integer;
struct Seed;
impl RandGen for Seed {
    fn r#gen(&mut self) -> u32 {
        // not really random
        0x8CEF_7310
    }
}
let mut seed = Seed;

let mut i = Integer::from(15);
i.random_below_mut(&mut rand);
println!("0 ≤ {} < 15", i);

```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rand.rs.html#354-359)#### pub unsafe fn [from_raw](https://docs.rs#method.from_raw)(raw: [randstate_t](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.randstate_t.html)) -> [RandState](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html)<'static>

#### pub unsafe fn [from_raw](https://docs.rs#method.from_raw)(raw: [randstate_t](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.randstate_t.html)) -> [RandState](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html)<'static>

Creates a random generator from an initialized [GMP random
generator](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.randstate_t.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The value must be initialized as a valid `randstate_t`
- The `randstate_t`
- The object must be thread safe.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::rand::RandState;
let mut rand = unsafe {
    let mut raw = MaybeUninit::uninit();
    gmp::randinit_default(raw.as_mut_ptr());
    let raw = raw.assume_init();
    // raw is initialized and unique
    RandState::from_raw(raw)
};
let u = rand.bits(32);
println!("32 random bits: {:032b}", u);
// since rand is a RandState now, deallocation is automatic
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rand.rs.html#392-401)#### pub fn [into_raw](https://docs.rs#method.into_raw)(self) -> [randstate_t](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.randstate_t.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rug/rand.rs.html#392-401)

#### pub fn [into_raw](https://docs.rs#method.into_raw)(self) -> [randstate_t](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.randstate_t.html)

Converts a random generator into a [GMP random generator](https://docs.rs/gmp-mpfr-sys/1.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/gmp_mpfr_sys/gmp/struct.randstate_t.html).

The returned object should be freed to avoid memory leaks.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This method panics if the [ RandState](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html) object was created using

[, as the borrow into the custom generator would be terminated once](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html#method.new_custom)

`new_custom``self` is consumed. This would lead to undefined
behavior if the returned object is used. This method does work with
objects created using [.](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html#method.new_custom_boxed)

`new_custom_boxed`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use gmp_mpfr_sys::gmp;
use rug::rand::RandState;
let rand = RandState::new();
let mut raw = rand.into_raw();
unsafe {
    let u = gmp::urandomb_ui(&mut raw, 32) as u32;
    println!("32 random bits: {:032b}", u);
    // free object to prevent memory leak
    gmp::randclear(&mut raw);
}
```

#### pub fn [into_custom_boxed](https://docs.rs#method.into_custom_boxed)(self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [RandGen](https://docs.rs/trait.RandGen.html)>, Self>

Converts a random generator into [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [RandGen](https://docs.rs/trait.RandGen.html)>

If the conversion is not possible, [Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)(self)

This conversion is always possible when the random generator was created
with [ new_custom_boxed](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html#method.new_custom_boxed). It is also possible if the generator was
cloned, directly or indirectly, from another generator that was created
with

[or](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html#method.new_custom)

`new_custom`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html#method.new_custom_boxed)

`new_custom_boxed`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use rug::rand::{RandGen, RandState};
struct Seed;
impl RandGen for Seed {
    fn r#gen(&mut self) -> u32 {
        // not really random
        0x8CEF_7310
    }
}
let seed = Box::new(Seed);
let rand = RandState::new_custom_boxed(seed);
let mut back_to_seed = rand.into_custom_boxed().unwrap();
assert_eq!(back_to_seed.r#gen(), 0x8CEF_7310);
```
Seeds the random generator.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
use rug::Integer;
let seed = Integer::from(123456);
let mut rand = RandState::new();
rand.seed(&seed);
let u1a = rand.bits(32);
let u1b = rand.bits(32);
// reseed with the same seed
rand.seed(&seed);
let u2a = rand.bits(32);
let u2b = rand.bits(32);
assert_eq!(u1a, u2a);
assert_eq!(u1b, u2b);
```
Generates a random number below the given boundary value.

This function can never return the maximum 32-bit value; in order to
generate a 32-bit random value that covers the whole range, use the
[ bits](https://docs.rs/struct.RandState.html#method.bits) method with

`bits` set to 32.[§](https://docs.rs#panics-2)Panics

Panics if the boundary value is zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use rug::rand::RandState;
let mut rand = RandState::new();
let u = rand.below(10000);
assert!(u < 10000);
println!("0 ≤ {} < 10000", u);
```

- [Complete](https://docs.rs/trait.CompleteRound.html)- Round

- [DivAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.DivAssignRound.html)- Round
- Compound division and assignment with a specified rounding method.
- [DivFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.DivFrom.html)
- Compound division and assignment to the rhs operand.
- [DivFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.DivFromRound.html)- Round
- Compound division and assignment to the rhs operand with a specified rounding method.
- [DivRounding](https://docs.rs/trait.DivRounding.html)
- Rounding variants of division.
- [DivRounding](https://docs.rs/trait.DivRoundingAssign.html)- Assign
- Compound assignment and rounding variants of division.
- [DivRounding](https://docs.rs/trait.DivRoundingFrom.html)- From
- Compound assignment to the rhs operand and rounding variants of division.
- [MulAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.MulAssignRound.html)- Round
- Compound multiplication and assignment with a specified rounding method.
- [MulFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.MulFrom.html)
- Compound multiplication and assignment to the rhs operand.
- [MulFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.MulFromRound.html)- Round
- Compound multiplication and assignment to the rhs operand with a specified rounding method.
- [NegAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NegAssign.html)
- Compound negation and assignment.
- [NotAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NotAssign.html)
- Compound bitwise complement and assignement.
- [Pow](https://docs.rs/trait.Pow.html)
- Binary operator for raising a value to a power.
- [PowAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.PowAssign.html)
- Compound power operation and assignment.
- [PowAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.PowAssignRound.html)- Round
- Compound power operation and assignment with a specified rounding method.
- [PowFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.PowFrom.html)
- Compound power operation and assignment to the rhs operand.
- [PowFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.PowFromRound.html)- Round
- Compound power operation and assignment to the rhs operand with a specified rounding method.
- [RemAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.RemAssignRound.html)- Round
- Compound remainder operation and assignment with a specified rounding method.
- [RemFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.RemFrom.html)
- Compound remainder operation and assignment to the rhs operand.
- [RemFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.RemFromRound.html)- Round
- Compound remainder operation and assignment to the rhs operand with a specified rounding method.
- [RemRounding](https://docs.rs/trait.RemRounding.html)
- Rounding variants of the remainder operation.
- [RemRounding](https://docs.rs/trait.RemRoundingAssign.html)- Assign
- Compound assignment and rounding variants of the remainder operation.
- [RemRounding](https://docs.rs/trait.RemRoundingFrom.html)- From
- Compound assignment to the rhs operand and rounding variants of the remainder operation.
- [ShlFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.ShlFrom.html)
- Compound left shift and assignment to the rhs operand.
- [ShrFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.ShrFrom.html)
- Compound right shift and assignment to the rhs operand.
- [SubAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.SubAssignRound.html)- Round
- Compound subtraction and assignment with a specified rounding method.
- [SubFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.SubFrom.html)
- Compound subtraction and assignment to the rhs operand.
- [SubFrom](https://docs.rs/trait.SubFromRound.html)- Round
- Compound subtraction and assignment to the rhs operand with a specified rounding method.

# rug 1.30.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rug/latest/source/README.md

```
Rug provides integers and floating-point numbers with arbitrary precision and
correct rounding:
  *   *  *  *
Rug is a high-level interface to the following [GNU] libraries:
  *   *  *
Rug is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms
of the GNU Lesser General Public License as published by the Free Software
Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later
version. See the full text of the [GNU LGPL] and [GNU GPL] for details.
  *      *     *     *     *  *     *
  *   *  *     *     *     *
Details on other releases can be found in [*RELEASES.md*].
```rust
use rug::{Assign, Integer};
let mut int = Integer::new();
assert_eq!(int, 0);
int.assign(14);
assert_eq!(int, 14);
let decimal = "98_765_432_109_876_543_210";
int.assign(Integer::parse(decimal).unwrap());
assert!(int > 100_000_000);
let hex_160 = "ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000ffff0000";
int.assign(Integer::parse_radix(hex_160, 16).unwrap());
assert_eq!(int.significant_bits(), 160);
int = (int >> 128) - 1;
assert_eq!(int, 0xfffe_ffff_u32);
```
  *   *  *  *  *
With Rust primitive types, arithmetic operators usually operate on two values of
the same type, for example `12i32 + 5i32`. Unlike primitive types, conversion to
and from Rug types can be expensive, so the arithmetic operators are overloaded
to work on many combinations of Rug types and primitives. More details are
available in the [documentation][primitive types].
Operators are overloaded to work on Rug types alone or on a combination of Rug
types and Rust primitives. When at least one operand is an owned value of a Rug
type, the operation will consume that value and return a value of the Rug type.
For example
```rust
use rug::Integer;
let a = Integer::from(10);
let b = 5 - a;
assert_eq!(b, 5 - 10);
```
Here `a` is consumed by the subtraction, and `b` is an owned [`Integer`].
If on the other hand there are no owned Rug types and there are references
instead, the returned value is not the final value, but an
incomplete-computation value. For example
```rust
use rug::Integer;
let (a, b) = (Integer::from(10), Integer::from(20));
let incomplete = &a - &b;
// This would fail to compile: assert_eq!(incomplete, -10);
let sub = Integer::from(incomplete);
assert_eq!(sub, -10);
```
Here `a` and `b` are not consumed, and `incomplete` is not the final value. It
still needs to be converted or assigned into an [`Integer`]. This is covered in
more detail in the documentation’s [*Incomplete-computation values*] section.
More details on operators are available in the [documentation][operators].
Rug is available on [crates.io][rug crate]. To use Rug in your crate, add it as
a dependency inside [*Cargo.toml*]:
```toml
[dependencies]
rug = "1.30"
```
Rug requires rustc version 1.85.0 or later.
Rug also depends on the [GMP], [MPFR] and [MPC] libraries through the low-level
FFI bindings in the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate][sys crate], which needs some setup to
build; the [gmp-mpfr-sys documentation][sys] has some details on usage under
[GNU/Linux][sys gnu], [macOS][sys mac] and [Windows][sys win].
The Rug crate has six optional features:
 1.  2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7.
The first six optional features are enabled by default; to use features
selectively, you can add the dependency like this to [*Cargo.toml*]:
```toml
[dependencies.rug]
version = "1.30"
default-features = false
features = ["integer", "float", "std"]
```
Here only the `integer`, `float` and `rand` features are enabled. If none of the
features are selected, the [gmp-mpfr-sys crate][sys crate] is not required and
thus not enabled. In that case, only the [`Assign`] trait and the traits that
are in the [`ops`] module are provided by the crate.
It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features
are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor
version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be
updated to an incompatible newer version.
 1.  2. 3. 4.
```

  *   *      *      *      *  *  *  *  *  *  *  *
Compatibility note
The implementations of [`PartialOrd`] and [`PartialEq`] between
[`Rational`][rat-1-22] numbers and tuples of two primitive integers were
breaking the transitivity property of the two traits in question. Since the
implementations necessarily break the trait guarantees, having the traits
implemented is considered a bug (see [issue 58] for more details). These buggy
implementations were removed. To fix code that used these comparisons without
adding extra allocations, [`SmallRational`][smr-1-22] can be used. For example
`rational == (1, 3)` can be replaced with
`rational == SmallRational::from((1, 3))`.

# az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/az/1.3.0/target-redirect/az/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#numeric-casts)Numeric casts

This crate provides casts and checked casts.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-examples)Quick examples

```
use az::{Az, OverflowingAs, WrappingAs};
use core::num::Wrapping;
// Panics on overflow with `debug_assertions`, otherwise wraps
assert_eq!(12i32.az::<u32>(), 12u32);
// Always wraps
let wrapped = 1u32.wrapping_neg();
assert_eq!((-1).wrapping_as::<u32>(), wrapped);
assert_eq!((-1).overflowing_as::<u32>(), (wrapped, true));
// Wrapping can also be obtained using `Wrapping`
assert_eq!((-1).az::<Wrapping<u32>>().0, wrapped);
```
Conversions from floating-point to integers are also supported.
Numbers are rounded towards zero, but the [ Round](https://docs.rs/struct.Round.html) wrapper can be
used to convert floating-point numbers to integers with rounding to
the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

```
use az::{Az, CheckedAs, Round, SaturatingAs};
assert_eq!(15.7.az::<i32>(), 15);
assert_eq!(Round(15.5).az::<i32>(), 16);
assert_eq!(1.5e20.saturating_as::<i32>(), i32::max_value());
assert_eq!(f32::NAN.checked_as::<i32>(), None);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-casts-for-other-types)Implementing casts for other types

To provide casts for another type, you should implement the [ Cast](https://docs.rs/trait.Cast.html) trait and
if necessary the

[,](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedCast.html)

`CheckedCast`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.StrictCast.html)

`StrictCast`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.SaturatingCast.html)

`SaturatingCast`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.WrappingCast.html)

`WrappingCast`[traits. The](https://docs.rs/trait.OverflowingCast.html)

`OverflowingCast`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.Az.html)

`Az`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedAs.html)

`CheckedAs`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.StrictAs.html)

`StrictAs`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.SaturatingAs.html)

`SaturatingAs`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.WrappingAs.html)

`WrappingAs`[traits are already implemented for all types using blanket implementations that make use of the former traits.](https://docs.rs/trait.OverflowingAs.html)

`OverflowingAs`The cast traits can also be implemented for references. This can be
useful for expensive types that are not [ Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html). For example if you
have your own integer type that does not implement

[, you could implement casts like in the following example. (The type](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html)

`Copy``I` could be
an expensive type, for example a bignum integer, but for the example
it is only a wrapped [.)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.i32.html)

`i32````
use az::{Az, Cast};
use core::borrow::Borrow;
struct I(i32);
impl Cast<i64> for &'_ I {
    fn cast(self) -> i64 { self.0.cast() }
}
let owned = I(12);
assert_eq!((&owned).az::<i64>(), 12);
// borrow can be used if chaining is required
assert_eq!(owned.borrow().az::<i64>(), 12);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-az-crate)Using the *az* crate

# Cast in az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/az/^1.3/trait.Cast.html

```
pub trait Cast<Dst> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[cast](https://docs.rs#tymethod.cast)(self) -> Dst;
}## Expand description

Used to cast values.

It is normally easier to use the [ Az](https://docs.rs/trait.Az.html) trait instead of this trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

When debug assertions are enabled, this trait’s method panics if the
value does not fit in the destination. When debug assertions are *not*
enabled (usual in release mode), the wrapped value can be returned,
but it is not considered a breaking change if in the future it panics;
if wrapping is required use [ WrappingCast](https://docs.rs/trait.WrappingCast.html) instead.

This trait’s method also panics with no debug assertions if the value does not fit and cannot be wrapped, for example when trying to cast floating-point ∞ into an integer type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use az::Cast;
let a: u32 = 5i32.cast();
assert_eq!(a, 5);
assert_eq!(Cast::<u8>::cast(17.1f32), 17);
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# CheckedCast in az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/az/^1.3/trait.CheckedCast.html

```
pub trait CheckedCast<Dst> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[checked_cast](https://docs.rs#tymethod.checked_cast)(self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Dst>;
}## Expand description

Used for checked casts.

This trait’s method returns [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if the value does not fit.

It is normally easier to use the [ CheckedAs](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckedAs.html) trait instead of this trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use az::CheckedCast;
let a: Option<u32> = 5i32.checked_cast();
assert_eq!(a, Some(5));
assert_eq!(CheckedCast::<u32>::checked_cast(-5i32), None);
assert_eq!(CheckedCast::<u8>::checked_cast(17.1f32), Some(17));
let b: Option<u8> = f32::NAN.checked_cast();
assert_eq!(b, None);
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# StrictCast in az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/az/^1.3/trait.StrictCast.html

```
pub trait StrictCast<Dst> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[strict_cast](https://docs.rs#tymethod.strict_cast)(self) -> Dst;
}## Expand description

Used to cast values, panicking if the value does not fit.

It is normally easier to use the [ StrictAs](https://docs.rs/trait.StrictAs.html) trait instead of this trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This trait’s method panics if the value does not fit in the destination, even when debug assertions are not enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use az::StrictCast;
let a: u32 = 5i32.strict_cast();
assert_eq!(a, 5);
assert_eq!(StrictCast::<u8>::strict_cast(17.1f32), 17);
```
The following panics because of overflow.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# SaturatingCast in az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/az/^1.3/trait.SaturatingCast.html

```
pub trait SaturatingCast<Dst> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[saturating_cast](https://docs.rs#tymethod.saturating_cast)(self) -> Dst;
}## Expand description

Used to cast into the destination type, saturating if the value does not fit.

It is normally easier to use the [ SaturatingAs](https://docs.rs/trait.SaturatingAs.html) trait instead of this trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This trait’s method panics if the value does not fit and saturation does not make sense, for example when trying to cast floating-point NaN into an integer type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use az::SaturatingCast;
let a: u32 = (-1).saturating_cast();
assert_eq!(a, 0);
assert_eq!(SaturatingCast::<u8>::saturating_cast(17.0 + 256.0), 255);
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# WrappingCast in az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/az/^1.3/trait.WrappingCast.html

```
pub trait WrappingCast<Dst> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[wrapping_cast](https://docs.rs#tymethod.wrapping_cast)(self) -> Dst;
}## Expand description

Wrapping cast.

It is normally easier to use the [ WrappingAs](https://docs.rs/trait.WrappingAs.html) trait instead of this trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This trait’s method panics if the value does not fit and cannot be wrapped, for example when trying to cast floating-point ∞ into an integer type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use az::WrappingCast;
let a: u32 = (-1).wrapping_cast();
assert_eq!(a, u32::max_value());
assert_eq!(WrappingCast::<u8>::wrapping_cast(17.0 + 256.0), 17);
```

# OverflowingCast in az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/az/^1.3/trait.OverflowingCast.html

```
pub trait OverflowingCast<Dst> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[overflowing_cast](https://docs.rs#tymethod.overflowing_cast)(self) -> (Dst, [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html));
}## Expand description

Used for overflowing casts.

This trait’s method returns a [tuple](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.tuple.html) of the value and a [ bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html),
indicating whether an overflow has occurred. On overflow, the wrapped
value is returned.

It is normally easier to use the [ OverflowingAs](https://docs.rs/trait.OverflowingAs.html) trait instead of this trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use az::OverflowingCast;
let a: (u8, bool) = 17i32.overflowing_cast();
assert_eq!(a, (17, false));
assert_eq!(OverflowingCast::<u32>::overflowing_cast(-1), (u32::max_value(), true));
assert_eq!(OverflowingCast::<u8>::overflowing_cast(17.0 + 256.0), (17, true));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This trait’s method panics if the value does not fit and cannot be wrapped, for example when trying to cast floating-point ∞ into an integer type.

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Az in az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/az/^1.3/trait.Az.html

## Expand description

Used to cast values.

This is a convenience trait to enable writing
`src.`. This would not work with
the [az](https://docs.rs/trait.Az.html#tymethod.az)::<Dst>()[Cast](https://docs.rs/trait.Cast.html)::[cast](https://docs.rs/trait.Cast.html#tymethod.cast)[ Cast](https://docs.rs/trait.Cast.html) trait is generic while its

[method is not generic.](https://docs.rs/trait.Cast.html#tymethod.cast)

`cast`This trait’s method is suitable for chaining.

If there is an implementation of
[Cast](https://docs.rs/trait.Cast.html)<Dst>`&Src` but not for `Src`,
and the variable `src` is of type `Src`, then
`src.` would not work and
[az](https://docs.rs/trait.Az.html#tymethod.az)::<Dst>()`(&src).` is not easy to use with
chaining, but
[az](https://docs.rs/trait.Az.html#tymethod.az)::<Dst>()`src.` works.[borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html#tymethod.borrow)().[az](https://docs.rs/trait.Az.html#tymethod.az)::<Dst>()

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

When debug assertions are enabled, this trait’s method panics if the
value does not fit in the destination. When debug assertions are *not*
enabled (usual in release mode), the wrapped value can be returned,
but it is not considered a breaking change if in the future it panics;
if wrapping is required use [ WrappingAs](https://docs.rs/trait.WrappingAs.html) instead.

This trait’s method also panics with no debug assertions if the value does not fit and cannot be wrapped, for example when trying to cast floating-point ∞ into an integer type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use az::Az;
assert_eq!(5i32.az::<u32>(), 5);
assert_eq!(17.1f32.az::<u8>(), 17);
```
The following example shows how this trait can be used when [ Cast](https://docs.rs/trait.Cast.html)
is implemented for a reference type.

```
use az::{Az, Cast};
use core::borrow::Borrow;
struct I(i32);
impl Cast<i64> for &'_ I {
    fn cast(self) -> i64 { self.0.cast() }
}
let r = &I(-5);
assert_eq!(r.az::<i64>(), -5);
let owned = I(12);
assert_eq!(owned.borrow().az::<i64>(), 12);
```

This would not work with the
[unwrapped_as](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedAs.html#tymethod.unwrapped_as)::<Dst>()[UnwrappedCast](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedCast.html)::[unwrapped_cast](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedCast.html#tymethod.unwrapped_cast)[ UnwrappedCast](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedCast.html) trait is generic while its

[method is not generic.](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedCast.html#tymethod.unwrapped_cast)

`UnwrappedCast::unwrapped_cast`This trait’s method is suitable for chaining.

If there is an implementation of
[UnwrappedCast](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedCast.html)<Dst>`&Src`
but not for `Src`, and the variable `src` is of type `Src`, then
`src.`
would not work and
[unwrapped_as](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedAs.html#tymethod.unwrapped_as)::<Dst>()`(&src).`
is not easy to use with chaining, but
[unwrapped_as](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedAs.html#tymethod.unwrapped_as)::<Dst>()`src.`
works.[borrow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html#tymethod.borrow)().[unwrapped_as](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedAs.html#tymethod.unwrapped_as)::<Dst>()

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This trait’s method panics if the value does not fit in the destination, even when debug assertions are not enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#planned-deprecation)Planned deprecation

This trait will be deprecated in version 1.4.0. Use [ StrictAs](https://docs.rs/trait.StrictAs.html) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use az::UnwrappedAs;
assert_eq!(5i32.unwrapped_as::<u32>(), 5);
assert_eq!(17.1f32.unwrapped_as::<u8>(), 17);
```
The following panics because of overflow.

The following example shows how this trait can be used when
[ UnwrappedCast](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedCast.html) is implemented for a reference type.

```
use az::{UnwrappedAs, UnwrappedCast};
use core::borrow::Borrow;
struct I(i32);
impl UnwrappedCast<i64> for &'_ I {
    fn unwrapped_cast(self) -> i64 { self.0.unwrapped_cast() }
}
let r = &I(-5);
assert_eq!(r.unwrapped_as::<i64>(), -5);
let owned = I(12);
assert_eq!(owned.borrow().unwrapped_as::<i64>(), 12);
```

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# UnwrappedCast in az - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/az/^1.3/trait.UnwrappedCast.html

```
pub trait UnwrappedCast<Dst> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[unwrapped_cast](https://docs.rs#tymethod.unwrapped_cast)(self) -> Dst;
}## Expand description

Used to cast values, panicking if the value does not fit.

It is normally easier to use the [ UnwrappedAs](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrappedAs.html) trait instead of this trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This trait’s method panics if the value does not fit in the destination, even when debug assertions are not enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#planned-deprecation)Planned deprecation

This trait will be deprecated in version 1.4.0. Use [ StrictCast](https://docs.rs/trait.StrictCast.html) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use az::UnwrappedCast;
let a: u32 = 5i32.unwrapped_cast();
assert_eq!(a, 5);
assert_eq!(UnwrappedCast::<u8>::unwrapped_cast(17.1f32), 17);
```
The following panics because of overflow.
